they agree on a + shared local resource. +- Sidecars are the first named single-node pattern in the course. + +## Before Starting + +- Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Chapter 3, Sidecar Pattern. +- References: + - Node.js `fs` module + - `setInterval` + - Compose volumes + - `docker compose restart` + +## Notes Example + +Starting problem: + +- One `app.js` both serves HTTP and syncs content. +- That gives one file/process two unrelated reasons to change: + - request serving logic + - content refresh logic + +Split version: + +- `app.js`: reads `./content/index.html` and serves it on port 3000. +- `sync.js`: writes `./content/index.html` on an interval. +- They cooperate only through the shared `./content` directory. + +Key observation: + +- The timestamp updates without `app.js` calling `sync.js`. +- Sync behavior can change without modifying serving behavior. + +## Exercise + +Modify only `sync.js`: + +- Change sync interval from 10 seconds to 3 seconds. +- Add a counter that increments on every sync. +- Page should show timestamp and sync count. + +Success condition: + +- Reloading `http://localhost:3000` shows count climbing every ~3 seconds. +- `app.js` is untouched. + +## Real World / Compose Version + +Use two containers and one named volume: + +- `app` service: + - runs `node app.js` + - exposes `3000:3000` + - mounts `content:/usr/src/app/content` +- `sync` service: + - runs `node sync.js` + - mounts the same `content` volume +- top-level named volume: `content:` + +Dockerfile: + +```Dockerfile +FROM node:24 +WORKDIR /usr/src/app +COPY . . +RUN mkdir -p content +``` + +Compose proves the pattern: + +- `docker compose up` +- Open `http://localhost:3000` +- `docker compose restart sync` pauses/restarts sync only; `app` keeps serving. + +## Home Exercise + +Add a second sidecar: + +- `monitor.js` polls `index.html` every 2 seconds. +- It logs when content changes. +- Add `monitor` service to Compose. +- It uses the same image, runs `node monitor.js`, and mounts the same `content` + volume. + +Success: + +- `docker compose logs monitor` shows a line whenever `sync` updates the file. +- No changes to `app.js` or `sync.js` are needed. + +## What To Look Closer At + +- Sidecar is about adding capability without editing the primary service. +- The shared resource here is a volume, not memory and not direct HTTP calls. +- Each container has a narrow job and can be restarted independently. +- Multiple sidecars can attach to one primary. +- This pattern is useful for sync, logging, monitoring, proxy helpers, and other + auxiliary behavior. + +## Looking Ahead + +Unit 7 introduces the ambassador pattern: a helper container in front of +outgoing calls, used for proxying, sharding, or experimentation without the +primary service knowing. + *** Add File: course-docs/pages/unit-6-sidecar-pattern/source.md +# Unit 6: The Sidecar Pattern: Extending Services Without Changing Them + +Source: COMPSCI 426 Canvas page pasted by the user. + +## Introduction + +Chapter 3 of the textbook introduces the sidecar as the first named single-node pattern. Chapter 1 explains why patterns matter: they give practitioners a shared vocabulary for describing arrangements that would otherwise have to be described from scratch every time. The sidecar solves a problem that appears as soon as a service acquires a second job: a process that serves HTTP and also syncs content has two reasons to change, two teams that might need to edit it, and two separate failure modes to worry about at once. The pattern's answer is a second container, attached to the first, that handles the second job without either container needing to know much about the other. + +Unit 5 introduced Docker Compose as the tool for declaring and running multi-container systems. This unit uses that foundation to implement the sidecar: two containers sharing a named volume, where one serves and one syncs, and neither calls the other directly. It is the first unit where the unit of execution is a whole container rather than a function call, and the first where the coordination mechanism is a shared volume rather than a shared variable. + +## Before You Start + +Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 3 (Sidecar Pattern) + +## References + +Node.js fs module — https://nodejs.org/api/fs.htmlLinks to an external site. +setInterval — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/setIntervalLinks to an external site. +Compose volumes — https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/volumes/Links to an external site. +docker compose restart — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/restart/Links to an external site. + +## Notes + +### The starting problem + +Here's a tiny Node.js server that serves a content directory. To keep that content fresh, it also syncs new content into that directory on a timer, right inside the same file. + +```js +// app.js +import http from 'node:http'; +import fs from 'node:fs'; +import path from 'node:path'; + +const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; + +const syncContent = () => { + // stands in for pulling the latest content: a git repo, a CMS, an S3 bucket + fs.writeFileSync( + path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'), + `

Updated at ${new Date().toISOString()}

`, + ); +}; + +fs.mkdirSync(CONTENT_DIR, { recursive: true }); +syncContent(); +setInterval(syncContent, 10000); + +http.createServer((req, res) => { + const html = fs.readFileSync(path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html')); + res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' }); + res.end(html); +}).listen(3000, () => console.log('Serving on port 3000')); +``` + +This works fine. But notice that app.js now has two jobs that have nothing to do with each other: serving HTTP requests, and knowing how content gets refreshed. If you wanted to change where content comes from, how often it refreshes, or swap in a completely different sync mechanism, you'd have to edit and redeploy the exact same file that handles requests — even though the request-handling logic never changed. + +### Extending the example + +Split the two jobs into two separate processes that agree on nothing except a shared directory. One serves. One syncs. Neither calls the other directly. + +```js +// app.js — serves only +import http from 'node:http'; +import fs from 'node:fs'; +import path from 'node:path'; + +const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; + +http.createServer((req, res) => { + const html = fs.readFileSync(path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html')); + res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' }); + res.end(html); +}).listen(3000, () => console.log('Serving on port 3000')); +``` + +```js +// sync.js — syncs only +import fs from 'node:fs'; +import path from 'node:path'; + +const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; + +const syncContent = () => { + fs.writeFileSync( + path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'), + `

Updated at ${new Date().toISOString()}

`, + ); + console.log('Content synced'); +}; + +fs.mkdirSync(CONTENT_DIR, { recursive: true }); +syncContent(); +setInterval(syncContent, 10000); +``` + +Create a package.json so Node.js treats these as ES modules: + +```json +{ + "type": "module" +} +``` + +Open two terminals. In the first, run node app.js. In the second, run node sync.js. Open http://localhost:3000 and reload every few seconds. The timestamp keeps updating, exactly like before, but app.js and sync.js never call each other. They cooperate purely by reading and writing the same directory. + +### Naming the pattern + +What you just built is the sidecar pattern: a second process attached to a primary process, sharing a local resource with it so it can add a capability the primary needs without modifying the primary's code. The primary (app.js) has no dependency on the sidecar's implementation. You could replace sync.js with something that pulls from a git repo, fetches from S3, or syncs on a completely different schedule, and app.js would never need to change. + +The sidecar runs as its own independent process, but is deployed and managed together with its primary as one unit. That independence is what makes the pattern work cleanly: app.js only reads the shared file, sync.js only writes it, so there is no shared mutable state being raced over the way there was in Unit 1. The coordination happens through a resource built for exactly this — a shared file — rather than through memory two processes are racing to update. + +## Exercise + +Task: Change the sync interval in sync.js from 10 seconds to 3 seconds, and add a counter that increments on every sync so the page shows both a timestamp and a sync count. + +Starting point: The two-file version from the Notes above (the app.js + sync.js split). + +You'll know it works when: refreshing http://localhost:3000 shows the sync count climbing roughly every 3 seconds, and you were able to make this entire change inside sync.js without touching app.js at all. + +## Real World + +The Notes version runs both processes on your local machine sharing a directory. In production, the primary service and its sidecar run as separate containers — but the coordination mechanism is exactly the same: a shared volume that both containers can read and write. + +Docker Compose lets you define the two containers and their shared volume in a single file. Create Dockerfile: + +```Dockerfile +FROM node:24 +WORKDIR /usr/src/app +COPY . . +RUN mkdir -p content +``` + +Create docker-compose.yml: + +```yaml +services: + app: + build: . + command: node app.js + ports: + - "3000:3000" + volumes: + - content:/usr/src/app/content + + sync: + build: . + command: node sync.js + volumes: + - content:/usr/src/app/content + +volumes: + content: +``` + +Run docker compose up. Open http://localhost:3000 and reload every few seconds. Chapter 1 explains why patterns matter: they give practitioners a shared vocabulary for describing arrangements that would otherwise have to be described from scratch every time. The sidecar solves a problem that appears as soon as a service acquires a second job: a process that serves HTTP and also syncs content has two reasons to change, two teams that might need to edit it, and two separate failure modes to worry about at once. The pattern's answer is a second container, attached to the first, that handles the second job without either container needing to know much about the other. Unit 5 introduced Docker Compose as the tool for declaring and running multi-container systems. This unit uses that foundation to implement the sidecar: two containers sharing a named volume, where one serves and one syncs, and neither calls the other directly. It is the first unit where the unit of execution is a whole container rather than a function call, and the first where the coordination mechanism is a shared volume rather than a shared variable. ## Before You Start Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 3 (Sidecar Pattern) ## References Node.js fs module — https://nodejs.org/api/fs.htmlLinks to an external site. setInterval — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/setIntervalLinks to an external site. Compose volumes — https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/volumes/Links to an external site. docker compose restart — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/restart/Links to an external site. ## Notes ### The starting problem Here's a tiny Node.js server that serves a content directory. To keep that content fresh, it also syncs new content into that directory on a timer, right inside the same file. ```js // app.js import http from 'node:http'; import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; const syncContent = () => { // stands in for pulling the latest content: a git repo, a CMS, an S3 bucket fs.writeFileSync( path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'), `

Updated at ${new Date().toISOString()}

`, ); }; fs.mkdirSync(CONTENT_DIR, { recursive: true }); syncContent(); setInterval(syncContent, 10000); http.createServer((req, res) => { const html = fs.readFileSync(path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html')); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' }); res.end(html); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Serving on port 3000')); ``` This works fine. But notice that app.js now has two jobs that have nothing to do with each other: serving HTTP requests, and knowing how content gets refreshed. If you wanted to change where content comes from, how often it refreshes, or swap in a completely different sync mechanism, you'd have to edit and redeploy the exact same file that handles requests — even though the request-handling logic never changed. ### Extending the example Split the two jobs into two separate processes that agree on nothing except a shared directory. One serves. One syncs. Neither calls the other directly. ```js // app.js — serves only import http from 'node:http'; import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; http.createServer((req, res) => { const html = fs.readFileSync(path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html')); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' }); res.end(html); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Serving on port 3000')); ``` ```js // sync.js — syncs only import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; const syncContent = () => { fs.writeFileSync( path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'), `

Updated at ${new Date().toISOString()}

`, ); console.log('Content synced'); }; fs.mkdirSync(CONTENT_DIR, { recursive: true }); syncContent(); setInterval(syncContent, 10000); ``` Create a package.json so Node.js treats these as ES modules: ```json { "type": "module" } ``` Open two terminals. In the first, run node app.js. In the second, run node sync.js. Open http://localhost:3000 and reload every few seconds. The timestamp keeps updating, exactly like before, but app.js and sync.js never call each other. They cooperate purely by reading and writing the same directory. ### Naming the pattern What you just built is the sidecar pattern: a second process attached to a primary process, sharing a local resource with it so it can add a capability the primary needs without modifying the primary's code. The primary (app.js) has no dependency on the sidecar's implementation. You could replace sync.js with something that pulls from a git repo, fetches from S3, or syncs on a completely different schedule, and app.js would never need to change. The sidecar runs as its own independent process, but is deployed and managed together with its primary as one unit. That independence is what makes the pattern work cleanly: app.js only reads the shared file, sync.js only writes it, so there is no shared mutable state being raced over the way there was in Unit 1. The coordination happens through a resource built for exactly this — a shared file — rather than through memory two processes are racing to update. ## Exercise Task: Change the sync interval in sync.js from 10 seconds to 3 seconds, and add a counter that increments on every sync so the page shows both a timestamp and a sync count. Starting point: The two-file version from the Notes above (the app.js + sync.js split). You'll know it works when: refreshing http://localhost:3000 shows the sync count climbing roughly every 3 seconds, and you were able to make this entire change inside sync.js without touching app.js at all. ## Real World The Notes version runs both processes on your local machine sharing a directory. In production, the primary service and its sidecar run as separate containers — but the coordination mechanism is exactly the same: a shared volume that both containers can read and write. Docker Compose lets you define the two containers and their shared volume in a single file. Create Dockerfile: ```Dockerfile FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY . . RUN mkdir -p content ``` Create docker-compose.yml: ```yaml services: app: build: . command: node app.js ports: - "3000:3000" volumes: - content:/usr/src/app/content sync: build: . command: node sync.js volumes: - content:/usr/src/app/content volumes: content: ``` Run docker compose up. Open http://localhost:3000 and reload every few seconds. The timestamp keeps updating. app and sync are now isolated containers — different process namespaces, different filesystems — but they cooperate through the content named volume exactly the way the two local processes cooperated through ./content/. To verify the independence: run docker compose restart sync while the page is open. The app container keeps serving without interruption; only the sync pauses and resumes. ## Home Exercise The sidecar pattern composes: you can attach more than one sidecar to a primary container. Add a second sidecar, monitor.js, that polls index.html every 2 seconds and logs a message whenever the file changes: ```js // monitor.js import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; const FILE = path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'); let lastContent = ''; setInterval(() => { try { const current = fs.readFileSync(FILE, 'utf8'); if (current !== lastContent) { console.log(`[monitor] content changed at ${new Date().toISOString()}`); lastContent = current; } } catch { // file not yet written } }, 2000); ``` Add a monitor service to docker-compose.yml that uses the same image, runs node monitor.js, and mounts the same content volume. You'll know it's working when docker compose logs monitor shows a line every time sync updates the file — and you added this capability without touching app.js or sync.js at all. ## Looking Ahead Unit 7 keeps the same two-container shape but flips the direction. Instead of a sidecar helping the primary container do its job better, an ambassador sits in front of outgoing calls and reshapes them — which is how you add proxying, sharding, or experimentation without the primary container knowing any of it is happening. Description The web has become a large and complex area for application development. Access to an abundance of open source languages, libraries, and frameworks has led to the quick and easy construction of a variety of applications with several moving parts working in coordination to present to the user the illusion of a single program. In reality, web applications are extremely difficult to get right. They involve a large collection of coordinated services, multiple databases, complicated user interfaces, security and performance issues, and ever changing third party services, spread across physical and virtual machines. These complications are further stressed by the large number of concurrent users that access these applications every second. This course investigates several well known web-based applications and the technology and software architecture used to scale them. We will also study specific topics related to scalability in software design in the context of web application architecture. This course is hands-on and heavily project-based; students will build, monitor, and load test a distributed system composed of coordinated services. This course counts as an Elective for the CS and INFORM Majors. This course is concept-first and experiential. You will build and break real scalable systems before we put names to the patterns you discover. The vocabulary of the field, sidecars, ambassadors, sharding, scatter/gather, comes after you have already felt why each pattern exists. Staff Instructor: Tim Richards Email: tdr@umass.edu Office Hours: By appointment, via Google Meet Teaching Assistant: Miles (Mingzhe) Li Email: mingzhel@umass.edu Learning Objectives By the end of this course, students will be able to: Configure and use a devcontainer-based development environment with Docker and VS Code for a reproducible, team-consistent workspace. Explain the core properties of distributed systems, including latency, reliability, idempotency, and delivery semantics, and reason about the trade-offs between them. Containerize an application with Docker and orchestrate multiple coordinated services with Docker Compose. Apply single-node patterns, including the sidecar, ambassador, and adapter patterns, to extend services without modifying them. Design and reason about serving patterns, including replication, caching, sharding with consistent hashing, and scatter/gather. Measure system behavior under load using k6, and interpret latency percentiles, throughput, and error rates. Build event-driven and queue-based systems, including work queues, pub/sub pipelines, and dead letter queues. Reason about distributed coordination, including locks, leases, ownership election, and concurrent data manipulation. Instrument a system for observability using structured logging, metrics, and tracing. Diagnose common distributed failure patterns, including thundering herd, versioning errors, and cascading failure. Use Git and GitHub for version control, branching, and pull request workflows on a shared team repository. Plan, build, and present a complete, scalable web system simulation as a team. Time Commitment A three credit course does not get smaller when you compress it into six weeks; it gets denser. Plan for roughly twenty-two to twenty-three hours a week. UMass Amherst defines course workload by a standard credit hour rule. The guiding rule is forty five hours of work per semester for each unit of credit, on the assumption that each credit hour generates two hours of assigned work for every hour of in class contact. By that rule a three credit course represents about one hundred thirty five hours of total work, and the University expects the total workload for a three credit course to be at least 135 hours. That total is fixed. It is the same whether the course runs across a full semester or across a summer. What changes is how those hours are distributed. In a normal fifteen week semester, one hundred thirty five hours works out to about nine hours per week. This section is taught asynchronously over six weeks, so the same one hundred thirty five hours are compressed into roughly six weeks of effort, which comes to about twenty-two to twenty-three hours per week. There is no reduction in scope to go with the shorter calendar; you are doing a full three credit course in forty percent of the usual time, so the weekly pace is about two and a half times what the same course would demand in the fall or spring. Twenty-two hours a week is a serious commitment, and you should plan your summer around that reality. Spread across six working days it is just under four hours a day. Because each day's material builds directly on the day before, and because this is a systems course where one misconfigured service can block everything downstream, the work does not compress well into a weekend burst. Students who treat this as a part time effort fall behind quickly, and in a six week term there is very little room to recover. For that reason I strongly advise against pairing this course with another demanding summer course or with full time employment. If your situation makes twenty-two hours a week difficult, email me at tdr@umass.edu before the term begins so we can be honest about whether the timing works for you. To make the number concrete, your weekly hours go toward the same components described elsewhere in this syllabus: working through several Knowledge Units, since the eighteen KUs are spread across the six weeks, including their preparatory reading, the activity, and the exercises; and steadily advancing your team's sprint project, which on its own accounts for a substantial share of your time over the term. The weekly quizzes are the clearest early signal of whether you are keeping pace. If you find yourself consistently spending far more than this, or far less and still finishing everything, let me know, because that is useful feedback on the course and may also be a sign we should look at how you are approaching the work. Sprints A simulated scalable system built incrementally: each sprint applies only what the previous week taught. The Sprints are the team project itself, carried forward in stages rather than assembled at the end. Each sprint is due during the week after the Knowledge Units that inform it are covered, so the system grows in lockstep with the course material. You cannot design the full architecture at the start; you do not yet know the patterns. Instead the simulation is extended one layer at a time: Sprint 0 forms the team and stakes out a domain idea; Sprint 1 frames the scalability problem using the distributed systems vocabulary from Week 1; Sprint 2 produces the first containerized services running under Docker Compose; Sprint 3 adds serving patterns (replication, caching, load balancing) and a first k6 load test; Sprint 4 introduces async processing and resilience; and Sprint 5 instruments the system with observability, runs a final load test, and delivers the four capstone artifacts. The system you build throughout is a simulation: data is synthetic, latency is injected, failures are scripted, and computation is modeled. This is a deliberate choice, not a shortcut. Building a production system from scratch in six weeks is not realistic, and the goal of this course is not deployment; it is design, engineering, and measurement. Simulation lets you practice every pattern the course covers, instrument and break the system intentionally, and measure it under realistic load, without the operational complexity of real data pipelines or live traffic. The skills you develop, structuring services, reasoning about coordination, interpreting latency percentiles, are the same ones a team would use on a real system. Sprints introduce no new instruction. They are where you apply the current state of the Knowledge Units to the simulated system your team is building. Teams are assigned by the instructor and are 2–3 members for this six-week section. Because this course has no separate lab sequence, the professional workflow skills that labs would otherwise carry, clean commits, pull requests, code review, conflict resolution, are practiced and assessed directly inside the sprints. Because impressions are unreliable, your sprint contribution is assessed against objective GitHub evidence, your commits, the pull requests you authored and reviewed, and the merge history, rather than against anyone's sense of who did what. Sprints 0 and 1 are half-weight (each worth half a full sprint); Sprints 2, 3, and 4 are full-weight. Sprint 5 is graded as the Project Final (20%) rather than as part of the Sprints category. Sprint 0: Team Formation and Project Concept Week 0 covered setting up the development environment and GitHub. Sprint 0 is about getting organized as a team and staking out a project idea while that setup is still fresh. No architecture decisions are required yet; students do not have the vocabulary for them. Shared GitHub repository created with all team members added as collaborators README with team roster A short paragraph describing the domain the team wants to simulate and a first guess at what makes it interesting from a scalability standpoint: what would a real system in this domain need to handle that a single server could not? Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing Week 1 covered why distributed systems exist, the core trade-offs between latency and reliability, and the semantics of idempotency and message delivery. Sprint 1 asks the team to apply that vocabulary to their chosen domain. No code is expected yet; this is design thinking grounded in the concepts just studied. A refined project description: what domain, what scalability problem, and why this problem is meaningful (the Computing for the Common Good framing) An initial list of services the simulation might include, with one sentence on what each does; this is a first guess, not a commitment, and it will evolve as more patterns are introduced A short statement of the system's latency and reliability requirements: what does "fast enough" mean for this domain, and what happens if a component fails? Sprint 2: First Containerized System Week 2 covered Docker fundamentals, Docker Compose, the sidecar pattern, and the ambassador pattern. Sprint 2 is the first time the team writes code. The goal is a multi-service simulation running under Docker Compose with at least one pattern from Week 2 applied. At least two services containerized and running under Docker Compose, each with its own HTTP endpoint returning domain-relevant simulated data At least one sidecar or ambassador pattern applied alongside a primary service as a separate container A docker-compose.yml committed to the repository that starts the whole system with a single command Sprint 3: Serving Patterns and First Load Test Week 3 covered the adapter pattern, replicated services with load balancing and caching, sharded services, and scatter/gather. Sprint 3 extends the existing simulation with at least one serving pattern and adds the first measurement. At least one service running with multiple replicas behind Caddy as a load balancer A caching layer (Redis) integrated into at least one service path, with simulated cache hits and misses A k6 load test script that exercises the replicated service, with a written summary of the p50, p95, and p99 latency results Sprint 4: Async Processing and Resilience Week 4 covered resilience and failure modes, event-driven processing, work queue systems, and pub/sub pipelines. Sprint 4 adds an asynchronous processing path to the simulation and introduces controlled failures to show the system can handle them. At least one async processing path: a work queue or pub/sub channel backed by Redis Health check endpoints on all services, wired into Docker Compose healthcheck configuration At least one scripted failure scenario: a service that can be made to fail or slow down, with a brief written description of how the system responds Sprint 5: Observability, Final Measurement, and Delivery Week 5 covered coordinated batch processing, ownership election, and observability. Sprint 5 instruments the simulation, produces the final load test evidence, and assembles the four capstone deliverables. Prometheus metrics exposed by all custom services, scraped by a Prometheus instance defined in Docker Compose A Grafana dashboard showing at minimum: request rate, error rate, and p95 latency for the main service path Structured JSON log output from all custom services A final k6 load test with a written interpretation: what the latency distribution shows, how it compares to the Sprint 3 baseline, and where the bottleneck appears to be GitHub repository URL: code committed, README complete, system starts with a single command Recorded video demonstration (10 minutes or less): the system starting with docker compose up, at least one endpoint responding, the Grafana dashboard live during a k6 load test, and an explanation of one design decision and its trade-off Project poster: the problem, the architecture, the patterns demonstrated, and the key trade-offs, formatted as a one-page PDF Individual reflection: submitted separately by each team member covering what you contributed, what you learned, and what you would do differently Project The capstone: a simulated scalable system that demonstrates the design, engineering, and measurement skills of the course. The Project is the summative destination the entire course is aimed at, and in this section it is fully asynchronous. Working in a team, you choose a problem domain in the spirit of Computing for the Common Good and design a meaningful but achievable scalable application. You then build a simulation of that application: services that model realistic behavior using synthetic data, injected latency, and scripted failures, orchestrated with Docker Compose and measured under load with k6. The simulation is not a stripped-down version of a real system; it is the full architecture, with coordinated services, asynchronous pipelines, caching, and observability, implemented in a way that makes every pattern visible and every failure intentional. The goal is to demonstrate that you understand how such a system is designed, how its components interact, and how its behavior changes under load. You submit four deliverables: the source code in your shared GitHub repository, a recorded video walkthrough of the running system, a poster presenting the problem, the architecture, and the trade-offs you made, and an individual written reflection from each team member on their own contribution and what they learned. You are assessed on collaborative practice, on meeting the sprint deliverable deadlines that pace the project from Week 1, and on professional conduct throughout, with contribution again read from objective GitHub evidence and the grade trajectory-weighted across the term. Deployment to a public host is not required and is not taught here; the destination is a complete, multi-service simulation running under Docker Compose in the dev container and demonstrated on video. The terminal is a completely different way of talking to your computer, and it requires a different mental model. This primer explains what the terminal is, why it exists, why it matters for a course like this one, and what you need to know to use it without confusion. What the Terminal Is Your operating system — macOS, Windows, Linux — is a layer of software that manages the hardware underneath your applications. Every time you create a file, open a browser, or install a program, the operating system is doing the actual work. A graphical interface gives you buttons and menus to make requests to the operating system. The terminal does the same thing, but through text. When you open a terminal, you see a cursor waiting for input. That interface is called the command line. You type a command, press Enter, and the operating system executes it. The output, if there is any, appears as text below your command. Then the cursor reappears and waits for the next one. That is the entire interaction model. The program that reads your input and coordinates with the operating system is called a shell. On macOS and Linux, the default shell is usually bash or zsh. On Windows with WSL, you also get bash. The shell is not the terminal window itself — the terminal is the visual container, and the shell is the program running inside it. The distinction rarely matters in practice, but you will see both words used in documentation. Why the Terminal Exists and Why It Matters The terminal is not a relic from before graphical interfaces were invented. It is still the primary tool for technical work because it is fast, precise, scriptable, and universal. Most of the tools used in professional software development — version control, build systems, test runners, package managers, servers, deployment scripts — are built to be operated from the command line. They have no graphical interface at all, or their graphical interface exposes far less than the command line does. git, npm, node, docker, psql: every tool you will use in this course is a command-line program. You will install packages by typing npm install. You will run your server by typing node server.js. You will interact with a database by typing commands. None of this happens through a menu. There is a second reason the terminal matters: it is the same everywhere. A command that works on your laptop works on your classmates' laptops and on a remote server in a data center. When you deploy an application to production, there is no graphical interface available — there is only a shell. Learning to work in the terminal now means the jump to professional environments is not a surprise later. Terminology You Need to Know Before touching any commands, you need a shared vocabulary. The file system is the structure your operating system uses to organize all stored data. Everything — your documents, your code, your programs — lives somewhere in the file system. A directory is a container that holds files and other directories. You may know this concept as a "folder." In the terminal, the word "directory" is standard. Directories nest inside each other, forming a tree. The root directory is the top of that tree. On macOS and Linux it is written as /. On Windows with WSL it is also / inside the Linux environment. Everything else in the file system is inside the root directory, directly or indirectly. Your home directory is the directory assigned to your user account. On macOS it is typically /Users/yourname. On Linux it is typically /home/yourname. The ~ character is shorthand for your home directory in most shells. The working directory is the directory the terminal is currently "inside." When you open a terminal, it starts in your home directory. When you run a command, the command executes relative to the working directory unless you specify otherwise. Understanding what your working directory is at any moment is one of the most important habits in terminal use. A path is the address of a file or directory in the file system. An absolute path starts from the root and describes the full address: /home/yourname/cs326/project/server.js. A relative path starts from the current working directory: if your working directory is /home/yourname/cs326, then project/server.js is a relative path to the same file. A command is a text instruction you give to the shell. Commands are usually short programs that live somewhere on your file system. When you type a command name, the shell searches a list of known locations to find and run it. An argument is additional information passed to a command. When you type node server.js, node is the command and server.js is an argument telling it which file to run. A flag (also called an option) is a special kind of argument that modifies a command's behavior. Flags usually start with - or --. For example, ls -l runs ls with the -l flag, which changes the output format. A script is a text file containing a sequence of commands. Instead of typing ten commands manually, you put them in a script file and run the whole file at once. Scripts are how automation works in the terminal. Permissions control who is allowed to read, write, or execute a file. Every file and directory in the file system has a set of permissions attached to it. Permissions matter when you try to run a script or access a file and the operating system refuses — understanding permissions tells you why and how to fix it. Standard output (stdout) is where a command sends its normal output — the text you see printed in the terminal after a command runs. Standard error (stderr) is a separate channel for error messages. Both appear in the terminal by default, but they can be separated and redirected independently. A process is a running instance of a program. When you run node server.js, you start a process. That process runs until it finishes or you stop it. Pressing Ctrl+C in the terminal sends a signal to the current process telling it to stop. The Commands You Need First These are the commands you will use constantly. Learn what they do before you need them in an activity. pwd: Print the working directory. Outputs the absolute path of the directory the terminal is currently in. When you are disoriented, run this first. pwd ls: List files and directories. Shows the files and directories inside the working directory. Running ls -l shows a detailed view including permissions, owner, size, and modification date. ls ls -l cd: Change directory. Moves the terminal's working directory to the path you specify. cd cs326 cd .. cd ~ cd /home/yourname/cs326 cd .. moves up one level to the parent directory. cd ~ moves to your home directory. cd with no argument also moves to your home directory. mkdir: Make a directory. Creates a new directory with the name you provide. mkdir project mkdir -p project/src/routes The -p flag creates intermediate directories as needed. Without it, mkdir project/src/routes fails if project or project/src do not already exist. touch: Creates an empty file if it does not exist, or update the modification timestamp. Commonly used to create placeholder files. touch server.ts cp: Copy file or directory. Copies a file from one location to another. cp server.ts server.backup.ts cp -r src src-backup The -r flag copies recursively, which is required when copying a directory. mv: Move file or directory. Moves a file to a new location, or renames it if the destination is in the same directory. mv server.ts app.ts mv server.js src/server.js rm: Remove file or directory. Deletes a file or directory. This is permanent — there is no trash or undo. rm server.backup.ts rm -r src-backup The -r flag removes a directory and everything inside it recursively. Use it carefully. cat: Concatenate a file. Prints the contents of a file to the terminal. Used constantly for quickly reading short files. cat package.json less: Pages content from a file. Shows the contents of a file one screen at a time, letting you scroll through output that is too long to read in a single terminal view. Unlike cat, it does not dump everything at once. Use the arrow keys or j/k to scroll, space to jump a full page, and q to exit. less server.ts less package.json You will use less any time a file is long enough that cat makes it scroll past before you can read it. It is also how man displays its pages internally, the same navigation keys apply (see below). echo: Print text to standard output. Useful in scripts and for quick checks. echo "hello" echo $PATH clear: Clear the terminal screen. Your command history is not deleted; the display is just scrolled. It clears things up. man: Manual. Open the manual page for a command. On macOS and Linux, nearly every command has a manual page. Use the arrow keys or j/k to scroll, space to jump a full page, and q to exit. Press q to exit. man ls man cp Running a Script Basics A script is an executable text file. To run one, you call it like a command: node server.js Some scripts are written for the shell directly, not for a runtime like Node. Those files typically end in .sh. To run a shell script, you first need to make sure it has execute permission, then call it: chmod +x setup.sh ./setup.sh chmod +x adds execute permission to the file. The ./ prefix tells the shell to look for the file in the current directory — without it, the shell only searches its known program locations and will not find your script. The Shebang (#!) The first line of a shell script that tells the operating system which interpreter to use to run the file. When you execute a script, the operating system reads the first two characters. If they are #!, it treats the rest of that line as the path to the program that should run the script. #!/bin/bash #!/usr/bin/env bash #!/usr/bin/env node #!/usr/bin/env python3 Without a shebang, the operating system does not know what kind of script it is looking at. It may refuse to run it, or it may guess wrong. With a shebang, running ./setup.sh works exactly the same as running bash setup.sh — the shebang makes the file self-describing. The second form, #!/usr/bin/env node, is more portable than a hardcoded path like #!/usr/local/bin/node. The env program searches your PATH for the named interpreter, so the script works regardless of where Node is installed on a given machine. You will see this form in most modern scripts that target Node or Python. The shebang line is ignored as a comment by the interpreter itself, # starts a comment in bash, Python, and most scripting languages, so it causes no errors when the interpreter processes the rest of the file. Here is a simple Node script that prints a greeting to the terminal: #!/usr/bin/env node const name = process.argv[2] ?? "stranger"; console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`); Save this as greet.js, make it executable, and run it: chmod +x greet.js ./greet.js ./greet.js Alice Output: Hello, stranger! Hello, Alice! process.argv is an array Node populates with the command-line arguments passed to the script. The first two entries are always the path to Node and the path to the script itself, so index 2 is where your first real argument lives. The ?? operator supplies a default if no argument was given. Without the shebang, you would have to type node greet.js Alice every time. With it, ./greet.js Alice works -- the script knows how to run itself. Permissions in Brief When you run ls -l, each entry starts with a string like -rwxr-xr--. That string encodes the permissions on the file. The characters map to three groups: the owner, the group, and everyone else. For each group, there are three possible permissions: read (r), write (w), and execute (x). A - means that permission is not granted. You will encounter permissions issues most often when trying to run a script that the operating system refuses to execute. The fix is usually chmod +x filename, which adds execute permission for the owner. The course activities will tell you when this is necessary. What Happens When Something Goes Wrong The terminal is unforgiving in one specific way: it does what you say, not what you meant. If you mistype a filename, it will tell you the file does not exist. If you run a command in the wrong directory, the results will be wrong. If you delete something with rm, it is gone. Developing three habits will prevent most problems. First, always know your working directory. Run pwd whenever you are uncertain. Second, use ls before and after operations that create or move files. Third, read error messages carefully -- they almost always tell you exactly what went wrong. "No such file or directory" means your path is wrong. "Permission denied" means you do not have the right access level. "Command not found" means the program is not installed or not on your PATH. There is no way to learn the terminal except by using it. The commands above will get you through everything in this course. You will be slow at first and faster within a week. A Note on This Course In this course you will use the terminal constantly. Every activity, every project sprint, every interaction with git, npm, node, and the Gantry container runs through the command line. If you setup the development environment and reach the integrated terminal inside VS Code, you are already in the right place. The shell running there is the same shell described in this primer. Every command here works exactly the same inside that terminal as it would in a standalone terminal application. The course uses a constrained subset of the language to keep examples consistent and readable across all units. Read through this before starting the units and return to it when you need a reminder. Two rules apply everywhere in the course: Functions are always defined as arrow functions: const fn = () => ... Classes are never used; objects are plain literals with arrow function methods Variables Use const for values that will not be reassigned. Use let for values that will change. Avoid var. const port = 3000; const name = "Alice"; let count = 0; count = count + 1; Reassigning a const is a runtime error. For objects and arrays, const prevents reassignment of the variable itself, not mutation of its contents. const config = { port: 3000 }; config.port = 4000; // allowed — mutating the object config = {}; // TypeError — reassigning the variable MDN: constLinks to an external site. | MDN: letLinks to an external site. Data Types JavaScript has six primitive types and two compound types. Primitives: string — text: 'hello', "world", `template` number — integers and floats: 42, 3.14, NaN, Infinity boolean — true or false null — explicit absence of a value undefined — a variable declared but not yet assigned symbol — unique identifiers (rarely used in this course) Compound: object — key/value pairs array — ordered list (technically also an object) Use typeof to inspect a type at runtime: typeof "hello"; // 'string' typeof 42; // 'number' typeof true; // 'boolean' typeof null; // 'object' — a known JS quirk typeof undefined; // 'undefined' typeof {}; // 'object' typeof []; // 'object' Array.isArray([]); // true MDN: JavaScript data typesLinks to an external site. Strings String literals use single quotes, double quotes, or backticks. Backtick strings (template literals) support embedded expressions and multi-line text. const greeting = "Hello"; const name = "world"; const message = `${greeting}, ${name}!`; // 'Hello, world!' const multiline = ` Line one Line two `; Common string methods: const s = " Hello, World! "; s.length; // 17 s.trim(); // 'Hello, World!' s.toLowerCase(); // ' hello, world! ' s.toUpperCase(); // ' HELLO, WORLD! ' s.includes("World"); // true s.startsWith(" Hello"); // true s.endsWith("! "); // true s.indexOf("World"); // 9 s.slice(2, 7); // 'Hello' s.replace("World", "Alice"); // ' Hello, Alice! ' s.split(", "); // [' Hello', 'World! '] "abc".repeat(3); // 'abcabcabc' "5".padStart(3, "0"); // '005' MDN: StringLinks to an external site. | MDN: Template literalsLinks to an external site. Numbers JavaScript uses 64-bit floating-point for all numbers. Integer arithmetic behaves as expected for typical values. const a = 10; const b = 3; a + b; // 13 a - b; // 7 a * b; // 30 a / b; // 3.3333... a % b; // 1 (remainder) a ** b; // 1000 (exponentiation) The Math object provides common utilities: Math.floor(3.9); // 3 Math.ceil(3.1); // 4 Math.round(3.5); // 4 Math.abs(-5); // 5 Math.min(1, 2, 3); // 1 Math.max(1, 2, 3); // 3 Math.sqrt(16); // 4 Math.pow(2, 10); // 1024 Math.random(); // random float in [0, 1) Convert between strings and numbers: Number("42"); // 42 Number("abc"); // NaN parseInt("42px"); // 42 parseFloat("3.14"); // 3.14 String(42)( // '42' 42, ).toString(); // '42' Check for special values: Number.isNaN(NaN); // true Number.isFinite(Infinity); // false Number.isInteger(4.0); // true MDN: NumberLinks to an external site. | MDN: MathLinks to an external site. Booleans and Comparison true && false; // false (logical AND) true || false; // true (logical OR) !true; // false (logical NOT) Use === (strict equality) and !== (strict inequality). Avoid == and !=, which coerce types in surprising ways. 1 === 1; // true 1 === "1"; // false — different types 1 == "1"; // true — type coercion (avoid this) Truthy and falsy: false, 0, '', null, undefined, and NaN are falsy. Everything else is truthy. if (0) { /* never runs */ } if ("") { /* never runs */ } if (null) { /* never runs */ } if ([]) { /* runs — empty array is truthy */ } if ({}) { /* runs — empty object is truthy */ } MDN: Equality comparisonsLinks to an external site. | MDN: Logical operatorsLinks to an external site. Arrow Functions Arrow functions are the only function syntax used in this course. // no arguments const greet = () => "Hello!"; // one argument — parentheses are optional, but include them for consistency const double = (n) => n * 2; // multiple arguments const add = (a, b) => a + b; // multi-line body — braces required, return must be explicit const clamp = (value, min, max) => { if (value < min) return min; if (value > max) return max; return value; }; // implicit return of an object — wrap in parentheses to avoid ambiguity const makePoint = (x, y) => ({ x, y }); Default parameters: const connect = (host = "localhost", port = 3000) => `${host}:${port}`; connect(); // 'localhost:3000' connect("example.com", 443); // 'example.com:443' Async arrow functions: const fetchData = async (url) => { const response = await fetch(url); return response.json(); }; Arrow functions do not have their own this binding. In this course that is rarely relevant because we reference objects by name rather than via this. MDN: Arrow function expressionsLinks to an external site. | MDN: Default parametersLinks to an external site. Arrays Arrays are ordered lists. Indices start at 0. const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]; fruits[0]; // 'apple' fruits.length; // 3 fruits[fruits.length - 1]; // 'cherry' (last element) Mutating methods (modify the array in place): const a = [1, 2, 3]; a.push(4); // appends 4; returns new length (4) a.pop(); // removes and returns last element (4) a.unshift(0); // prepends 0; returns new length a.shift(); // removes and returns first element (0) a.splice(1, 1); // removes 1 element at index 1; returns removed elements a.reverse(); // reverses in place a.sort(); // sorts in place (lexicographic by default) Non-mutating methods (return a new value, original unchanged): const nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]; nums.slice(2, 5); // [4, 1, 5] — copy from index 2 up to (not including) 5 nums.concat([7, 8]); // [3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6,7,8] nums.includes(4); // true nums.indexOf(1); // 1 — first occurrence nums .join(", ") // '3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6' [(1, [2, [3]])].flat() // [1, 2, [3]] — one level deep [(1, [2, [3]])].flat(Infinity); // [1, 2, 3] — fully flattened Sorting with a comparator: const sorted = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 1, 3, 4, 5] MDN: ArrayLinks to an external site. Functional Array Methods These are the primary iteration tools in this course. Each takes an arrow function as its argument and does not modify the original array. .map() Transforms every element; returns a new array of the same length. const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]; const doubled = numbers.map((n) => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6, 8] const labels = numbers.map((n) => `item-${n}`); // ['item-1', 'item-2', ...] .filter() Keeps elements for which the callback returns true; returns a new (possibly shorter) array. const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]; const evens = numbers.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0); // [2, 4, 6] const big = numbers.filter((n) => n > 3); // [4, 5, 6] .reduce() Accumulates a single value from all elements. The second argument to reduce is the initial accumulator value. const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]; const sum = numbers.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0); // 10 const max = numbers.reduce((acc, n) => (n > acc ? n : acc), -Infinity); // 4 Building an object from an array: const words = ["cat", "dog", "cat", "bird", "dog", "dog"]; const counts = words.reduce((acc, word) => { acc[word] = (acc[word] ?? 0) + 1; return acc; }, {}); // { cat: 2, dog: 3, bird: 1 } .find() and .findIndex() Return the first matching element or its index. Return undefined / -1 if not found. const users = [ { id: 1, name: "Alice" }, { id: 2, name: "Bob" }, ]; users.find((u) => u.id === 2); // { id: 2, name: 'Bob' } users.findIndex((u) => u.id === 2); // 1 .some() and .every() Return a boolean. const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; nums.some((n) => n > 4); // true — at least one element matches nums.every((n) => n > 0); // true — all elements match nums.every((n) => n > 2); // false .forEach() Runs a callback for side effects; returns undefined. Prefer .map() when you need the results. [1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => console.log(n)); .flatMap() Maps then flattens one level. Useful when each element produces an array of results. const sentences = ["hello world", "foo bar"]; const words = sentences.flatMap((s) => s.split(" ")); // ['hello', 'world', 'foo', 'bar'] MDN: Array.prototype.mapLinks to an external site. | MDN: filterLinks to an external site. | MDN: reduceLinks to an external site. Objects Objects are key/value pairs. Keys are strings (or symbols); values can be anything. const server = { host: "localhost", port: 3000, tls: false, }; server.host; // 'localhost' — dot notation server["port"]; // 3000 — bracket notation (useful for dynamic keys) Shorthand property names: when a variable name matches the key, you can omit the value. const host = "localhost"; const port = 3000; const config = { host, port }; // same as { host: host, port: port } Computed property names: const key = "status"; const obj = { [key]: 200 }; // { status: 200 } Methods as arrow function properties: this is how functions are attached to objects in this course. const counter = { value: 0, increment: () => { counter.value++; }, reset: () => { counter.value = 0; }, get: () => counter.value, }; counter.increment(); counter.get(); // 1 Note: arrow functions do not bind this, so methods reference the object by its variable name rather than via this. Object utility methods: const obj = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }; Object.keys(obj); // ['a', 'b', 'c'] Object.values(obj); // [1, 2, 3] Object.entries(obj); // [['a', 1], ['b', 2], ['c', 3]] Object.fromEntries([ ["a", 1], ["b", 2], ]); // { a: 1, b: 2 } Object.assign({}, obj, { d: 4 }); // { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4 } Spread operator on objects (shallow copy / merge): const base = { host: "localhost", port: 3000 }; const override = { port: 8080, tls: true }; const merged = { ...base, ...override }; // { host: 'localhost', port: 8080, tls: true } MDN: ObjectLinks to an external site. | MDN: Spread syntaxLinks to an external site. Destructuring Destructuring extracts values from objects and arrays into named variables. Object destructuring: const config = { host: "localhost", port: 3000, tls: false }; const { host, port } = config; // host = 'localhost', port = 3000 // rename while destructuring const { host: serverHost } = config; // serverHost = 'localhost' // default values (used when the key is absent) const { timeout = 5000 } = config; // timeout = 5000 Array destructuring: const [first, second, ...rest] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]; // first = 10, second = 20, rest = [30, 40, 50] const [, second] = [10, 20, 30]; // skip first element In function parameters: const greet = ({ name, greeting = "Hello" }) => `${greeting}, ${name}!`; greet({ name: "Alice" }); // 'Hello, Alice!' greet({ name: "Bob", greeting: "Hi" }); // 'Hi, Bob!' MDN: Destructuring assignmentLinks to an external site. Spread and Rest Spread expands an iterable into individual elements. Rest collects remaining elements into an array. Both use .... // spread an array into function arguments const nums = [1, 2, 3]; Math.max(...nums); // 3 // copy and extend an array const a = [1, 2]; const b = [...a, 3, 4]; // [1, 2, 3, 4] // rest parameters — collect extra arguments const sum = (first, ...others) => others.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, first); sum(1, 2, 3, 4); // 10 MDN: Rest parametersLinks to an external site. | MDN: Spread syntaxLinks to an external site. Control Flow if / else: const classify = (n) => { if (n > 0) return "positive"; else if (n < 0) return "negative"; else return "zero"; }; Ternary operator — for simple conditional expressions: const label = (n) => (n >= 0 ? "non-negative" : "negative"); switch: const describe = (status) => { switch (status) { case 200: return "OK"; case 404: return "Not Found"; case 500: return "Server Error"; default: return "Unknown"; } }; Short-circuit evaluation: const name = user.name || "Anonymous"; // use 'Anonymous' if name is falsy const port = options.port ?? 3000; // use 3000 only if port is null/undefined user.isAdmin && performAdminTask(); // call only if isAdmin is truthy MDN: if...elseLinks to an external site. | MDN: Conditional (ternary) operatorLinks to an external site. | MDN: switchLinks to an external site. Iteration .map(), .filter(), .reduce() handle synchronous iteration over arrays. See the Functional Array Methods section above. for...of iterates over any iterable (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets). Use it when you need sequential await inside the loop body. const urls = ["https://api.example.com/a", "https://api.example.com/b"]; for (const url of urls) { const data = await fetch(url); // awaited one at a time, in order console.log(data); } Iterating object entries: const scores = { Alice: 95, Bob: 87, Carol: 92 }; for (const [name, score] of Object.entries(scores)) { console.log(`${name}: ${score}`); } MDN: for...ofLinks to an external site. Promises A Promise represents a value that will be available in the future. Most async APIs in Node.js return promises. You will mostly use async/await rather than .then() chains, but several Promise utility functions are useful. // run multiple promises in parallel; fail fast if any one fails const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([fetchUser(id), fetchPosts(id)]); // run multiple promises in parallel; collect all outcomes regardless of failure const results = await Promise.allSettled([fetchA(), fetchB()]); results.forEach((r) => { if (r.status === "fulfilled") console.log(r.value); else console.error(r.reason); }); // return the result of whichever promise settles first const fastest = await Promise.race([slowFetch(), fastFetch()]); Creating a promise manually (useful for wrapping callback-based APIs or for delays): const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); await delay(1000); // pause for 1 second MDN: PromiseLinks to an external site. | MDN: Promise.allLinks to an external site. | MDN: Promise.allSettledLinks to an external site. Async/Await async and await let you write asynchronous code that reads like synchronous code. An async arrow function always returns a Promise. const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); const run = async () => { console.log("start"); await delay(1000); console.log("one second later"); await delay(500); console.log("done"); }; run(); Parallel execution with Promise.all: const fetchUserAndPosts = async (userId) => { const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([ fetchUser(userId), fetchPosts(userId), ]); return { user, posts }; }; Both fetches start at the same time instead of waiting for each other in sequence. MDN: async function expressionLinks to an external site. | MDN: awaitLinks to an external site. Error Handling try / catch: const parseJSON = (text) => { try { return JSON.parse(text); } catch (err) { console.error("Invalid JSON:", err.message); return null; } }; try / catch with async/await: const loadData = async (url) => { try { const response = await fetch(url); if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`); return await response.json(); } catch (err) { console.error("Failed to load:", err.message); return null; } }; Throwing errors: const divide = (a, b) => { if (b === 0) throw new Error("Cannot divide by zero"); return a / b; }; finally — runs whether or not an error was thrown: const withCleanup = async () => { const resource = await acquire(); try { return await use(resource); } finally { await release(resource); } }; MDN: try...catchLinks to an external site. | MDN: ErrorLinks to an external site. ES6 Modules The course uses ES6 modules throughout. Files use .js extensions and package.json must set "type": "module". Named exports: // math.js export const add = (a, b) => a + b; export const multiply = (a, b) => a * b; Named imports: import { add, multiply } from "./math.js"; add(2, 3); // 5 multiply(2, 3); // 6 Default export: // logger.js const logger = { info: (msg) => console.log(`[INFO] ${msg}`), error: (msg) => console.error(`[ERROR] ${msg}`), }; export default logger; Default import: import logger from "./logger.js"; logger.info("Server started"); Re-export: export { add } from "./math.js"; Note: if you see require() in an example outside this course, it uses CommonJS, which predates ES6 modules. Node.js supports both, but this course uses import/export exclusively. MDN: exportLinks to an external site. | MDN: importLinks to an external site. Useful Operators Optional chaining (?.) — access a property only if the preceding value is not null/undefined: const user = { profile: { name: "Alice" } }; user.profile?.name; // 'Alice' user.address?.city; // undefined — no error even though address is absent user.greet?.(); // undefined — safe method call Nullish coalescing (??) — return the right side only when the left is null or undefined. Unlike ||, it does not trigger on 0 or ''. const port = process.env.PORT ?? 3000; // 3000 if PORT is not set 0 || "default"; // 'default' — 0 is falsy 0 ?? "default"; // 0 — 0 is not null/undefined Logical assignment: let a = null; a ??= "fallback"; // assigns only if null or undefined let b = 0; b ||= 42; // assigns if falsy let c = 5; c &&= c * 2; // assigns if truthy MDN: Optional chainingLinks to an external site. | MDN: Nullish coalescingLinks to an external site. JSON JSON is the standard data format for APIs and configuration files. const obj = { name: "Alice", scores: [95, 87, 92] }; const json = JSON.stringify(obj); // '{"name":"Alice","scores":[95,87,92]}' const pretty = JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2); // { // "name": "Alice", // "scores": [ // 95, // 87, // 92 // ] // } const parsed = JSON.parse(json); // { name: 'Alice', scores: [95, 87, 92] } JSON.stringify and JSON.parse throw on invalid input, so wrap them in try/catch when handling untrusted data. MDN: JSONLinks to an external site. Maps and Sets Map stores key/value pairs where keys can be any type, not just strings. It preserves insertion order and is more predictable than using a plain object as a dictionary. const cache = new Map(); cache.set("user:1", { name: "Alice" }); cache.get("user:1"); // { name: 'Alice' } cache.has("user:1"); // true cache.size; // 1 cache.delete("user:1"); for (const [key, value] of cache) { console.log(key, value); } Set stores unique values; duplicates are silently ignored. const ids = new Set([1, 2, 3, 2, 1]); ids.size; // 3 — duplicates removed ids.has(2); // true ids.add(4); ids.delete(1); // convert to array const unique = [...new Set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3])]; // [1, 2, 3] MDN: MapLinks to an external site. | MDN: SetLinks to an external site. The system is a simulation: its data is synthetic, its latency is injected, its failures are scripted, and its computation is modeled. This is a deliberate design choice, not a shortcut. A production system built from scratch in six weeks is not realistic, and that is not the goal. The goal is design, engineering, and measurement. Simulation lets your team practice every pattern covered in the course, break the system intentionally, and measure it under realistic load, without the operational complexity of real data pipelines or live traffic. Every pattern you study in the units is first presented as a simulation. By the time you reach the project, you will know exactly how to model latency, inject failures, and observe behavior, because the units showed you how. The project is where those techniques are applied to a coherent system of your team's own design. Computing for the Common Good Your project domain must serve a real community or address a genuine societal need. This is not a theme layer on top of the technical work; it shapes what services exist, what the latency and reliability requirements mean, and who is affected when the system fails. A system that routes community food pantry inventory across multiple locations has different failure consequences than one that serves movie recommendations, and reasoning about those consequences is part of the design work. Domains that fit this framing include, for example: a public health outbreak alert and notification service; a community library catalog with digital resource lending; a municipal transit real-time information and disruption alert system; an emergency shelter capacity and resource tracking system; or a neighborhood mutual aid request coordination platform. Domains that do not fit include commercial recommendation engines, advertising platforms, social media analytics, or entertainment applications. When choosing a domain, ask: who benefits if this system is reliable and fast, and who is harmed when it is not? If the answer involves a specific real community, you are in the right territory. What the System Must Demonstrate Every project, regardless of domain, must demonstrate the following: Reliability: Services have health check endpoints. The system can recover from at least one scripted failure scenario. Latency: At least one service path is measured under load with k6. Results are reported as p50, p95, and p99 percentiles. Resiliency: The system handles at least one simulated failure (a slow service, a crashing service, or a queue backlog) without total collapse. Observability: At least two services expose Prometheus metrics. A Grafana dashboard displays request rate, error rate, and p95 latency. At least one service writes structured log output. Patterns: The system must implement patterns covered in the course across its services. [TBD: minimum required pattern list and count] Technical Constraints The same constraints that apply to the course units apply to the project: JavaScript only, using the course subset: arrow functions, no classes, ES6 modules, functional iteration preferred. All services and infrastructure are orchestrated with Docker Compose. The entire system must start with a single docker compose up command. Services are written in Node.js with Express for HTTP. Load testing uses k6. Caching and async processing use Redis. Reverse proxying and load balancing use Caddy. No new tools may be introduced unless approved in advance. Team Structure Teams are assigned by the instructor. Team size depends on the course version: 2–3 members in the 6-week summer or winter version, 3–7 members in the 13-week regular semester. Each team targets one custom service per team member plus one shared service (team_size + 1, minimum 3): a 2-person summer team targets 3 services; a 3-person team targets 4; a 5-person semester team targets 6. Infrastructure containers (Caddy, Redis, Prometheus, Grafana) do not count. Services are added incrementally: 2 in Sprint 2, at least one more in Sprint 4, reaching the full target by Sprint 5. Each team member is expected to contribute meaningfully and independently. Contribution is assessed from objective GitHub evidence: commits, pull requests authored and reviewed, and merge history. Because the later sprints are more integrative than the earlier ones, sprint grading is trajectory-weighted across the term. [TBD: trajectory-weighting formula.] Non-contributing members do not receive credit for work they did not do. [TBD: non-contributing member policy and process.] Repository Your team shares one GitHub repository, created during Sprint 0. All work is committed to this repository. The instructor has read access throughout the term and uses the commit and pull request history to assess individual contribution. Patterns, Trade-Offs, and the Design Mindset Introduction A scalable web system is a distributed system. The terms are nearly synonymous because web applications are almost always the systems that reach the scale at which a single machine can no longer keep up. When that happens, you add more machines, and those machines coordinate over HTTP: the same protocol users use to reach the application in the first place. Chapter 1 of the textbook makes this case directly: modern always-on, instantly scalable services are built from many independent services working in coordination, all presenting to the user the appearance of a single unified application. The patterns this course covers, sidecars, ambassadors, queues, and the rest, are the toolkit for building and maintaining that appearance. Before those patterns can be useful, though, you need to feel the problem they exist to solve. A web application that serves one request at a time will eventually stop keeping up. The obvious fix is to handle requests concurrently: start the next request before the previous one finishes. This speeds things up, but it introduces a coordination problem that does not exist when only one request is in flight. You will watch this happen in about 30 lines of Node.js code. The tension it reveals is the one every pattern in the textbook exists to manage: more concurrency means more speed, but it also means more coordination, and coordination has its own cost and its own failure modes. Before You Start This chapter sets up the vocabulary and motivation for everything that follows, so it's worth reading closely even though it has no code of its own. Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 1 (Introduction) References Promise.all — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/allLinks to an external site. setTimeout — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/setTimeoutLinks to an external site. Node.js event loop — https://nodejs.org/en/docs/guides/event-loop-timers-and-nexttickLinks to an external site. Express API — https://expressjs.com/en/4x/api.htmlLinks to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here is a program that handles five requests, one at a time. const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); const handleRequest = async (userId) => { console.log(`Handling request from user ${userId}`); await delay(1000); // stands in for real work: a database lookup, a computation, a file read console.log(`Finished request from user ${userId}`); }; const main = async () => { const start = Date.now(); for (const userId of [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]) { await handleRequest(userId); } const end = Date.now(); console.log(`Total time: ${(end - start) / 1000} seconds`); }; main(); Run it and you'll see it take about five seconds. That should not be surprising: each await in the loop waits for the request before it to finish before starting the next one. This is the simplest possible web service, and for a long time it's also a perfectly fine one. The problem only shows up once enough users show up at once that "one at a time" stops being fast enough. Extending the example The obvious fix is to stop waiting for each request to finish before starting the next. Promise.all lets you kick off all five requests at once and let the event loop interleave them. const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); let sharedCounter = 0; const handleRequest = async (userId) => { await delay(1000); const current = sharedCounter; await delay(1); // widens the window enough to see the problem sharedCounter = current + 1; }; const main = async () => { const start = Date.now(); await Promise.all([0, 1, 2, 3, 4].map(handleRequest)); const end = Date.now(); console.log(`Total time: ${(end - start) / 1000} seconds`); console.log(`Expected counter value: 5, actual: ${sharedCounter}`); }; main(); The total time drops to about one second, which is the win you'd expect. But run it a few times and look at the printed counter value. It is frequently not 5. Two calls to handleRequest both read sharedCounter, both see the same value, and both write back the same incremented result, so one of the increments is silently lost. This is worth pausing on, because JavaScript is single-threaded. There is no OS-level thread switching happening here, and yet the problem still shows up. The event loop can still suspend handleRequest at the await delay(1) line and let a different call to handleRequest run in the gap, which is enough interleaving to lose an update. Notice what happened: the original problem was "handle requests fast enough." Running them concurrently solved that, but it created a new problem that didn't exist when there was only one request in flight at a time: now the in-flight requests have to agree on the value of something they all touch. Naming the pattern That second problem, getting independent units of work to agree on shared state, is not a bug in this particular program. It is the central tension underneath every pattern in this course. The moment you have more than one unit of work in flight, whether that's threads, processes, async tasks on a single event loop, containers, or machines on a network, you gain speed and resilience, but you take on the job of coordinating those units, and coordination has its own cost and its own failure modes. The JavaScript example above is a useful reminder that this has nothing to do with literal parallelism. It shows up the moment work can interleave, even on a single thread. This is also what the course description means by describing web applications as "a large collection of coordinated services... working in coordination to present to the user the illusion of a single program." A distributed system is not one program. It's several independent units of work arranged so carefully that users can't tell the difference. Every pattern you'll meet in this course, sidecar, ambassador, scatter/gather, consistent hashing, is a named, reusable answer to some version of the trade-off you just watched play out: more concurrency means more speed, but it also means more coordination. This is the design mindset the course title refers to: instead of asking "is this program correct," you start asking "what am I trading away to get this property," because in a distributed system you are always trading something. Exercise JavaScript doesn't have a built-in lock the way some languages do, but you can build an equivalent out of a single chained promise. Here is a small helper: const createLock = () => { let chain = Promise.resolve(); return (fn) => { const result = chain.then(fn); chain = result.catch(() => {}); return result; }; }; Task: Use createLock to wrap the critical section in handleRequest (the read, the delay, and the write) so the five calls run that part one at a time instead of interleaving. Starting point: The second code block in the Notes section above, plus the createLock helper. You'll know it works when: running the program ten times in a row always prints actual: 5. Once it does, add a one-line comment in your code noting whether the total runtime changed compared to the unsynchronized version, and a short guess at why. Real World The JavaScript examples above run in Node.js and use setTimeout to stand in for real work. A real web server does the same thing structurally: it receives requests, does some work (database queries, downstream calls), and sends back responses. The coordination problem is identical. Express is the most widely used Node.js HTTP framework. Here is the same sequential-vs-concurrent pattern, but now it's a real server that a real HTTP client can hit. import express from 'express'; const app = express(); let sharedCounter = 0; const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); app.get('/increment', async (req, res) => { const current = sharedCounter; await delay(10); // simulate async work: a database read, a downstream call sharedCounter = current + 1; res.json({ counter: sharedCounter }); }); app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000')); Rather than reloading browser tabs to generate concurrent requests, write a small bash script using curl in a file called sequ.sh. This is the very primitive and manual version of what a load testing tool like k6 does automatically, with configurable concurrency, duration, and built-in result reporting — you will use it in later units. State that multiple requests can race to update belongs in a system that supports atomic operations — a database with transactions, or a cache like Redis that has an INCR command which reads, increments, and writes in a single uninterruptible step.
