An SLO is a formal statement of how a service performs, capturing two things separately: how fast it responds under normal and worst-case conditions, and how often it succeeds at all. In a scalable web system, where many services call each other over HTTP, SLOs are what allow one team's service to become a reliable building block for another team's work. Without them, "fast" and "reliable" remain assumptions rather than commitments. Unit 1 showed that concurrency creates a speed-versus-coordination trade-off but left "faster" as a word rather than a number. This unit supplies the measurements that make SLOs concrete: latency percentiles, which reveal what a typical and a worst-case response actually look like, and a reliability rate, which captures how often calls succeed. You will compute both by hand from a simulated API call, then produce the same numbers from a real HTTP server under concurrent load using k6, the load testing tool used throughout this course. Before You Start Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 2. References Array.prototype.sort — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/sortLinks to an external site. Array.prototype.reduce — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/reduceLinks to an external site. k6 docs — https://k6.io/docs/Links to an external site. k6 end-of-test summary — https://k6.io/docs/results-output/end-of-test/Links to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here's a function that stands in for calling a weather API. In the real world, calls like this don't all take the same amount of time, so this version picks a random delay each time, mostly fast, occasionally slow. const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); const randomLatency = () => Math.random() < 0.95 ? 5 + Math.random() * 15 // fast path: 5 to 20 ms : 100 + Math.random() * 200; // slow path: 100 to 300 ms const callWeatherApi = async () => { const latency = randomLatency(); await delay(latency); return latency; }; const main = async () => { const latencies = []; for (const _ of Array.from({ length: 100 })) { latencies.push(await callWeatherApi()); } const average = latencies.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l, 0) / latencies.length; console.log(`Average latency: ${average.toFixed(1)} ms`); }; main(); Run it and you'll probably see an average somewhere around 15 to 25 ms, which sounds fine. But that single number is hiding something: a small number of those 100 calls took 100 to 300 ms, and the average doesn't tell you how many users had that worse experience, or how much worse it was. Extending the example Two things are missing from the picture above. First, an average flattens out the slow calls instead of showing them to you. Second, real calls don't just run slow, they sometimes fail outright, and that's a different problem than slowness. Let's track both. const percentile = (sortedLatencies, p) => { const index = Math.ceil((p / 100) * sortedLatencies.length) - 1; return sortedLatencies[index]; }; const callWeatherApi = async () => { const latency = randomLatency(); await delay(latency); if (Math.random() < 0.03) { throw new Error("weather service unavailable"); } return latency; }; const main = async () => { const latencies = []; let failures = 0; for (const _ of Array.from({ length: 100 })) { try { latencies.push(await callWeatherApi()); } catch (err) { failures++; } } latencies.sort((a, b) => a - b); const average = latencies.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l, 0) / latencies.length; console.log( `Average latency (successful calls only): ${average.toFixed(1)} ms`, ); console.log(`p50 latency: ${percentile(latencies, 50).toFixed(1)} ms`); console.log(`p95 latency: ${percentile(latencies, 95).toFixed(1)} ms`); console.log(`p99 latency: ${percentile(latencies, 99).toFixed(1)} ms`); console.log(`Failures: ${failures} of 100 calls`); }; main(); Now look at the gap between p50 and p99. p50 looks a lot like the average did before, but p99 is much higher, because it's showing you the slow path that the average was smoothing over. And the failure count is tracked completely separately from latency, because a call that throws an error didn't have a latency at all. It just didn't work. Naming the pattern Three ideas are sitting inside the code you just wrote. Resiliency. The function callWeatherApi is an API: a contract between the caller and whatever does the work. Most API contracts describe the happy path, what comes back when things go well, but they often leave out exactly the two properties you just measured: how long a call might take, and how often it might fail outright. A well designed API contract says something about both, not just about the shape of the return value. Latency is the raw measurement you collected in the latencies array, the time between making a call and getting a response. A percentile is a way of summarizing a pile of latency measurements honestly. The p50, or median, is roughly "what a typical call looks like." The p95 and p99 describe the tail: the experience of the unluckiest 5% or 1% of calls. Real systems are usually judged by their tail, not their median, because a typical user doesn't notice the median, they notice when their own request happens to land in the slow 1%. Reliability is the third idea, and it's independent of latency. A system can be fast and unreliable, slow and reliable, or any combination. That's why production systems usually publish two separate numbers, something like "99.9% of calls succeed" and "p99 latency under 300 ms," rather than a single combined score. Designing an API well means deciding, on purpose, what you're promising for each of these, instead of letting them fall out of whatever the implementation happens to do. Exercise Task: Increase the loop in the second code block from 100 calls to 1000, and add a p99.9 calculation alongside the existing percentiles. Starting point: The second code block in the Notes section above. You'll know it works when: the program prints a p99.9 value in addition to p50, p95, and p99. Run the program a few times at 1000 iterations and add a one-line comment noting which percentile, p50 or p99.9, jumps around more from run to run, and why that might matter when deciding how many samples you need before trusting a percentile measurement. In a scalable web system, any HTTP call between services can fail: the network drops a packet, the server processes a request but the response never arrives, a connection resets mid-flight. Chapter 2 introduces delivery semantics to describe what systems can guarantee in those situations: at-least-once delivery ensures nothing is silently lost but allows duplicates; at-most-once delivery prevents duplicates but can lose requests entirely. Idempotency is what resolves that tension. An operation that produces the same result whether it runs once or ten times can safely use at-least-once delivery, because repeating it on failure costs nothing. Unit 2 measured how often calls fail. This unit asks what callers should do about it. The intuitive answer is to retry until the call succeeds, but without idempotency that is dangerous: if the server processed the request and only the response was lost, retrying causes a duplicate effect. You will watch this happen with a simulated payment API, then fix it with an idempotency key, a design decision made before writing the first retry loop that transforms retries from a source of corruption into a reliable recovery mechanism. Before You Start Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 2 References Map — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/MapLinks to an external site. Idempotency keys (Stripe) — https://stripe.com/docs/api/idempotent_requestsLinks to an external site. express.json() — https://expressjs.com/en/4x/api.html#express.jsonLinks to an external site. HTTP status codes — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/StatusLinks to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here's a function that simulates charging a credit card. The network is flaky: 30% of the time, the charge actually succeeds on the server, but the response never makes it back to the client. From the client's point of view, that looks exactly like a failed request, so the client retries. let totalCharged = 0; const chargeCard = (amount) => { totalCharged += amount; const responseArrives = Math.random() > 0.3; if (!responseArrives) { throw new Error("timed out waiting for a response"); } return { status: "charged", amount }; }; const chargeWithRetry = async (amount) => { for (const attempt of [1, 2, 3]) { try { return chargeCard(amount); } catch (err) { console.log(`Attempt ${attempt} failed: ${err.message}, retrying...`); } } throw new Error("all retries failed"); }; const main = async () => { await chargeWithRetry(20).catch(() => {}); console.log(`Total charged: $${totalCharged}`); }; main(); Run this a handful of times. Sometimes totalCharged is $20, like you'd expect. Other times it's $40 or $60. The retry logic did exactly what you'd want from a client that doesn't want to give up too early — it kept trying until it got a real response — but chargeCard had already taken effect on earlier attempts that the client thought had failed. The client and the true state of the world disagree, and the client has no way to tell from the outside. Extending the example The fix isn't to retry less. It's to make the operation safe to repeat. Give each logical charge a unique key, generated once per operation rather than once per attempt, and have the server remember which keys it has already handled. let totalCharged = 0; const processedKeys = new Map(); const chargeCard = (amount, idempotencyKey) => { if (processedKeys.has(idempotencyKey)) { return processedKeys.get(idempotencyKey); } totalCharged += amount; const result = { status: "charged", amount }; processedKeys.set(idempotencyKey, result); const responseArrives = Math.random() > 0.3; if (!responseArrives) { throw new Error("timed out waiting for a response"); } return result; }; const chargeWithRetry = async (amount, idempotencyKey) => { for (const attempt of [1, 2, 3]) { try { return chargeCard(amount, idempotencyKey); } catch (err) { console.log(`Attempt ${attempt} failed: ${err.message}, retrying...`); } } throw new Error("all retries failed"); }; const main = async () => { const idempotencyKey = "order-48213"; // generated once for this logical operation, not once per attempt await chargeWithRetry(20, idempotencyKey).catch(() => {}); console.log(`Total charged: $${totalCharged}`); }; main(); Run this several times. totalCharged stays at $20 no matter how many of the three attempts time out, because the server recognizes the key on every retry and hands back the result it already computed instead of charging again. Naming the pattern An operation is idempotent if doing it once and doing it five times leave the world in the same state. chargeCard on its own was not idempotent: each call had its own effect. What you built was an idempotent API around a non-idempotent action, by attaching an identity to the operation (the key) and having the server deduplicate on that identity rather than trusting the client to only ask once. This connects directly to delivery semantics — the promises a system makes about how many times an operation might actually run: At-most-once: never duplicates an effect, but can silently lose one. Giving up after a single failed attempt means a true failure and a lost response look identical. At-least-once: never silently loses an effect, but can duplicate one unless the operation is idempotent. This is what the retry loop above does. Exactly-once: the thing everyone wants and almost no real network can promise end to end. In practice it is approximated by combining at-least-once delivery with an idempotent operation — often called effectively-once behavior — which is exactly the combination you just built. Notice how this differs from the coordination problem in Unit 1. There, multiple workers disagreed with each other about shared state. Here, it is a single client and a single server that can disagree about whether something happened, purely because the network in between is unreliable. That disagreement is itself a data consistency problem: in the broken version, the client believed one charge had happened while the stored totalCharged reflected two or three. Consistency is not only about concurrent writers stepping on each other — it is also about a delivery layer that cannot fully tell the truth about what already happened. Exercise Task: Add a second, legitimate charge of $20 using a new idempotency key ("order-48214"), then call chargeWithRetry for "order-48213" a second time to simulate a client that didn't hear back and retried. Starting point: The second code block in the Notes section above. You'll know it works when: totalCharged reliably ends at $40 no matter how many internal retries happen on either call. Add a one-line comment explaining why the idempotency key — not the dollar amount — is what determines whether two calls count as "the same" operation. Real World The Notes example runs entirely in memory. A real payment API uses the same concept: the client sends an Idempotency-Key HTTP header with each request, and the server deduplicates on it. This is exactly how Stripe works. Express is already set up from earlier units. Add express.json() middleware to parse the request body. Create server.js: import express from 'express'; const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); let totalCharged = 0; const processedKeys = new Map(); app.post('/charge', (req, res) => { const idempotencyKey = req.headers['idempotency-key']; if (!idempotencyKey) { return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key header is required' }); } if (processedKeys.has(idempotencyKey)) { return res.json({ ...processedKeys.get(idempotencyKey), duplicate: true }); } const { amount } = req.body; totalCharged += amount; const result = { status: 'charged', amount, totalCharged }; processedKeys.set(idempotencyKey, result); res.json(result); }); app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000')); npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module && npm install express Start the server (node server.js) and test it with two curl commands — one original charge and one retry using the same key: # First attempt curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/charge \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: order-48213" \ -d '{"amount": 20}' # Retry — same key, should not double-charge curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/charge \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: order-48213" \ -d '{"amount": 20}' The first response has no duplicate field. Before containers, the patterns the book describes existed as ideas but not as reusable, portable artifacts: you could implement a sidecar in code, but the deployment unit was just "some process" that had to be configured, versioned, and reproduced by hand on every machine it ran on. Containers changed that. When a service and everything it depends on are packaged into a single image, you have something that runs identically anywhere Docker is installed, that can be composed with other services by name, and that other teams can depend on without knowing what it is built from. Units 1 through 3 covered the logical challenges of distributed services: concurrency, measurement, and safe retries. Before any of those patterns can run in production, each service needs to be packaged as an image. A Node.js server that works on your machine may fail on a teammate's machine, in CI, or in production, because none of its dependencies are written down anywhere. This unit fixes that. You will write a Dockerfile, build it into an image, and run it as a container. By the end, those words stop being vocabulary and become two specific things you watched happen. Before You Start Read: Docker's overview of images and containers — https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/Links to an external site. References Dockerfile reference — https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/Links to an external site. docker build — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/build/Links to an external site. docker run — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/Links to an external site. docker ps / docker logs / docker rm — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/Links to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here's a tiny web server. // server.js import http from 'node:http'; http.createServer((req, res) => { res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' }); res.end('Hello from a plain Node process\n'); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000')); You also need a package.json so Node treats the file as an ES module: { "type": "module" } Run it with node server.js, then visit localhost:3000 or run curl localhost:3000. It works, but notice everything it's quietly depending on: this exact machine has Node installed, at some version, with nothing else conflicting. None of that is written down anywhere. If you sent server.js to a teammate, it would either work by luck or fail in some way that has nothing to do with the code itself. Extending the example Write down exactly what this code needs to run, in a file called a Dockerfile, then build that description into an image. # Dockerfile FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY . . EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "server.js"] Each line does one specific thing. FROM node:24 starts from a base image that already has Node 24 installed. WORKDIR sets the directory inside the image where the following commands run. COPY . . brings everything from your current directory into the image. EXPOSE documents which port the container expects to be reached on. CMD is the command that runs when a container starts from this image. Build it, then run it: docker build -t hello-server . docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-server docker build reads the Dockerfile and produces an image named hello-server. docker run starts a container — a running instance of that image — and -p 3000:3000 connects port 3000 on your machine to port 3000 inside the container. Visit localhost:3000 again. Same response as before, but now it's coming from inside an isolated container built from a file that says exactly what it needs. Managing containers and images docker run blocks your terminal because the container's output goes there. To start a container in the background, add -d (detached mode). Give it a name with --name so you can refer to it by something other than its ID: docker run -d --name my-server -p 3000:3000 hello-server Check what's running: docker ps docker ps lists every running container: its ID, image, when it started, and the port mapping. To include containers that have stopped, use docker ps -a. To see the output from a detached container: docker logs my-server When you're done, stop the container and remove it: docker stop my-server docker rm my-server docker stop sends a signal that gives the process a moment to shut down cleanly. docker rm removes the stopped container — until you do this, the container still exists on disk (visible in docker ps -a) even after it stops. To skip the two steps, docker rm -f my-server stops and removes in one command. Images accumulate too. To see what images are installed on your machine: docker images To remove an image (only works if no containers — running or stopped — are using it): docker rmi hello-server To remove all unused images at once: docker image prune Naming the pattern An image is a packaged, read-only blueprint: your code plus everything it depends on to run, frozen into a single artifact. A container is a running instance of that image, the way a process is a running instance of a program. You can start several containers from the same image at once, and they won't interfere with each other — each one gets its own isolated filesystem and process space. The Dockerfile is the recipe that produces the image, and each instruction in it becomes a layer that Docker can cache. That's why rebuilding an image after a small code change is usually much faster than the first build: Docker reuses unchanged layers and only reruns the steps that changed. Two things worth keeping straight: EXPOSE just documents intent inside the Dockerfile. The -p flag on docker run is what actually connects a port on your machine to a port inside the running container. EXPOSE without -p doesn't open anything. This is the foundation everything from Unit 6 onward sits on top of. Multi-container patterns — sidecars, proxies, workers — are just multiple containers, each one a running instance of some image, deliberately sharing a little while staying isolated in every other way. You'll know it works when: docker run -d --name server-3000 -e PORT=3000 -p 3000:3000 hello-server docker run -d --name server-3001 -e PORT=3001 -p 3001:3001 hello-server docker ps — both containers are listed as running docker logs server-3000 — shows "Listening on port 3000" docker logs server-3001 — shows "Listening on port 3001" curl localhost:3000 and curl localhost:3001 both return a response Cleanup: docker stop server-3000 server-3001 then docker rm server-3000 server-3001 Real World Most Node.js projects have npm dependencies. That changes the Dockerfile in one important way: you need to install them inside the image before copying your source code. Create an Express app: // server.js import express from 'express'; const app = express(); const port = process.env.PORT || 3000; app.get('/', (req, res) => { res.send('Hello from Express in a container\n'); }); app.listen(port, () => console.log(`Listening on port ${port}`)); { "type": "module", "dependencies": { "express": "^4.18.0" } } Run npm install once locally to generate package-lock.json. Then write the Dockerfile: FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY package*.json . RUN npm install COPY . . EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "server.js"] The key change is the order: copy package*.json first, run npm install, then copy the rest of the source. Docker caches each layer — so as long as package.json doesn't change, npm install is skipped on every subsequent rebuild. If you copied everything first and then ran npm install, any change to any file would invalidate the install layer and force a full reinstall. Add a .dockerignore file to prevent the local node_modules from being copied into the image (which would overwrite what npm install just put there): node_modules Build and run: npm install docker build -t hello-express . docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-express curl localhost:3000 returns the response from Express running inside the container. In production, that role is played by Kubernetes. At the scale of a single developer or a small team, Docker Compose fills the same conceptual role. Instead of a sequence of imperative commands that must be typed in the right order with the right flags every time, Compose lets you declare what containers you want, how they are connected, and what volumes they share, then brings the whole arrangement up or down with a single command. Unit 4 built one container from a Dockerfile and ran it with docker run. The moment you need two containers sharing a volume, that one command becomes four, each one with flags that must match exactly, in the right order, every time you want to bring the system up. This unit introduces Compose as the tool that replaces that sequence with a file you can read, share, and check into version control. Every multi-container setup from Unit 6 onward will be expressed as a docker-compose.yml, so the goal here is to make that format completely familiar before the patterns begin. Before You Start Read: Docker's Compose overview — https://docs.docker.com/compose/Links to an external site. References Compose file reference — https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/Links to an external site. docker compose CLI — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/Links to an external site. Named volumes — https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/Links to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here are two small scripts. One writes a timestamp to a shared file every five seconds. The other serves whatever is currently in that file over HTTP. // writer.js import fs from 'node:fs'; setInterval(() => { fs.writeFileSync( '/data/message.txt', `Last updated: ${new Date().toISOString()}\n`, ); }, 5000); // reader-server.js import http from 'node:http'; import fs from 'node:fs'; http.createServer((req, res) => { const message = fs.existsSync('/data/message.txt') ? fs.readFileSync('/data/message.txt', 'utf8') : 'no data yet\n'; res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' }); res.end(message); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000')); Using what you learned in Unit 4, running both of these as containers that share a volume takes a sequence like this: docker build -t demo-app . docker volume create shared-data docker run -d --name writer -v shared-data:/data demo-app node writer.js docker run -d --name reader -p 3000:3000 -v shared-data:/data demo-app node reader-server.js That's already four commands, each one easy to get slightly wrong, and you'd have to remember this exact sequence, in this exact order, every single time you wanted to bring this up again. Tearing it down means stopping and removing two containers and a volume by hand too. Extending the example Describe the same two containers and the volume they share in a single file instead. # docker-compose.yml services: writer: build: . command: node writer.js volumes: - shared-data:/data reader: build: . command: node reader-server.js ports: - "3000:3000" volumes: - shared-data:/data volumes: shared-data: Now bring both containers up with one command: docker compose up Visit localhost:3000 a few times over thirty seconds and watch the timestamp update. When you're done, docker compose down removes both containers and cleans up after itself. Same two containers, same shared volume, same result as the four commands above — but now the whole arrangement lives in a file you can read top to bottom, hand to a teammate, and check into version control. You also need a Dockerfile so Compose knows how to build the image: FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY . . There's no CMD here — each service in docker-compose.yml provides its own command, so the Dockerfile just handles the image and leaves the command to Compose. Managing a Compose project docker compose up runs in the foreground — all service output streams to your terminal. To start in the background instead, add -d: docker compose up -d Check the status of every service in the project: docker compose ps To stream logs as they arrive: docker compose logs -f # all services docker compose logs -f writer # one service only To restart a single service without touching the others: docker compose restart writer To stop all services without removing the containers: docker compose stop docker compose down goes further — it stops and removes all containers. By default it leaves named volumes alone. To remove volumes too and wipe all stored data: docker compose down --volumes To open a shell inside a running service for debugging: docker compose exec reader sh Naming the pattern docker-compose.yml is a declarative description of a multi-container application. Each entry under services is one container's blueprint: where to build it from, what command to run, which ports to expose, which volumes to mount. A named volume like shared-data is declared once under volumes and referenced by any service that needs it — which is how two otherwise unrelated containers end up sharing the same files. Compose itself isn't a new pattern. It's a tool for describing an arrangement of containers that you've already decided on, the same way a recipe describes a dish without being the dish. The patterns themselves — sidecar, ambassador, and the ones still ahead — are about why containers are arranged a certain way. Compose is just how that arrangement gets written down in one place instead of typed by hand every time. From Unit 6 onward, every multi-container example in this course will be expressed as a docker-compose.yml. It shares the shared-data volume but doesn't expose any port — it only reads from the shared file and logs to its own console. // logger.js import fs from 'node:fs'; setInterval(() => { const message = fs.existsSync('/data/message.txt') ? fs.readFileSync('/data/message.txt', 'utf8') : 'no data yet'; console.log(message.trim()); }, 5000); Starting point: The docker-compose.yml and Dockerfile from the Notes above, plus the logger.js file. Add a logger service to docker-compose.yml. You'll know it works when: docker compose up -d --build docker compose ps — all three services listed as running docker compose logs logger — shows the same timestamp the reader is serving over HTTP, updating every five seconds curl localhost:3000 — the reader responds with that same timestamp Cleanup: docker compose down Real World Volume sharing is one way containers cooperate. Chapter 1 explains why patterns matter: they give practitioners a shared vocabulary for describing arrangements that would otherwise have to be described from scratch every time. The sidecar solves a problem that appears as soon as a service acquires a second job: a process that serves HTTP and also syncs content has two reasons to change, two teams that might need to edit it, and two separate failure modes to worry about at once. The pattern's answer is a second container, attached to the first, that handles the second job without either container needing to know much about the other. Notes The starting problem Here's a tiny Node.js server that serves a content directory. To keep that content fresh, it also syncs new content into that directory on a timer, right inside the same file. // app.js import http from 'node:http'; import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; const syncContent = () => { // stands in for pulling the latest content: a git repo, a CMS, an S3 bucket fs.writeFileSync( path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'), `

Updated at ${new Date().toISOString()}

`, ); }; fs.mkdirSync(CONTENT_DIR, { recursive: true }); syncContent(); setInterval(syncContent, 10000); http.createServer((req, res) => { const html = fs.readFileSync(path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html')); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' }); res.end(html); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Serving on port 3000')); This works fine. But notice that app.js now has two jobs that have nothing to do with each other: serving HTTP requests, and knowing how content gets refreshed. If you wanted to change where content comes from, how often it refreshes, or swap in a completely different sync mechanism, you'd have to edit and redeploy the exact same file that handles requests — even though the request-handling logic never changed. Extending the example Split the two jobs into two separate processes that agree on nothing except a shared directory. One serves. One syncs. Neither calls the other directly. // app.js — serves only import http from 'node:http'; import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; http.createServer((req, res) => { const html = fs.readFileSync(path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html')); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' }); res.end(html); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Serving on port 3000')); // sync.js — syncs only import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; const syncContent = () => { fs.writeFileSync( path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'), `

Updated at ${new Date().toISOString()}

`, ); console.log('Content synced'); }; fs.mkdirSync(CONTENT_DIR, { recursive: true }); syncContent(); setInterval(syncContent, 10000); Create a package.json so Node.js treats these as ES modules: { "type": "module" } Open two terminals. In the first, run node app.js. In the second, run node sync.js. Open http://localhost:3000 and reload every few seconds. The timestamp keeps updating, exactly like before, but app.js and sync.js never call each other. They cooperate purely by reading and writing the same directory. Naming the pattern What you just built is the sidecar pattern: a second process attached to a primary process, sharing a local resource with it so it can add a capability the primary needs without modifying the primary's code. The primary (app.js) has no dependency on the sidecar's implementation. You could replace sync.js with something that pulls from a git repo, fetches from S3, or syncs on a completely different schedule, and app.js would never need to change. The sidecar runs as its own independent process, but is deployed and managed together with its primary as one unit. That independence is what makes the pattern work cleanly: app.js only reads the shared file, sync.js only writes it, so there is no shared mutable state being raced over the way there was in Unit 1. The coordination happens through a resource built for exactly this — a shared file — rather than through memory two processes are racing to update. Starting point: The two-file version from the Notes above (the app.js + sync.js split). You'll know it works when: refreshing http://localhost:3000 shows the sync count climbing roughly every 3 seconds, and you were able to make this entire change inside sync.js without touching app.js at all. Real World The Notes version runs both processes on your local machine sharing a directory. In production, the primary service and its sidecar run as separate containers — but the coordination mechanism is exactly the same: a shared volume that both containers can read and write. Docker Compose lets you define the two containers and their shared volume in a single file. Create Dockerfile: FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY . . RUN mkdir -p content Create docker-compose.yml: services: app: build: . command: node app.js ports: - "3000:3000" volumes: - content:/usr/src/app/content sync: build: . command: node sync.js volumes: - content:/usr/src/app/content volumes: content: Run docker compose up. Open http://localhost:3000 and reload every few seconds. The timestamp keeps updating. app and sync are now isolated containers — different process namespaces, different filesystems — but they cooperate through the content named volume exactly the way the two local processes cooperated through ./content/. To verify the independence: run docker compose restart sync while the page is open. The app container keeps serving without interruption; only the sync pauses and resumes. Traffic grows to the point where one instance cannot keep up, so your team splits the data across two servers: even-numbered user IDs go to one, odd-numbered IDs go to another. You update app.js to route each call to the right server. Three months later a third server is added, and you update app.js again. A second internal service also looks up users, so the routing logic is duplicated there too. Whenever the sharding strategy changes, every service that calls users-service has to change with it. This is the problem Chapter 4 of the textbook targets with the ambassador pattern: routing decisions, retries, and traffic shaping belong in the infrastructure, not inside every application that happens to make a call. The ambassador is a proxy container that intercepts a primary container's outgoing calls and makes those decisions on its behalf, while the primary keeps calling a fixed local address as if nothing has changed. Unit 6 introduced the sidecar: a helper container that adds capability beside the primary by sharing a named volume with it. The ambassador keeps the two-container shape but flips the concern: instead of adding something the primary was missing, it intercepts something the primary was already doing, its outgoing calls to other services, and takes over the routing. This unit uses network_mode: "service:..." in Docker Compose to give the ambassador container access to the primary container's localhost interface. By the end you will have a working sharding ambassador that routes traffic to two backend instances based on user ID, and you will extend it to run a canary experiment on top of the existing routing logic. Before You Start Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 4 (Ambassador Pattern) References Node.js http module: https://nodejs.org/api/http.htmlLinks to an external site. fetch global (Node.js 18+): https://nodejs.org/api/globals.html#fetchLinks to an external site. Compose network_mode: https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/#network_modeLinks to an external site. Caddy reverse_proxy directive: https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/directives/reverse_proxyLinks to an external site. Notes The starting problem Your application calls users-service to look up user data. There is one instance, one hostname, and the call is direct. // app.js import http from 'node:http'; const getUser = async (userId) => { const res = await fetch(`http://users-service:5000/users/${userId}`); return res.json(); }; http.createServer(async (req, res) => { const userId = req.url.split('/').pop(); const user = await getUser(userId); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(JSON.stringify(user)); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('App listening on port 3000')); This works as long as there is exactly one users-service to call. The moment you want to split requests across two backend instances, or send a fraction of traffic to a new version you are testing, you have nowhere to put that decision except inside app.js, mixed into code whose job is to handle requests, not manage routing. Extending the example Change one line: instead of calling the real backend's hostname, app.js calls localhost. A separate container, the ambassador, listens on that same localhost interface and decides where each request actually goes. // app.js — now calls localhost instead of the real backend import http from 'node:http'; const getUser = async (userId) => { const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:5000/users/${userId}`); return res.json(); }; http.createServer(async (req, res) => { const userId = req.url.split('/').pop(); const user = await getUser(userId); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(JSON.stringify(user)); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('App listening on port 3000')); // ambassador.js import http from 'node:http'; const forwardTo = async (host, userId, res) => { const r = await fetch(`http://${host}/users/${userId}`); const data = await r.text(); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(data); }; http.createServer((req, res) => { const userId = parseInt(req.url.split('/').pop(), 10); const host = userId % 2 === 0 ? 'users-service-a:5000' : 'users-service-b:5000'; console.log(`Routing user ${userId} to ${host}`); forwardTo(host, userId, res); }).listen(5000, () => console.log('Ambassador listening on port 5000')); // backend.js — used by both users-service-a and users-service-b import http from 'node:http'; http.createServer((req, res) => { const userId = req.url.split('/').pop(); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(JSON.stringify({ id: userId, servedBy: process.env.LABEL })); }).listen(5000, () => console.log(`Backend ${process.env.LABEL} listening on port 5000`)); Create a package.json to enable ES modules: { "type": "module" } # docker-compose.yml services: app: build: . command: node app.js ports: - "3000:3000" ambassador: build: . command: node ambassador.js network_mode: "service:app" users-service-a: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=A users-service-b: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=B # Dockerfile FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY . . network_mode: "service:app" puts the ambassador inside the same network namespace as app, so they share localhost the same way containers in the same pod would in production. Run docker compose up, then try: curl localhost:3000/users/42 curl localhost:3000/users/43 One comes back with "servedBy": "A" and the other with "servedBy": "B", even though app.js only ever called localhost:5000 and has no idea two backends exist. Naming the pattern This is the ambassador pattern: a proxy container placed in the path of a primary container's outgoing calls, making routing decisions on its behalf, while the primary container keeps calling a fixed local address and stays completely unaware of sharding, retries, or anything else the ambassador might be doing. The primary container's code does not change when you add sharding, retry logic, or an experiment. It is worth comparing this directly to Unit 6's sidecar. Both patterns deploy a helper container alongside a primary one and share a local resource with it. But a sidecar sits beside the primary doing auxiliary work the primary would otherwise have to do itself, like syncing content into a shared volume. An ambassador sits in the path of calls the primary was already going to make, intercepting and reshaping them. Sharding, what you just built, routes requests across multiple backend instances based on a key. The same shape supports a second use case called a canary deployment. The name comes from the mining practice of sending a canary into a coal mine ahead of workers: if the canary was harmed by toxic gas, miners knew to stay out. A canary deployment works the same way. When you have a new version of a service that you are not yet confident in, you route a small percentage of real production traffic to it, say 10%, and leave the rest on the stable version. If the new version has a bug or a performance problem, only that fraction of users is affected, and you can pull it back immediately. Ninety percent of traffic never touched it. Once you gain confidence, you raise the percentage until the new version handles everything. An ambassador makes this straightforward: instead of routing by user ID, it rolls a random number on each incoming request and sends a configurable fraction to the new version. The primary container's code never changes. The experiment can be started, adjusted, or cancelled by modifying the ambassador alone. Exercise Task: Add a canary experiment to ambassador.js. On top of the existing even-or-odd sharding, make 20% of all requests, regardless of user ID, go to users-service-b instead, chosen at random. Starting point: The ambassador.js and docker-compose.yml from the Notes above. You'll know it works when: sending 20 requests for the same even-numbered user ID results in most responses showing "servedBy": "A", but a noticeable fraction showing "servedBy": "B", and app.js did not need a single line changed. Real World The Notes version builds its own ambassador in JavaScript. In production, most teams use an existing reverse proxy for this role. This section replaces ambassador.js with Caddy, a lightweight web server and reverse proxy, to show that the ambassador pattern is not a coding exercise: it is an arrangement that already exists inside tools you can drop in. Create a Caddyfile that configures Caddy to listen on port 5000 and round-robin between two backends: :5000 { reverse_proxy users-service-a:5000 users-service-b:5000 { lb_policy round_robin } } Replace the ambassador service in docker-compose.yml with a Caddy container. The network_mode entry stays the same: services: app: build: . command: node app.js ports: - "3000:3000" caddy: image: caddy:2 volumes: - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile network_mode: "service:app" users-service-a: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=A users-service-b: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=B Run docker compose up, then send several requests: for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -s localhost:3000/users/2 | grep servedBy; done You should see alternating A and B responses. app.js is unchanged; the only thing that changed is which container acts as the ambassador. Caddy's reverse_proxy directive handles round-robin distribution, health checking, and connection pooling that you would otherwise have to implement yourself. Home Exercise Caddy's reverse_proxy accepts additional upstream addresses alongside the existing two. Add a third backend, users-service-c, to both the Caddyfile and docker-compose.yml: Update the Caddyfile: :5000 { reverse_proxy users-service-a:5000 users-service-b:5000 users-service-c:5000 { lb_policy round_robin } } Add to docker-compose.yml: users-service-c: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=C You'll know it works when: sending 30 requests for the same user ID produces a mix of A, B, and C responses in roughly equal proportions, and you made this change entirely in Caddyfile and docker-compose.yml without touching app.js or backend.js. Looking Ahead Unit 8 introduces the third shape for a helper container. Unlike the sidecar, which adds capability beside the primary, or the ambassador, which intercepts the primary's outgoing calls, the adapter intercepts what the primary already produces and transforms it into a format that something else expects. The system uses only Express; no other libraries are needed. This assignment is framed around real marine science: at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, Associate Scientist Loretta Roberson researches large-scale offshore seaweed farming as a source of sustainable biomass, aimed at bioremediation and at protecting sensitive ecosystems like coral reefs. She leads a DOE ARPA-E-funded initiative farming tropical seaweed off Puerto Rico and works on refining Sargassum into an alternative biomass feedstock. A real deployment of that kind of research depends on exactly the kind of system you will build here: a network of monitoring stations, one per farm site, coordinated and routed reliably enough that no single site's software has to know about the others. When you are done you will have one shared Docker image, one docker-compose.yml, and four small service files (a farm-monitoring service, a regional-aggregator sidecar, a routing ambassador, and a buoy gateway) — hands-on evidence that the patterns from class compose together into a real distributed system. Setup Inside your Gantry devcontainer, create a working directory for this homework: mkdir hw02 && cd hw02 npm init -y npm pkg set type=module npm install express You will create seven files: farm-service.js, sidecar-sync.js, ambassador.js, buoy-gateway.js, Dockerfile, .dockerignore, and docker-compose.yml. Part 1: Containerizing a Farm Site (Unit 4) Your farm monitoring service represents one offshore farm site. It must expose two endpoints, and be entirely configured through environment variables so the same image can run as any farm site. Environment variables PORT — port to listen on FARM_ID — this farm's identifier (e.g. farm-a) DATA_DIR — directory to persist readings to (default ./data) CALIBRATION — sensor calibration version (default v1) GET /status Returns the farm's identity and every reading recorded so far. 200 OK { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] } POST /reading Records a sensor reading. The request body must include metric (a string, e.g. "growthRateCm") and value (a number). Appends the reading (with a server-generated timestamp) to an in-memory array and to ${DATA_DIR}/readings.json. 200 OK { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.4, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } } The Dockerfile Write a Dockerfile that builds an image any farm site can run from: FROM node:24 (or a version you have installed) WORKDIR set to your app directory Copy package*.json first and run npm install, then copy the rest of your source — in that order, so Docker only reinstalls dependencies when package.json actually changes EXPOSE the port your service listens on A default CMD that starts farm-service.js Add a .dockerignore that excludes node_modules. You'll know it works when: running docker build -t seagrid . docker run -e FARM_ID=farm-a -p 3000:3000 seagrid and then curl http://localhost:3000/status returns { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "readings": [] }. Part 2: Orchestrating the Farm Network (Unit 5) Write a docker-compose.yml that runs the whole farm network as one system: farm-a, farm-b, farm-c — three farm-service instances, each built from the same image, each with its own FARM_ID and DATA_DIR, each mapped to its own host port farm-a-v2 — a fourth farm-service instance with FARM_ID=farm-a, a separate DATA_DIR, and CALIBRATION=v2 — a calibration trial running alongside farm-a itself A single named volume mounted into every farm service (all four) so their data directories persist and can be read by the sidecar you will add in Part 3 You'll know it works when: running docker compose up --build starts all four farm containers, each independently reachable on its own host port, and a reading posted to farm-a never appears when you GET /status on farm-b or farm-c. Part 3: The Regional Aggregator Sidecar (Unit 6) Add sidecar-sync.js: a background process with no HTTP server of its own, that periodically reads every farm's readings.json from the shared volume and writes a rolled-up summary — without farm-service.js ever knowing it exists. Environment variables DATA_ROOT — the shared volume's mount path FARM_IDS — comma-separated list of farm ids to summarize (e.g. farm-a,farm-b,farm-c) SYNC_INTERVAL_MS — how often to re-read and rewrite the summary (default 5000) Behavior On every interval tick, for each farm id in FARM_IDS, read ${DATA_ROOT}//readings.json (treat a missing file as zero readings), then write ${DATA_ROOT}/regional-summary.json: { "generatedAt": "2026-07-10T12:00:05.000Z", "farms": { "farm-a": { "count": 3, "avgValue": 2.1 }, "farm-b": { "count": 1, "avgValue": 4.0 } }, "regionalAvgValue": 2.35 } regionalAvgValue is the mean of every reading from every farm pooled together — not the mean of the per-farm averages. (With farm-a's three readings averaging 2.1 and farm-b's one reading at 4.0, the pooled mean of all four numbers — not the average of 2.1 and 4.0 — is what belongs here.) Add sidecar as a service in your docker-compose.yml, sharing the same named volume, with depends_on on the three farms. You'll know it works when: after posting a few readings to two or more farms and waiting one sync interval, docker compose exec sidecar cat /data/regional-summary.json shows the correct per-farm count and avgValue, and a regionalAvgValue that matches the pooled-mean formula above. Part 4: The Ambassador (Unit 7) Add two more files: buoy-gateway.js — the primary service a real buoy would talk to. Exposes POST /submit-reading (body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }) and forwards it verbatim to a fixed AMBASSADOR_URL. It contains no routing logic of its own — it always calls the same local address, the same way Unit 7's own primary service did. ambassador.js — shares buoy-gateway's network namespace (via network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" in Compose) and makes the actual routing decision on buoy-gateway's behalf. ambassador.js: POST /reading Body: { "farmId", "metric", "value" }. Unknown farmId → 404 { "error": "unknown farmId: farm-x" } farmId === "farm-b" or "farm-c" → forwarded to that farm's fixed URL every time farmId === "farm-a" → forwarded to farm-a-v2 roughly CANARY_PERCENT percent of the time (default 20), and to farm-a the rest of the time — a canary trial of the new calibration Response (whichever farm actually handled it): 200 OK { "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "farmId": "farm-a", "calibration": "v1", "count": 1, "latest": { "metric": "growthRateCm", "value": 2.0, "timestamp": "2026-07-10T12:00:00.000Z" } } } buoy-gateway.js: POST /submit-reading Forwards the request body to ${AMBASSADOR_URL}/reading and returns: 200 OK { "receivedBy": "buoy-gateway", "routedTo": "farm-a", "farmResponse": { "...": "..." } } Wiring it in docker-compose.yml Add buoy-gateway and ambassador services. The ambassador must not declare its own ports: — network_mode: "service:buoy-gateway" and ports: cannot be used together on the same service; Compose will reject it. Expose the port through buoy-gateway instead. You'll know it works when: Repeatedly submitting readings for farm-b or farm-c always routes to that same farm. Submitting around 100 readings for farm-a results in roughly 10-30 of them landing on farm-a-v2 (check GET /status on each afterward) — not exactly 20 every time, but in that range. Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing Schedule: Week 2 (Jul 13–17) Grade entry: Sprint 2 (half weight) Purpose Week 1 introduced the vocabulary of distributed systems: why latency and reliability are the two properties you measure first, what idempotency means and why it matters when services retry, and how concurrency creates coordination problems that do not exist on a single machine. Sprint 1 asks your team to apply that vocabulary to your chosen domain. No code is expected in this sprint. This is design thinking grounded in the concepts just studied. The deliverables are written artifacts that demonstrate you can reason about your system before you build it. Deliverables All three deliverables are committed to the team repository under a docs/ directory and linked from the README.md. 1. Refined project description (docs/PROJECT.md) Write a short document called docs/PROJECT.md (roughly one page) that refines the domain paragraph from Sprint 0 into a complete project description. It must address: Domain: What kind of system is this, and who does it serve? Scalability problem: What specific load or coordination challenge makes this domain require a scalable distributed web system? Be concrete: what happens when demand spikes, when a service goes down, or when data must be shared across multiple nodes? Computing for the Common Good framing: Who benefits when this system works correctly? Who is harmed when it fails or is slow? Also note like what goes into the course and what to be on\\n\\nany extra information you need access to from this leave in 'syllabus.md' \\nSkip To Content\\nDashboard\\nAustin Fairbanks\\nAccount\\nDashboard\\nCourses\\nGroups\\nCalendar\\nInbox\\nHistory\\nStudio\\nPortfolio\\n4 unread release notes.4\\nHelp\\nCOMPSCI 426 (170735) SUM26Pages⚖️ 426 U26 Syllabus (Summer Session II)\\n\\nSummer 2026\\nHome\\nAnnouncements\\nModules\\nGradescope\\nAssignments\\nQuizzes\\nDiscussions\\nPeople\\nIgniteAI Search\\n⚖️ 426 U26 Syllabus (Summer Session II)\\nCOMPSCI 426 Scalable Web Systems\\nNumber: COMPSCI 426\\nTitle: Scalable Web Systems\\nInstructor: Tim Richards\\nCanvas: https://umamherst.instructure.com/courses/38093\\nSemester: Summer Session II 2026\\nMode: Online, Asynchronous\\nScheduled Meetings: There are no scheduled meetings for this course. It is online and asynchronous.\\nExams: There are no exams in this course\\nGroups: There is group work in this course\\nCredits: 3\\nPrerequisites: COMPSCI 320 or COMPSCI 326 with a grade of C or better. If you are from another academic institution or have unique circumstances, you must submit an override requestLinks to an external site. to be considered for enrollment.\\nDescription\\nThe web has become a large and complex area for application development. Access to an abundance of open source languages, libraries, and frameworks has led to the quick and easy construction of a variety of applications with several moving parts working in coordination to present to the user the illusion of a single program. In reality, web applications are extremely difficult to get right. They involve a large collection of coordinated services, multiple databases, complicated user interfaces, security and performance issues, and ever changing third party services, spread across physical and virtual machines. These complications are further stressed by the large number of concurrent users that access these applications every second. This course investigates several well known web-based applications and the technology and software architecture used to scale them. We will also study specific topics related to scalability in software design in the context of web application architecture. This course is hands-on and heavily project-based; students will build, monitor, and load test a distributed system composed of coordinated services. This course counts as an Elective for the CS and INFORM Majors.\\n\\nThis course is concept-first and experiential. You will build and break real scalable systems before we put names to the patterns you discover. The vocabulary of the field, sidecars, ambassadors, sharding, scatter/gather, comes after you have already felt why each pattern exists.\\n\\nStaff\\nInstructor: Tim Richards\\nEmail: tdr@umass.edu\\nOffice Hours: By appointment, via Google Meet\\nTeaching Assistant: Miles (Mingzhe) Li\\nEmail: mingzhel@umass.edu\\nLearning Objectives\\nBy the end of this course, students will be able to:\\n\\nConfigure and use a devcontainer-based development environment with Docker and VS Code for a reproducible, team-consistent workspace.\\n\\nExplain the core properties of distributed systems, including latency, reliability, idempotency, and delivery semantics, and reason about the trade-offs between them.\\n\\nContainerize an application with Docker and orchestrate multiple coordinated services with Docker Compose.\\n\\nApply single-node patterns, including the sidecar, ambassador, and adapter patterns, to extend services without modifying them.\\n\\nDesign and reason about serving patterns, including replication, caching, sharding with consistent hashing, and scatter/gather.\\n\\nMeasure system behavior under load using k6, and interpret latency percentiles, throughput, and error rates.\\n\\nBuild event-driven and queue-based systems, including work queues, pub/sub pipelines, and dead letter queues.\\n\\nReason about distributed coordination, including locks, leases, ownership election, and concurrent data manipulation.\\n\\nInstrument a system for observability using structured logging, metrics, and tracing.\\n\\nDiagnose common distributed failure patterns, including thundering herd, versioning errors, and cascading failure.\\n\\nUse Git and GitHub for version control, branching, and pull request workflows on a shared team repository.\\n\\nPlan, build, and present a complete, scalable web system simulation as a team.\\n\\nTime Commitment\\nA three credit course does not get smaller when you compress it into six weeks; it gets denser. Plan for roughly twenty-two to twenty-three hours a week.\\n\\nUMass Amherst defines course workload by a standard credit hour rule. The guiding rule is forty five hours of work per semester for each unit of credit, on the assumption that each credit hour generates two hours of assigned work for every hour of in class contact. By that rule a three credit course represents about one hundred thirty five hours of total work, and the University expects the total workload for a three credit course to be at least 135 hours. That total is fixed. It is the same whether the course runs across a full semester or across a summer.\\n\\nWhat changes is how those hours are distributed. In a normal fifteen week semester, one hundred thirty five hours works out to about nine hours per week. This section is taught asynchronously over six weeks, so the same one hundred thirty five hours are compressed into roughly six weeks of effort, which comes to about twenty-two to twenty-three hours per week. There is no reduction in scope to go with the shorter calendar; you are doing a full three credit course in forty percent of the usual time, so the weekly pace is about two and a half times what the same course would demand in the fall or spring.\\n\\nTwenty-two hours a week is a serious commitment, and you should plan your summer around that reality. Spread across six working days it is just under four hours a day. Because each day's material builds directly on the day before, and because this is a systems course where one misconfigured service can block everything downstream, the work does not compress well into a weekend burst. Students who treat this as a part time effort fall behind quickly, and in a six week term there is very little room to recover. For that reason I strongly advise against pairing this course with another demanding summer course or with full time employment. If your situation makes twenty-two hours a week difficult, email me at tdr@umass.edu before the term begins so we can be honest about whether the timing works for you.\\n\\nTo make the number concrete, your weekly hours go toward the same components described elsewhere in this syllabus: working through several Knowledge Units, since the eighteen KUs are spread across the six weeks, including their preparatory reading, the activity, and the exercises; and steadily advancing your team's sprint project, which on its own accounts for a substantial share of your time over the term. The weekly quizzes are the clearest early signal of whether you are keeping pace. If you find yourself consistently spending far more than this, or far less and still finishing everything, let me know, because that is useful feedback on the course and may also be a sign we should look at how you are approaching the work.\\n\\nCourse Structure Synopsis\\nAsynchronous Delivery\\nThis course is offered in an online, asynchronous format. All course materials will be available online on the course website. You are expected to engage with the content and complete assignments on your own schedule within the given deadlines. This course is designed to be experiential, meaning that you will learn by doing, and the course structure is built around active participation and hands-on activities.\\n\\nKnowledge Units (KUs)\\nThe primary way in which learning takes place is through knowledge units (KUs). Each KU is a self-contained module that includes preparatory reading, hands-on activities, and exercises. You are expected to complete each KU in order, as they build upon one another. The course is deliberately concept-first: most units ask you to build or observe something before the underlying pattern is named, so that the name lands on an experience you already have rather than on an abstraction. Each KU will have a set of activities that you must complete, including coding and load-testing exercises.\\n\\nCanvas\\nCanvas is where you will find links to all of the course material. The syllabus and schedule can be found on Canvas. All assignments will be posted on Canvas. Grades will be posted to Canvas. Announcements will be posted on Canvas. If in doubt, go to Canvas to find what you are looking for and follow links from there.\\n\\nGradescope\\nHomework assignments are submitted through Gradescope and graded automatically. When you submit, an autograder runs your code against a test suite and reports a score immediately; you do not have to wait for manual review to see how you did. If a test fails, the output includes enough information to diagnose and fix the issue before the deadline. You may resubmit as many times as you like before the deadline, and only your final submission is graded. Gradescope is accessible through Canvas.\\n\\nCommunication\\nEmail the instructor at tdr@umass.edu for all course-related questions and requests. Every email must include [426] at the start of the subject line — for example, [426] Sprint 3 question. Emails without this prefix may be missed. See the full Communication section for guidance on what to include in your message.\\n\\nSpire\\nFinal grades will be posted to Canvas before they are submitted to Spire. You are expected to check your grades in both places to ensure that everything adds up. You are responsible for ensuring that your grades are accurate and that you have received credit for all assignments that you submitted by the posted deadline. If you notice any discrepancies, you should contact the course staff immediately.\\n\\nRequired Books, Equipment, and Technology\\nOne textbook, one container that carries the entire stack, and a machine capable of running it.\\n\\nThis course uses one textbook: Designing Distributed Systems, 2nd EditionLinks to an external site., by Brendan Burns (O'Reilly). You have free access to the book by logging in using your UMass credentials under “Other login options” and selecting “Affiliated with a school or institution?” The book frames containers as the vehicle for every pattern we study, and its treatment of patterns like the sidecar, the work queue, and dead letter queues is unusually thorough. Preparatory reading for the Knowledge Units draws directly from it. Beyond the textbook, everything you need to read is provided through as Knowledge Units, primers, and linked documentation. Where you need a reference for a specific tool, the course points you to that tool's official documentation.\\n\\nWhat this course also requires is a computer you control and that is capable of running a containerized development environment. You need a reasonably current laptop or desktop running macOS, Windows, or Linux, with enough memory and disk space to run Docker comfortably; eight gigabytes of RAM is a practical minimum and sixteen is more comfortable, along with several gigabytes of free disk space for container images and your project. A Chromebook or a tablet is not sufficient for this course, because neither can run the local development environment. If your only computer cannot meet these requirements, email the course staff at tdr@umass.edu during the first few days so we can help you find an alternative such as a loaner machine through the University. We will try, but we can't guarantee.\\n\\nNearly all of the software for this course is delivered through a single prepared development environment, a Dev Container that bundles the entire technology stack so you do not have to install or configure each piece by hand.\\n\\nDevelopment Environment\\nThis course uses development containers (devcontainers) to provide a uniform and consistent development environment for all students. Devcontainers are a way to package and distribute development environments using Docker containers. This allows you to have a consistent environment across different machines and operating systems, and ensures that you have all the necessary tools and dependencies installed.\\n\\nYou are not required to know much about Docker or devcontainers to begin, but you will need to have Docker installed on your machine, and over the course of the term you will come to understand containers deeply, since they are the central building block of the entire course. You will be required to use the devcontainer for all course-related work, including coding exercises, load tests, and the project.\\n\\nThe core software you will need to install is VS Code, Docker Desktop, and the VS Code Remote Containers extension. The devcontainer is configured to include the tools and dependencies for the course, including Node.js, npm, the Docker CLI and Compose, the k6 load testing tool, and Caddy as a reverse proxy and load balancer. Services and worker processes in this course are written in Node.js and JavaScript. You should not install this software right now, as you will be instructed on how to do so as part of the course setup unit.\\n\\nAssignments\\nWe use several different methods to scaffold your learning and assess your understanding of the material covered in this course. We outline the various methods and the kind of assessment below so you can better understand and plan your learning path. We categorize assignments as either being formative (F), summative (S), or a combination (FS). A purely formative assignment is designed to build your understanding, low stakes, and doesn't have any or very little impact on your grade. A summative assignment is designed to measure your understanding of the material. A combination of formative/summative contains aspects of low stakes assessment with measurement.\\n\\nAssessment Type\\tCount\\tWeight\\nExercises\\tShort practice exercises\\tF\\t>10\\t0%\\nParticipation\\tWeekly discussions and reflections\\t\\t6\\t5%\\nQuizzes\\t\\t\\t\\t20%\\nWeekly Quiz\\tF\\t6\\t\\nHomework\\t\\t\\t\\t30%\\nHomework\\tF\\t4\\t\\nSprints\\t\\t\\t\\t25%\\nSprint 1\\tFS\\t1\\t\\nSprint 2\\tFS\\t1\\t\\nSprint 3\\tFS\\t1\\t\\nSprint 4\\tFS\\t1\\t\\nSprint 5\\tS\\t1\\t\\nProject\\t\\t\\t\\t20%\\nGitHub Repository URL\\tS\\t1\\t\\nRecorded Video Demonstration\\tS\\t1\\t\\nProject Poster\\tS\\t1\\t\\nReflection\\tS\\t1\\t\\nExercises\\nPractice embedded in every unit, not graded, but expected.\\n\\nExercises are short activities built into each Knowledge Unit. They are not submitted and they do not count toward your grade. Many ask you to run a service under load with k6, observe a latency percentile or an error rate, and interpret what you see. The goal is practice: try something, get it wrong safely, and learn from it. You are expected to do the exercises; they exist to make the hands-on work in the Knowledge Units land rather than to generate a score.\\n\\nParticipation\\nSmall, low-stakes tasks spread across the term that keep you engaged with the course and your teammates-to-be.\\n\\nEach of the six weeks, Week 0 through Week 5, carries one participation task delivered natively on Canvas: Week 0 is a public discussion where you introduce yourself before project teams form; Weeks 1 through 5 are a short, private reflection survey connecting that week's Knowledge Units to your own experience. Both are graded on completion, not correctness or length, and both are generated directly from this repository rather than written by hand in Canvas. Together the six tasks make up five percent of your final grade.\\n\\nWeekly Quizzes\\nA timed, summative check on the week's material, taken at your own pace within 3 days after the week's completion.\\n\\nAfter each of the six content weeks you complete a timed quiz covering that week's Knowledge Units. Each quiz is multiple choice, approximately twenty questions, and you have forty-five minutes. You may take each quiz up to three times; your highest score is recorded. The quiz for the final week is cumulative across the full course. Together the six quizzes make up twenty percent of your final grade. Quizzes are available on Canvas.\\n\\nHomework\\nFour hands-on assignments that build the skills the project depends on.\\n\\nThere are four homework assignments across the term, one roughly every week and a half. Each is a hands-on task that involves creating parts of a simulated distributed system using real tools and services: k6 for load testing, JavaScript for building services, and existing services such as Caddy, Redis, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Prometheus, and Grafana. Homework is submitted through Gradescope and graded automatically against a rubric; you will see your score as soon as the autograder runs. Together the four assignments make up thirty percent of your final grade. Your scores from Gradescope will be periodically synced to Canvas.\\n\\nSprints\\nA simulated scalable system built incrementally: each sprint applies only what the previous week taught.\\n\\nThe Sprints are the team project itself, carried forward in stages rather than assembled at the end. Each sprint is due during the week after the Knowledge Units that inform it are covered, so the system grows in lockstep with the course material. You cannot design the full architecture at the start; you do not yet know the patterns. Instead the simulation is extended one layer at a time: Sprint 0 forms the team and stakes out a domain idea; Sprint 1 frames the scalability problem using the distributed systems vocabulary from Week Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing\nSchedule: Week 2 (Jul 13–17)\n\nGrade entry: Sprint 2 (half weight)\n\nPurpose\nWeek 1 introduced the vocabulary of distributed systems: why latency and reliability are the two properties you measure first, what idempotency means and why it matters when services retry, and how concurrency creates coordination problems that do not exist on a single machine. Sprint 1 asks your team to apply that vocabulary to your chosen domain.\n\nNo code is expected in this sprint. This is design thinking grounded in the concepts just studied. The deliverables are written artifacts that demonstrate you can reason about your system before you build it.\n\nDeliverables\nAll three deliverables are committed to the team repository under a docs/ directory and linked from the README.md.\n\n1. Refined project description (docs/PROJECT.md)\nWrite a short document called docs/PROJECT.md (roughly one page) that refines the domain paragraph from Sprint 0 into a complete project description. It must address:\n\nDomain: What kind of system is this, and who does it serve?\nScalability problem: What specific load or coordination challenge makes this domain require a scalable distributed web system? Be concrete: what happens when demand spikes, when a service goes down, or when data must be shared across multiple nodes?\nComputing for the Common Good framing: Who benefits when this system works correctly? Who is harmed when it fails or is slow? This framing should motivate the latency and reliability requirements you will define below.\n2. Initial service list (docs/SERVICES.md)\nWrite a document called docs/SERVICES.md containing a bulleted list of the services your simulation will likely include, with one sentence describing what each service does. This is a first guess and will change as you learn more patterns in subsequent weeks.\n\nEach service entry should name the service and describe its role in one sentence:\n\ninventory-service: Manages stock levels for each pantry location and accepts update and query requests from the coordinator.\ncoordinator-service: Routes incoming distribution requests to the appropriate pantry location based on availability.\nThe target is team_size + 1 custom services: 3 for 2-person teams, 4 for 3-person teams, and one more per additional member. The extra service beyond per-member ownership is a shared component — a coordinator, gateway, or API layer that multiple members contribute to. Infrastructure containers (Caddy, Redis, Prometheus, Grafana) do not count. This list is a projection — you will not build all services in Sprint 1. Sprint 2 begins with 2; Sprint 4 adds at least one more.\n\n3. Service level objectives (docs/SLO.md)\nWrite a document called docs/SLO.md. It should be roughly half a page and define the system's service level objectives: the specific, measurable targets that describe what \"good enough\" looks like for your domain.\n\nFor each service you listed above, define at least two SLOs:\n\nLatency SLO: A percentile target and a threshold. For example: \"The inventory lookup endpoint must respond within 500 ms at the 95th percentile.\" Tie the target to the domain: name who is waiting and what happens when the threshold is exceeded.\nReliability SLO: A success rate target. For example: \"The distribution request endpoint must succeed at least 99% of the time.\" Reason about what at-least-once and at-most-once delivery semantics mean for each operation: a failed lookup is annoying; a double-counted distribution is a data integrity problem.\nThese SLOs do not need to be precise engineering targets yet. They are commitments that will inform your design decisions in later sprints and that you will measure against in Sprint 3 and Sprint 5. Write them as if you intend to hold your system to them.\n\nGrading\nSprint 1 is worth 50 points. It counts as half a sprint grade toward the Sprints total (30%).\n\nTeam (30 pts)\nCriterion\tPoints\ndocs/PROJECT.md, docs/SERVICES.md, and docs/SLO.md all exist in a docs/ directory and are linked from README.md\t5\ndocs/PROJECT.md: names a specific domain and community (5 pts); describes a concrete scalability problem with at least one named condition (5 pts); CFTCG framing names specific beneficiaries and a specific harm — not a restatement of the domain (5 pts)\t15\ndocs/SERVICES.md: lists team_size + 1 services; every entry has a formatted name (service-name) and a one-sentence role description\t5\ndocs/SLO.md: contains at least one latency SLO and at least one reliability SLO\t5\nAward 0 pts for a docs/PROJECT.md criterion if the content is absent or entirely generic (e.g. \"high traffic\" without a named condition). For docs/SERVICES.md, deduct 1 pt per entry missing a name or description, down to 0.\n\nIndividual (20 pts)\nGraded per student based on commit history and service ownership.\n\nCriterion\tPoints\nStudent has authored at least one commit to any of the three Sprint 1 documents before the deadline\t5\ndocs/SERVICES.md includes a service this student owns (identifiable by commit authorship in Sprint 2 onward) with a formatted name and one-sentence description\t5\ndocs/SLO.md contains both a latency SLO and a reliability SLO for their service; latency SLO names an endpoint, a percentile, and a threshold with units\t10\nA latency SLO without a percentile scores 5/10.
