Sprint 4 adds an asynchronous processing path to your simulation and introduces controlled failures that demonstrate the system can degrade gracefully rather than collapse completely. The distinction between synchronous and asynchronous processing matters for your domain. Some operations in your system should complete before a response is sent; others, particularly those that are expensive, retryable, or durable, belong in a queue. Sprint 4 asks you to identify at least one operation in your domain that fits the async pattern and build it that way. ## Deliverables ### 1. At least one async processing path The producer and consumer of an async path are typically separate services. For teams of 3 or more, the worker is a new standalone service. For 2-person teams, the worker logic can be added to an existing service rather than creating a new one. Either way, this sprint advances your team closer to the target of team_size + 1 custom services. Add at least one work queue or pub/sub channel, using the same tools Unit 14 and Unit 15 built them with: RabbitMQ for a work queue, Kafka for pub/sub. The choice of pattern should be motivated by your domain: Work queue (RabbitMQ): Use when a task needs to be picked up and processed by exactly one worker, and the result does not need to be returned to the original caller synchronously. Example: sending a notification after a distribution request is logged, or recalculating inventory totals after a batch update. Pub/sub (Kafka): Use when multiple downstream services need to react to the same event independently. Example: broadcasting an alert when a pantry location's stock drops below a threshold, so both the coordinator service and the notification service respond to the same event. The async path must be observable: log when a message is enqueued and when a worker picks it up and processes it. Add a rabbitmq or kafka service to your docker-compose.yml. This is new infrastructure, not the Redis cache from Sprint 3, which stays a cache. Give the broker its own healthcheck, matching the setup from Unit 14 or Unit 15, so any service that depends on it can use depends_on with condition: service_healthy rather than just waiting for the container to start. ### 2. Health check endpoints on all services Add a GET /health endpoint to every service in your system. The endpoint must return a JSON response indicating the service is running: { "status": "ok" } Wire these health check endpoints into the Docker Compose healthcheck configuration for each service so that Docker knows when a service is ready to receive traffic. Services that depend on other services must use depends_on with a condition: service_healthy check. ### 3. At least one scripted failure scenario Add a mechanism to one of your services that allows it to be made to fail or slow down on demand. This could be an environment variable that toggles a fault injection mode, an endpoint that forces the service to return errors or inject extra latency, or a script that kills a worker process. Write a short description (roughly half a page) committed to the repository as results/sprint-4-failure.md. The description must explain: What the failure scenario is How to trigger it How the system responds (does it degrade gracefully, queue up work, return errors, or something else?) What a real system would do differently in production ### 4. Updated system diagram (`docs/SERVICES.md`) Update the diagram in docs/SERVICES.md to add the async path: the producer, the RabbitMQ- or Kafka-backed queue or pub/sub channel, and the consumer or worker. As with Sprint 3, this should be the complete system diagram, not just the new pieces. ## Example Repository Structure This sprint adds the async path. For teams of three or more, the worker is a new standalone service and gets its own top-level directory, shown below as alert-worker/. For two-person teams, the worker logic can instead live inside an existing service’s code rather than a new directory. Either way, this sprint also adds results/sprint-4-failure.md alongside the load test summary from Sprint 3. 426-project-pantry-network/ ├── README.md ├── docker-compose.yml ├── docs/ │ ├── PROJECT.md │ ├── SERVICES.md │ └── SLO.md ├── results/ │ ├── sprint-3-load-test.md │ └── sprint-4-failure.md ├── load-tests/ │ └── sprint-3-load.js ├── caddy/ │ └── Caddyfile ├── inventory-service/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ ├── package.json │ └── src/ │ └── index.js ├── coordinator-service/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ ├── package.json │ └── src/ │ └── index.js ├── coordinator-sidecar/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ ├── package.json │ └── src/ │ └── index.js └── alert-worker/ ├── Dockerfile ├── package.json └── src/ └── index.js Health check endpoints do not add new files here since they are additions to each existing service’s own code and to the healthcheck blocks already in docker-compose.yml. ## Checking Your Work You'll know this sprint is complete when: docker compose up starts all services, including the RabbitMQ or Kafka broker, and all health checks pass. Submit the repository URL through Canvas by the Sprint 4 deadline. # 426-project--Team-9- Blue Light ## Team Roster | GitHub Username | UMass Email | |-----------------|-------------| |austinfairbanks|afairbanks@umass.edu| |Dos0n|bdo@umass.edu |ShriRadhakrishnan1|sradhakrishn@umass.edu| | | | ## Domain Description Our system simulates a distributed mobile blue-light emergency response network that routes emergency requests across multiple regions, including university campuses, transit hubs, stadiums, shopping centers, and other public venues. Users submit requests through a mobile application, and the system is responsible for determining the appropriate response, routing the request to the correct regional service, and keeping responders and users updated throughout the incident. A single server becomes insufficient when the system experiences sudden spikes in demand, such as during large public events, severe weather, or multiple simultaneous emergencies. During these periods, the system must rapidly process incoming requests, determine user locations, prioritize incidents based on severity, and notify the appropriate local responders without introducing delays. Distributing the workload across multiple servers allows the system to remain responsive and available even under heavy load. From a Computing for the Common Good perspective, a reliable emergency response system directly improves public safety. Students, commuters, event attendees, employees, and other members of the public all benefit from fast and dependable access to emergency services. When the system performs well, people receive timely police, medical, security, or crisis-response assistance. When it fails or becomes overloaded, delayed or misrouted requests can increase response times and potentially place people in dangerous situations. Each response exposes `servedBy` so replica selection is observable. `GET /route` is Redis-cached: the cache key normalizes `latitude`/`longitude` to six decimal places and combines it with `emergencyType`, so an exact repeated lookup (e.g. many requests during an event at the Mullins Center) becomes a cache hit shared across all three replicas, without merging distinct nearby venues into the same key. Each response's `cache` field reports `"HIT"` or `"MISS"`, and every replica logs the cache key and outcome for each request. If Redis is unreachable, a lookup falls back to computing the route directly rather than failing the request. - `regional-routing-load-balancer`: Caddy load balancer that checks each routing replica's `/health` endpoint and distributes requests across healthy replicas using round-robin selection. - `redis`: Shared Redis cache used by all three `regional-routing-service` replicas for `GET /route` results, keyed by rounded location and emergency type with a 30-second TTL (`ROUTE_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS`). - `regional-routing-ambassador` (Owner: `@ShriRadhakrishnan1`): Ambassador proxy in front of the routing load balancer; forwards lookups, applies timeout/retry under load, and logs each upstream attempt. - `incident-ambassador` (Owner: `@Dos0n`): Ambassador proxy in front of `incident-service`; forwards `GET` and `POST` requests, retries safe (`GET`/`HEAD`) requests on timeout or 5xx, never retries `POST /incidents` to avoid duplicate incident creation, applies a simulated request-inspection delay via `setTimeout` before replying, and logs each upstream attempt. - `responder-dispatch-service` (Owner: `@Dos0n`): Simulates notifying and assigning the appropriate security, medical, police, or crisis-response team via `POST /dispatches` (body: `incidentId`, `teamId`), tracks dispatch status through `GET /dispatches/:dispatchId` and `PATCH /dispatches/:dispatchId/status`, and lists the response-team roster via `GET /teams`. ## Current Sprint 4 Container Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR client[Phone / Web Client] subgraph compose[Docker Compose] incident[incident-service

GET /incidents/:incidentId| incidentAmbassador incidentAmbassador -->|Forward through Compose DNS| incident incident -->|Persistent job after valid POST /incidents| rabbitmq rabbitmq -->|Deliver to one consumer| notificationWorker client -->|GET /route
GET /regions| routingAmbassador routingAmbassador -->|One stable upstream| routingLoadBalancer routingLoadBalancer -->|Healthy upstream| routingA routingLoadBalancer -->|Healthy upstream| routingB routingLoadBalancer -->|Healthy upstream| routingC routingA -->|Cache GET/SET on /route| redis routingB -->|Cache GET/SET on /route| redis routingC -->|Cache GET/SET on /route| redis client -->|POST /dispatches
GET /dispatches/:dispatchId
GET /teams| dispatch ``` The primary HTTP services remain separate client-facing paths in Sprint 4; `incident-service`, `regional-routing-service`, and `responder-dispatch-service` do not call each other directly. A valid incident creation now branches into asynchronous work: `incident-service` publishes a persistent job to RabbitMQ and returns after broker confirmation without waiting for `emergency-notification-worker` to process it. RabbitMQ holds jobs while the worker is unavailable and redelivers a job when a worker disconnects before acknowledging it. Two primary services remain reachable through their observable ambassador containers: `incident-ambassador` is the public path to `incident-service`, and `regional-routing-ambassador` reaches the routing replicas through Caddy. `responder-dispatch-service` is reached directly, with no ambassador in front of it. Redis remains exclusively the shared routing cache and does not carry Sprint 4 notification work. The regional routing service is replicated because routing is naturally stateless. Every replica receives the location and emergency type, loads the same synthetic regional map, and computes the answer independently. No request depends on mutable state held by a particular replica. Caddy can therefore send a request to any healthy replica and remove a failed replica without changing routing results. ## Sprint 3 Routing Replication and Caddy Verification Run these commands from the Gantry devcontainer. Start the complete system and validate Caddy's loaded configuration: ```bash docker compose up --build -d docker compose exec regional-routing-load-balancer \ caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile docker compose ps ``` Send nine requests through the public routing ambassador. All three `servedBy` values should appear: ```bash for request_number in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9; do curl -fsS \ 'http://localhost:3002/route?latitude=42.3868&longitude=-72.5301&emergencyType=medical' \ | jq -r '.servedBy' done ``` Stop replica B, wait longer than Caddy's two-second health-check interval, and repeat the requests. Every request should still succeed, and only replicas A and C should appear: ```bash docker compose stop regional-routing-service-b sleep 3 for request_number in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -fsS \ 'http://localhost:3002/route?latitude=42.3868&longitude=-72.5301&emergencyType=medical' \ | jq -r '.servedBy' done ``` Restore replica B and confirm that the full system returns to a healthy state: ```bash docker compose start regional-routing-service-b docker compose ps ``` Regression-check the other existing service paths: ```bash curl -fsS http://localhost:3003/health | jq curl -fsS http://localhost:3004/health | jq ``` ### Recorded Validation: July 30, 2026 The complete system built and started with `docker compose up --build -d`, and every service with a configured health check reported healthy. Some operations in your system should complete before a response is sent; others, particularly those that are expensive, retryable, or durable, belong in a queue. Sprint 4 asks you to identify at least one operation in your domain that fits the async pattern and build it that way.\n\n## Deliverables\n### 1. At least one async processing path\nThe producer and consumer of an async path are typically separate services. For teams of 3 or more, the worker is a new standalone service. The choice of pattern should be motivated by your domain:\n\nWork queue (RabbitMQ): Use when a task needs to be picked up and processed by exactly one worker, and the result does not need to be returned to the original caller synchronously. Example: sending a notification after a distribution request is logged, or recalculating inventory totals after a batch update.\nPub/sub (Kafka): Use when multiple downstream services need to react to the same event independently. Example: broadcasting an alert when a pantry location's stock drops below a threshold, so both the coordinator service and the notification service respond to the same event.\nThe async path must be observable: log when a message is enqueued and when a worker picks it up and processes it. Add a rabbitmq or kafka service to your docker-compose.yml. This is new infrastructure, not the Redis cache from Sprint 3, which stays a cache. Give the broker its own healthcheck, matching the setup from Unit 14 or Unit 15, so any service that depends on it can use depends_on with condition: service_healthy rather than just waiting for the container to start.\n\n### 2. Description The web has become a large and complex area for application development. Access to an abundance of open source languages, libraries, and frameworks has led to the quick and easy construction of a variety of applications with several moving parts working in coordination to present to the user the illusion of a single program. In reality, web applications are extremely difficult to get right. They involve a large collection of coordinated services, multiple databases, complicated user interfaces, security and performance issues, and ever changing third party services, spread across physical and virtual machines. These complications are further stressed by the large number of concurrent users that access these applications every second. This course investigates several well known web-based applications and the technology and software architecture used to scale them. We will also study specific topics related to scalability in software design in the context of web application architecture. This course is hands-on and heavily project-based; students will build, monitor, and load test a distributed system composed of coordinated services. This course counts as an Elective for the CS and INFORM Majors. This course is concept-first and experiential. You will build and break real scalable systems before we put names to the patterns you discover. The vocabulary of the field, sidecars, ambassadors, sharding, scatter/gather, comes after you have already felt why each pattern exists. Staff Instructor: Tim Richards Email: tdr@umass.edu Office Hours: By appointment, via Google Meet Teaching Assistant: Miles (Mingzhe) Li Email: mingzhel@umass.edu Learning Objectives By the end of this course, students will be able to: Configure and use a devcontainer-based development environment with Docker and VS Code for a reproducible, team-consistent workspace. Explain the core properties of distributed systems, including latency, reliability, idempotency, and delivery semantics, and reason about the trade-offs between them. Containerize an application with Docker and orchestrate multiple coordinated services with Docker Compose. Apply single-node patterns, including the sidecar, ambassador, and adapter patterns, to extend services without modifying them. Design and reason about serving patterns, including replication, caching, sharding with consistent hashing, and scatter/gather. Measure system behavior under load using k6, and interpret latency percentiles, throughput, and error rates. Build event-driven and queue-based systems, including work queues, pub/sub pipelines, and dead letter queues. Reason about distributed coordination, including locks, leases, ownership election, and concurrent data manipulation. Instrument a system for observability using structured logging, metrics, and tracing. Diagnose common distributed failure patterns, including thundering herd, versioning errors, and cascading failure. Use Git and GitHub for version control, branching, and pull request workflows on a shared team repository. Plan, build, and present a complete, scalable web system simulation as a team. Time Commitment A three credit course does not get smaller when you compress it into six weeks; it gets denser. Plan for roughly twenty-two to twenty-three hours a week. UMass Amherst defines course workload by a standard credit hour rule. The guiding rule is forty five hours of work per semester for each unit of credit, on the assumption that each credit hour generates two hours of assigned work for every hour of in class contact. By that rule a three credit course represents about one hundred thirty five hours of total work, and the University expects the total workload for a three credit course to be at least 135 hours. That total is fixed. It is the same whether the course runs across a full semester or across a summer. What changes is how those hours are distributed. In a normal fifteen week semester, one hundred thirty five hours works out to about nine hours per week. This section is taught asynchronously over six weeks, so the same one hundred thirty five hours are compressed into roughly six weeks of effort, which comes to about twenty-two to twenty-three hours per week. There is no reduction in scope to go with the shorter calendar; you are doing a full three credit course in forty percent of the usual time, so the weekly pace is about two and a half times what the same course would demand in the fall or spring. Twenty-two hours a week is a serious commitment, and you should plan your summer around that reality. Spread across six working days it is just under four hours a day. Because each day's material builds directly on the day before, and because this is a systems course where one misconfigured service can block everything downstream, the work does not compress well into a weekend burst. Students who treat this as a part time effort fall behind quickly, and in a six week term there is very little room to recover. For that reason I strongly advise against pairing this course with another demanding summer course or with full time employment. If your situation makes twenty-two hours a week difficult, email me at tdr@umass.edu before the term begins so we can be honest about whether the timing works for you. To make the number concrete, your weekly hours go toward the same components described elsewhere in this syllabus: working through several Knowledge Units, since the eighteen KUs are spread across the six weeks, including their preparatory reading, the activity, and the exercises; and steadily advancing your team's sprint project, which on its own accounts for a substantial share of your time over the term. The weekly quizzes are the clearest early signal of whether you are keeping pace. If you find yourself consistently spending far more than this, or far less and still finishing everything, let me know, because that is useful feedback on the course and may also be a sign we should look at how you are approaching the work. Sprints A simulated scalable system built incrementally: each sprint applies only what the previous week taught. The Sprints are the team project itself, carried forward in stages rather than assembled at the end. Each sprint is due during the week after the Knowledge Units that inform it are covered, so the system grows in lockstep with the course material. You cannot design the full architecture at the start; you do not yet know the patterns. Instead the simulation is extended one layer at a time: Sprint 0 forms the team and stakes out a domain idea; Sprint 1 frames the scalability problem using the distributed systems vocabulary from Week 1; Sprint 2 produces the first containerized services running under Docker Compose; Sprint 3 adds serving patterns (replication, caching, load balancing) and a first k6 load test; Sprint 4 introduces async processing and resilience; and Sprint 5 instruments the system with observability, runs a final load test, and delivers the four capstone artifacts. The system you build throughout is a simulation: data is synthetic, latency is injected, failures are scripted, and computation is modeled. This is a deliberate choice, not a shortcut. Building a production system from scratch in six weeks is not realistic, and the goal of this course is not deployment; it is design, engineering, and measurement. Simulation lets you practice every pattern the course covers, instrument and break the system intentionally, and measure it under realistic load, without the operational complexity of real data pipelines or live traffic. The skills you develop, structuring services, reasoning about coordination, interpreting latency percentiles, are the same ones a team would use on a real system. Sprints introduce no new instruction. They are where you apply the current state of the Knowledge Units to the simulated system your team is building. Teams are assigned by the instructor and are 2–3 members for this six-week section. Because this course has no separate lab sequence, the professional workflow skills that labs would otherwise carry, clean commits, pull requests, code review, conflict resolution, are practiced and assessed directly inside the sprints. Because impressions are unreliable, your sprint contribution is assessed against objective GitHub evidence, your commits, the pull requests you authored and reviewed, and the merge history, rather than against anyone's sense of who did what. Sprints 0 and 1 are half-weight (each worth half a full sprint); Sprints 2, 3, and 4 are full-weight. Sprint 5 is graded as the Project Final (20%) rather than as part of the Sprints category. Sprint 0: Team Formation and Project Concept Week 0 covered setting up the development environment and GitHub. Sprint 0 is about getting organized as a team and staking out a project idea while that setup is still fresh. No architecture decisions are required yet; students do not have the vocabulary for them. Shared GitHub repository created with all team members added as collaborators README with team roster A short paragraph describing the domain the team wants to simulate and a first guess at what makes it interesting from a scalability standpoint: what would a real system in this domain need to handle that a single server could not? Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing Week 1 covered why distributed systems exist, the core trade-offs between latency and reliability, and the semantics of idempotency and message delivery. Sprint 1 asks the team to apply that vocabulary to their chosen domain. No code is expected yet; this is design thinking grounded in the concepts just studied. A refined project description: what domain, what scalability problem, and why this problem is meaningful (the Computing for the Common Good framing) An initial list of services the simulation might include, with one sentence on what each does; this is a first guess, not a commitment, and it will evolve as more patterns are introduced A short statement of the system's latency and reliability requirements: what does "fast enough" mean for this domain, and what happens if a component fails? Sprint 2: First Containerized System Week 2 covered Docker fundamentals, Docker Compose, the sidecar pattern, and the ambassador pattern. Sprint 2 is the first time the team writes code. The goal is a multi-service simulation running under Docker Compose with at least one pattern from Week 2 applied. At least two services containerized and running under Docker Compose, each with its own HTTP endpoint returning domain-relevant simulated data At least one sidecar or ambassador pattern applied alongside a primary service as a separate container A docker-compose.yml committed to the repository that starts the whole system with a single command Sprint 3: Serving Patterns and First Load Test Week 3 covered the adapter pattern, replicated services with load balancing and caching, sharded services, and scatter/gather. Sprint 3 extends the existing simulation with at least one serving pattern and adds the first measurement. At least one service running with multiple replicas behind Caddy as a load balancer A caching layer (Redis) integrated into at least one service path, with simulated cache hits and misses A k6 load test script that exercises the replicated service, with a written summary of the p50, p95, and p99 latency results Sprint 4: Async Processing and Resilience Week 4 covered resilience and failure modes, event-driven processing, work queue systems, and pub/sub pipelines. Sprint 4 adds an asynchronous processing path to the simulation and introduces controlled failures to show the system can handle them. At least one async processing path: a work queue or pub/sub channel backed by Redis Health check endpoints on all services, wired into Docker Compose healthcheck configuration At least one scripted failure scenario: a service that can be made to fail or slow down, with a brief written description of how the system responds Sprint 5: Observability, Final Measurement, and Delivery Week 5 covered coordinated batch processing, ownership election, and observability. Sprint 5 instruments the simulation, produces the final load test evidence, and assembles the four capstone deliverables. Prometheus metrics exposed by all custom services, scraped by a Prometheus instance defined in Docker Compose A Grafana dashboard showing at minimum: request rate, error rate, and p95 latency for the main service path Structured JSON log output from all custom services A final k6 load test with a written interpretation: what the latency distribution shows, how it compares to the Sprint 3 baseline, and where the bottleneck appears to be GitHub repository URL: code committed, README complete, system starts with a single command Recorded video demonstration (10 minutes or less): the system starting with docker compose up, at least one endpoint responding, the Grafana dashboard live during a k6 load test, and an explanation of one design decision and its trade-off Project poster: the problem, the architecture, the patterns demonstrated, and the key trade-offs, formatted as a one-page PDF Individual reflection: submitted separately by each team member covering what you contributed, what you learned, and what you would do differently Project The capstone: a simulated scalable system that demonstrates the design, engineering, and measurement skills of the course. The Project is the summative destination the entire course is aimed at, and in this section it is fully asynchronous. Working in a team, you choose a problem domain in the spirit of Computing for the Common Good and design a meaningful but achievable scalable application. You then build a simulation of that application: services that model realistic behavior using synthetic data, injected latency, and scripted failures, orchestrated with Docker Compose and measured under load with k6. The simulation is not a stripped-down version of a real system; it is the full architecture, with coordinated services, asynchronous pipelines, caching, and observability, implemented in a way that makes every pattern visible and every failure intentional. The goal is to demonstrate that you understand how such a system is designed, how its components interact, and how its behavior changes under load. You submit four deliverables: the source code in your shared GitHub repository, a recorded video walkthrough of the running system, a poster presenting the problem, the architecture, and the trade-offs you made, and an individual written reflection from each team member on their own contribution and what they learned. You are assessed on collaborative practice, on meeting the sprint deliverable deadlines that pace the project from Week 1, and on professional conduct throughout, with contribution again read from objective GitHub evidence and the grade trajectory-weighted across the term. Deployment to a public host is not required and is not taught here; the destination is a complete, multi-service simulation running under Docker Compose in the dev container and demonstrated on video. Description The web has become a large and complex area for application development. Access to an abundance of open source languages, libraries, and frameworks has led to the quick and easy construction of a variety of applications with several moving parts working in coordination to present to the user the illusion of a single program. In reality, web applications are extremely difficult to get right. They involve a large collection of coordinated services, multiple databases, complicated user interfaces, security and performance issues, and ever changing third party services, spread across physical and virtual machines. These complications are further stressed by the large number of concurrent users that access these applications every second. This course investigates several well known web-based applications and the technology and software architecture used to scale them. We will also study specific topics related to scalability in software design in the context of web application architecture. This course is hands-on and heavily project-based; students will build, monitor, and load test a distributed system composed of coordinated services. This course counts as an Elective for the CS and INFORM Majors. This course is concept-first and experiential. You will build and break real scalable systems before we put names to the patterns you discover. The vocabulary of the field, sidecars, ambassadors, sharding, scatter/gather, comes after you have already felt why each pattern exists. Staff Instructor: Tim Richards Email: tdr@umass.edu Office Hours: By appointment, via Google Meet Teaching Assistant: Miles (Mingzhe) Li Email: mingzhel@umass.edu Learning Objectives By the end of this course, students will be able to: Configure and use a devcontainer-based development environment with Docker and VS Code for a reproducible, team-consistent workspace. Explain the core properties of distributed systems, including latency, reliability, idempotency, and delivery semantics, and reason about the trade-offs between them. Containerize an application with Docker and orchestrate multiple coordinated services with Docker Compose. Apply single-node patterns, including the sidecar, ambassador, and adapter patterns, to extend services without modifying them. Design and reason about serving patterns, including replication, caching, sharding with consistent hashing, and scatter/gather. Measure system behavior under load using k6, and interpret latency percentiles, throughput, and error rates. Build event-driven and queue-based systems, including work queues, pub/sub pipelines, and dead letter queues. Reason about distributed coordination, including locks, leases, ownership election, and concurrent data manipulation. Instrument a system for observability using structured logging, metrics, and tracing. Diagnose common distributed failure patterns, including thundering herd, versioning errors, and cascading failure. Use Git and GitHub for version control, branching, and pull request workflows on a shared team repository. Plan, build, and present a complete, scalable web system simulation as a team. Time Commitment A three credit course does not get smaller when you compress it into six weeks; it gets denser. Plan for roughly twenty-two to twenty-three hours a week. UMass Amherst defines course workload by a standard credit hour rule. The guiding rule is forty five hours of work per semester for each unit of credit, on the assumption that each credit hour generates two hours of assigned work for every hour of in class contact. By that rule a three credit course represents about one hundred thirty five hours of total work, and the University expects the total workload for a three credit course to be at least 135 hours. That total is fixed. It is the same whether the course runs across a full semester or across a summer. What changes is how those hours are distributed. In a normal fifteen week semester, one hundred thirty five hours works out to about nine hours per week. This section is taught asynchronously over six weeks, so the same one hundred thirty five hours are compressed into roughly six weeks of effort, which comes to about twenty-two to twenty-three hours per week. There is no reduction in scope to go with the shorter calendar; you are doing a full three credit course in forty percent of the usual time, so the weekly pace is about two and a half times what the same course would demand in the fall or spring. Twenty-two hours a week is a serious commitment, and you should plan your summer around that reality. Spread across six working days it is just under four hours a day. Because each day's material builds directly on the day before, and because this is a systems course where one misconfigured service can block everything downstream, the work does not compress well into a weekend burst. Students who treat this as a part time effort fall behind quickly, and in a six week term there is very little room to recover. For that reason I strongly advise against pairing this course with another demanding summer course or with full time employment. If your situation makes twenty-two hours a week difficult, email me at tdr@umass.edu before the term begins so we can be honest about whether the timing works for you. To make the number concrete, your weekly hours go toward the same components described elsewhere in this syllabus: working through several Knowledge Units, since the eighteen KUs are spread across the six weeks, including their preparatory reading, the activity, and the exercises; and steadily advancing your team's sprint project, which on its own accounts for a substantial share of your time over the term. The weekly quizzes are the clearest early signal of whether you are keeping pace. If you find yourself consistently spending far more than this, or far less and still finishing everything, let me know, because that is useful feedback on the course and may also be a sign we should look at how you are approaching the work. Sprints A simulated scalable system built incrementally: each sprint applies only what the previous week taught. The Sprints are the team project itself, carried forward in stages rather than assembled at the end. Each sprint is due during the week after the Knowledge Units that inform it are covered, so the system grows in lockstep with the course material. You cannot design the full architecture at the start; you do not yet know the patterns. Instead the simulation is extended one layer at a time: Sprint 0 forms the team and stakes out a domain idea; Sprint 1 frames the scalability problem using the distributed systems vocabulary from Week 1; Sprint 2 produces the first containerized services running under Docker Compose; Sprint 3 adds serving patterns (replication, caching, load balancing) and a first k6 load test; Sprint 4 introduces async processing and resilience; and Sprint 5 instruments the system with observability, runs a final load test, and delivers the four capstone artifacts. The system you build throughout is a simulation: data is synthetic, latency is injected, failures are scripted, and computation is modeled. This is a deliberate choice, not a shortcut. Simulation lets you practice every pattern the course covers, instrument and break the system intentionally, and measure it under realistic load, without the operational complexity of real data pipelines or live traffic. The Project is the summative destination the entire course is aimed at, and in this section it is fully asynchronous. Working in a team, you choose a problem domain in the spirit of Computing for the Common Good and design a meaningful but achievable scalable application. You then build a simulation of that application: services that model realistic behavior using synthetic data, injected latency, and scripted failures, orchestrated with Docker Compose and measured under load with k6. The simulation is not a stripped-down version of a real system; it is the full architecture, with coordinated services, asynchronous pipelines, caching, and observability, implemented in a way that makes every pattern visible and every failure intentional. The goal is to demonstrate that you understand how such a system is designed, how its components interact, and how its behavior changes under load. You submit four deliverables: the source code in your shared GitHub repository, a recorded video walkthrough of the running system, a poster presenting the problem, the architecture, and the trade-offs you made, and an individual written reflection from each team member on their own contribution and what they learned. Description The web has become a large and complex area for application development. Access to an abundance of open source languages, libraries, and frameworks has led to the quick and easy construction of a variety of applications with several moving parts working in coordination to present to the user the illusion of a single program. In reality, web applications are extremely difficult to get right. They involve a large collection of coordinated services, multiple databases, complicated user interfaces, security and performance issues, and ever changing third party services, spread across physical and virtual machines. These complications are further stressed by the large number of concurrent users that access these applications every second. This course investigates several well known web-based applications and the technology and software architecture used to scale them. We will also study specific topics related to scalability in software design in the context of web application architecture. This course is hands-on and heavily project-based; students will build, monitor, and load test a distributed system composed of coordinated services. This course counts as an Elective for the CS and INFORM Majors. This course is concept-first and experiential. You will build and break real scalable systems before we put names to the patterns you discover. The vocabulary of the field, sidecars, ambassadors, sharding, scatter/gather, comes after you have already felt why each pattern exists. Staff Instructor: Tim Richards Email: tdr@umass.edu Office Hours: By appointment, via Google Meet Teaching Assistant: Miles (Mingzhe) Li Email: mingzhel@umass.edu Learning Objectives By the end of this course, students will be able to: Configure and use a devcontainer-based development environment with Docker and VS Code for a reproducible, team-consistent workspace. Explain the core properties of distributed systems, including latency, reliability, idempotency, and delivery semantics, and reason about the trade-offs between them. Containerize an application with Docker and orchestrate multiple coordinated services with Docker Compose. Apply single-node patterns, including the sidecar, ambassador, and adapter patterns, to extend services without modifying them. Design and reason about serving patterns, including replication, caching, sharding with consistent hashing, and scatter/gather. Measure system behavior under load using k6, and interpret latency percentiles, throughput, and error rates. Build event-driven and queue-based systems, including work queues, pub/sub pipelines, and dead letter queues. Reason about distributed coordination, including locks, leases, ownership election, and concurrent data manipulation. Instrument a system for observability using structured logging, metrics, and tracing. Diagnose common distributed failure patterns, including thundering herd, versioning errors, and cascading failure. Use Git and GitHub for version control, branching, and pull request workflows on a shared team repository. Plan, build, and present a complete, scalable web system simulation as a team. Time Commitment A three credit course does not get smaller when you compress it into six weeks; it gets denser. Plan for roughly twenty-two to twenty-three hours a week. UMass Amherst defines course workload by a standard credit hour rule. The guiding rule is forty five hours of work per semester for each unit of credit, on the assumption that each credit hour generates two hours of assigned work for every hour of in class contact. By that rule a three credit course represents about one hundred thirty five hours of total work, and the University expects the total workload for a three credit course to be at least 135 hours. That total is fixed. It is the same whether the course runs across a full semester or across a summer. What changes is how those hours are distributed. In a normal fifteen week semester, one hundred thirty five hours works out to about nine hours per week. This section is taught asynchronously over six weeks, so the same one hundred thirty five hours are compressed into roughly six weeks of effort, which comes to about twenty-two to twenty-three hours per week. There is no reduction in scope to go with the shorter calendar; you are doing a full three credit course in forty percent of the usual time, so the weekly pace is about two and a half times what the same course would demand in the fall or spring. Twenty-two hours a week is a serious commitment, and you should plan your summer around that reality. Spread across six working days it is just under four hours a day. Because each day's material builds directly on the day before, and because this is a systems course where one misconfigured service can block everything downstream, the work does not compress well into a weekend burst. Students who treat this as a part time effort fall behind quickly, and in a six week term there is very little room to recover. For that reason I strongly advise against pairing this course with another demanding summer course or with full time employment. If your situation makes twenty-two hours a week difficult, email me at tdr@umass.edu before the term begins so we can be honest about whether the timing works for you. To make the number concrete, your weekly hours go toward the same components described elsewhere in this syllabus: working through several Knowledge Units, since the eighteen KUs are spread across the six weeks, including their preparatory reading, the activity, and the exercises; and steadily advancing your team's sprint project, which on its own accounts for a substantial share of your time over the term. The weekly quizzes are the clearest early signal of whether you are keeping pace. If you find yourself consistently spending far more than this, or far less and still finishing everything, let me know, because that is useful feedback on the course and may also be a sign we should look at how you are approaching the work. Course Structure Synopsis Asynchronous Delivery This course is offered in an online, asynchronous format. All course materials will be available online on the course website. You are expected to engage with the content and complete assignments on your own schedule within the given deadlines. This course is designed to be experiential, meaning that you will learn by doing, and the course structure is built around active participation and hands-on activities. Knowledge Units (KUs) The primary way in which learning takes place is through knowledge units (KUs). Each KU is a self-contained module that includes preparatory reading, hands-on activities, and exercises. You are expected to complete each KU in order, as they build upon one another. The course is deliberately concept-first: most units ask you to build or observe something before the underlying pattern is named, so that the name lands on an experience you already have rather than on an abstraction. Each KU will have a set of activities that you must complete, including coding and load-testing exercises. Canvas Canvas is where you will find links to all of the course material. The syllabus and schedule can be found on Canvas. All assignments will be posted on Canvas. Grades will be posted to Canvas. Announcements will be posted on Canvas. If in doubt, go to Canvas to find what you are looking for and follow links from there. Gradescope Homework assignments are submitted through Gradescope and graded automatically. When you submit, an autograder runs your code against a test suite and reports a score immediately; you do not have to wait for manual review to see how you did. If a test fails, the output includes enough information to diagnose and fix the issue before the deadline. You may resubmit as many times as you like before the deadline, and only your final submission is graded. Gradescope is accessible through Canvas. Communication Email the instructor at tdr@umass.edu for all course-related questions and requests. Every email must include [426] at the start of the subject line — for example, [426] Sprint 3 question. Emails without this prefix may be missed. See the full Communication section for guidance on what to include in your message. Spire Final grades will be posted to Canvas before they are submitted to Spire. You are expected to check your grades in both places to ensure that everything adds up. You are responsible for ensuring that your grades are accurate and that you have received credit for all assignments that you submitted by the posted deadline. If you notice any discrepancies, you should contact the course staff immediately. Required Books, Equipment, and Technology One textbook, one container that carries the entire stack, and a machine capable of running it. This course uses one textbook: Designing Distributed Systems, 2nd EditionLinks to an external site., by Brendan Burns (O'Reilly). You have free access to the book by logging in using your UMass credentials under “Other login options” and selecting “Affiliated with a school or institution?” The book frames containers as the vehicle for every pattern we study, and its treatment of patterns like the sidecar, the work queue, and dead letter queues is unusually thorough. Preparatory reading for the Knowledge Units draws directly from it. Beyond the textbook, everything you need to read is provided through as Knowledge Units, primers, and linked documentation. Where you need a reference for a specific tool, the course points you to that tool's official documentation. What this course also requires is a computer you control and that is capable of running a containerized development environment. You need a reasonably current laptop or desktop running macOS, Windows, or Linux, with enough memory and disk space to run Docker comfortably; eight gigabytes of RAM is a practical minimum and sixteen is more comfortable, along with several gigabytes of free disk space for container images and your project. A Chromebook or a tablet is not sufficient for this course, because neither can run the local development environment. If your only computer cannot meet these requirements, email the course staff at tdr@umass.edu during the first few days so we can help you find an alternative such as a loaner machine through the University. We will try, but we can't guarantee. Nearly all of the software for this course is delivered through a single prepared development environment, a Dev Container that bundles the entire technology stack so you do not have to install or configure each piece by hand. Development Environment This course uses development containers (devcontainers) to provide a uniform and consistent development environment for all students. Devcontainers are a way to package and distribute development environments using Docker containers. This allows you to have a consistent environment across different machines and operating systems, and ensures that you have all the necessary tools and dependencies installed. You are not required to know much about Docker or devcontainers to begin, but you will need to have Docker installed on your machine, and over the course of the term you will come to understand containers deeply, since they are the central building block of the entire course. You will be required to use the devcontainer for all course-related work, including coding exercises, load tests, and the project. The core software you will need to install is VS Code, Docker Desktop, and the VS Code Remote Containers extension. The devcontainer is configured to include the tools and dependencies for the course, including Node.js, npm, the Docker CLI and Compose, the k6 load testing tool, and Caddy as a reverse proxy and load balancer. Services and worker processes in this course are written in Node.js and JavaScript. You should not install this software right now, as you will be instructed on how to do so as part of the course setup unit. Assignments We use several different methods to scaffold your learning and assess your understanding of the material covered in this course. We outline the various methods and the kind of assessment below so you can better understand and plan your learning path. We categorize assignments as either being formative (F), summative (S), or a combination (FS). A purely formative assignment is designed to build your understanding, low stakes, and doesn't have any or very little impact on your grade. A summative assignment is designed to measure your understanding of the material. A combination of formative/summative contains aspects of low stakes assessment with measurement. Participation Small, low-stakes tasks spread across the term that keep you engaged with the course and your teammates-to-be. Each of the six weeks, Week 0 through Week 5, carries one participation task delivered natively on Canvas: Week 0 is a public discussion where you introduce yourself before project teams form; Weeks 1 through 5 are a short, private reflection survey connecting that week's Knowledge Units to your own experience. Both are graded on completion, not correctness or length, and both are generated directly from this repository rather than written by hand in Canvas. Together the six tasks make up five percent of your final grade. Weekly Quizzes A timed, summative check on the week's material, taken at your own pace within 3 days after the week's completion. After each of the six content weeks you complete a timed quiz covering that week's Knowledge Units. Each quiz is multiple choice, approximately twenty questions, and you have forty-five minutes. You may take each quiz up to three times; your highest score is recorded. The quiz for the final week is cumulative across the full course. Together the six quizzes make up twenty percent of your final grade. Quizzes are available on Canvas. Homework Four hands-on assignments that build the skills the project depends on. There are four homework assignments across the term, one roughly every week and a half. Each is a hands-on task that involves creating parts of a simulated distributed system using real tools and services: k6 for load testing, JavaScript for building services, and existing services such as Caddy, Redis, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Prometheus, and Grafana. Homework is submitted through Gradescope and graded automatically against a rubric; you will see your score as soon as the autograder runs. Together the four assignments make up thirty percent of your final grade. Your scores from Gradescope will be periodically synced to Canvas. Sprints A simulated scalable system built incrementally: each sprint applies only what the previous week taught. The Sprints are the team project itself, carried forward in stages rather than assembled at the end. Each sprint is due during the week after the Knowledge Units that inform it are covered, so the system grows in lockstep with the course material. You cannot design the full architecture at the start; you do not yet know the patterns. Instead the simulation is extended one layer at a time: Sprint 0 forms the team and stakes out a domain idea; Sprint 1 frames the scalability problem using the distributed systems vocabulary from Week 1; Sprint 2 produces the first containerized services running under Docker Compose; Sprint 3 adds serving patterns (replication, caching, load balancing) and a first k6 load test; Sprint 4 introduces async processing and resilience; and Sprint 5 instruments the system with observability, runs a final load test, and delivers the four capstone artifacts. The system you build throughout is a simulation: data is synthetic, latency is injected, failures are scripted, and computation is modeled. This is a deliberate choice, not a shortcut. Building a production system from scratch in six weeks is not realistic, and the goal of this course is not deployment; it is design, engineering, and measurement. Simulation lets you practice every pattern the course covers, instrument and break the system intentionally, and measure it under realistic load, without the operational complexity of real data pipelines or live traffic. The skills you develop, structuring services, reasoning about coordination, interpreting latency percentiles, are the same ones a team would use on a real system. Sprints introduce no new instruction. They are where you apply the current state of the Knowledge Units to the simulated system your team is building. Teams are assigned by the instructor and are 2–3 members for this six-week section. Because this course has no separate lab sequence, the professional workflow skills that labs would otherwise carry, clean commits, pull requests, code review, conflict resolution, are practiced and assessed directly inside the sprints. Because impressions are unreliable, your sprint contribution is assessed against objective GitHub evidence, your commits, the pull requests you authored and reviewed, and the merge history, rather than against anyone's sense of who did what. Sprints 0 and 1 are half-weight (each worth half a full sprint); Sprints 2, 3, and 4 are full-weight. Sprint 5 is graded as the Project Final (20%) rather than as part of the Sprints category. The Project is the summative destination the entire course is aimed at, and in this section it is fully asynchronous. Working in a team, you choose a problem domain in the spirit of Computing for the Common Good and design a meaningful but achievable scalable application. You then build a simulation of that application: services that model realistic behavior using synthetic data, injected latency, and scripted failures, orchestrated with Docker Compose and measured under load with k6. The simulation is not a stripped-down version of a real system; it is the full architecture, with coordinated services, asynchronous pipelines, caching, and observability, implemented in a way that makes every pattern visible and every failure intentional. The goal is to demonstrate that you understand how such a system is designed, how its components interact, and how its behavior changes under load. You submit four deliverables: the source code in your shared GitHub repository, a recorded video walkthrough of the running system, a poster presenting the problem, the architecture, and the trade-offs you made, and an individual written reflection from each team member on their own contribution and what they learned. You are assessed on collaborative practice, on meeting the sprint deliverable deadlines that pace the project from Week 1, and on professional conduct throughout, with contribution again read from objective GitHub evidence and the grade trajectory-weighted across the term. Deployment to a public host is not required and is not taught here; the destination is a complete, multi-service simulation running under Docker Compose in the dev container and demonstrated on video. This guide will get your development environment up and running, even if you have never used Docker or a dev container before. Read through each section in order the first time, it only takes about 10 minutes. What is this, exactly? When you open the development environment folder in VS Code, it automatically builds a Linux environment that runs inside your computer. Think of it like a virtual machine, but lighter and faster. Inside that environment you get: Node.js (latest LTS) and all the tools you need for web development Optional databases (PostgreSQL, Redis, MongoDB, MySQL, and more) that you can turn on with a single command A pre-configured terminal with shortcuts that make common tasks faster Everything needed for web development, no manual installation required No matter whether you are on macOS, Windows, or Linux, everyone on the team gets the exact same environment. "It works on my machine" stops being an excuse. A note before you dive in: This document covers a lot of ground, and that is intentional. It is meant to be a reference you return to throughout the course, not something you need to absorb all at once. You will not use everything here, and that is completely fine. Many of the services, shortcuts, and tools listed are available if and when a homework or exercise calls for them. If you have never touched a terminal or typed a command before, do not worry. The terminal may look unfamiliar at first, but you will get comfortable with it gradually as we work through things together. Just follow the steps in order, and if something is confusing, set it aside for now. It will make more sense in context when we get there. Step 1: Install the prerequisites You need three things installed on your computer before you start. Click each link and follow the instructions for your operating system. Docker DesktopLinks to an external site. Docker is the engine that runs the dev environment. The Desktop app gives you a graphical dashboard too. Windows users: during installation, choose "Use WSL 2" if asked. After installing, open Docker Desktop once and let it finish starting up before moving on. Visual Studio CodeLinks to an external site. The code editor. Dev Containers extensionLinks to an external site. This VS Code extension makes the "open in container" magic work. Click the link, then click Install, and VS Code will open and install it automatically. Once all three are installed, make sure Docker Desktop is running (look for the Docker whale icon in your taskbar or menu bar) before continuing. Step 2: Download the development environment Go to the Gantry Dev Container ReleasesLinks to an external site.. Under "Assets," download the latest release by selecting the file named gantry-.zip. Do not download the "Source code" archives, that is not the release build. Save the file somewhere you can find it, such as your Desktop or your own folder for this course. Step 3: Extract the archive Extract gantry-.zip to your chosen folder location. Do not leave it in your Downloads folder, the container will store your course work inside this folder, so treat it as your course workspace. On macOS: double-click gantry-.zip to extract it. A folder named gantry- will appear alongside the archive. On Windows: right-click gantry-.zip and choose "Extract All." Select your destination folder and click Extract. A folder named gantry- will appear in the destination folder. On Linux: open a terminal and run unzip gantry-.zip. A folder named gantry- will appear in the destination folder. You may also use a zip extracting application provided by the particular Linux distribution you are using (e.g., Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch) Step 4: Open the Development Environment in VS Code Open VS Code. Go to File → Open Folder and select the development environment folder. VS Code will show a notification in the bottom-right corner (this may take a moment). Click "Reopen in Container". If you missed the notification, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows/Linux, Cmd+Shift+P on Mac), type "Reopen in Container", and press Enter. Wait for the build to finish. The first time takes 3–5 minutes while it downloads everything. You will see a progress bar in the bottom-right corner. Subsequent openings are almost instant. It is helpful to be on a fast WiFi connection for this part. When the build finishes, VS Code reloads and you are now inside the development environment. Step 5: Open the terminal The terminal is how you run code and commands. Inside VS Code: Go to Terminal → New Terminal in the menu bar, or press Ctrl+` (backtick). The Gantry banner confirms everything is working. The $ at the end of the last line is the prompt, it is waiting for you to type a command. New to the terminal? The terminal works by typing a command and pressing Enter. Commands are case-sensitive. If something goes wrong, you can usually press Ctrl+C to stop whatever is running. Common Tasks The following examples cover common tasks. Run them in the VS Code terminal (Terminal → New Terminal in the menu bar, or press Ctrl+` (backtick)). Run a Node.js script Let's confirm Node.js is ready. node --version You should see something like v22.x.x. Now create and run a tiny script: echo 'console.log("Hello from the dev container!")' > hello.js node hello.js Expected output: Hello from the dev container! Install npm packages and run a project If you have a package.json file in your workspace: npm install npm run dev The npm run dev command starts your project (exact behavior depends on the project). Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Shortcuts that save typing: Instead of You can type npm install ni npm run dev nrd npm run nr npm start ns npm test nt Start a database and connect to it Databases are off by default to save memory. Turn one on when you need it. Start PostgreSQL: dc-up postgres You will see Docker pulling the image and starting the container. Once it says the container is healthy, connect to it: psql-dev You are now inside the PostgreSQL shell. Try a quick command: \l This lists all databases. You should see devdb in the list. Type \q to exit. Start Redis: dc-up redis redis-dev ping Expected output: PONG Start MongoDB: dc-up mongo mongo-dev You are now in the MongoDB shell. Type show dbs to list databases. Type exit to leave. Stop everything when you're done: dc-down Check what is running dps This shows all running containers in a tidy table format. If nothing is running, you will see an empty table. To see the logs from a running service (like postgres), use: dc-logs postgres Press Ctrl+C to stop watching logs. Make an HTTP request and read JSON The environment comes with several tools for working with HTTP APIs. curl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1 The output is JSON but it is hard to read. Pipe it through jq to pretty-print it: curl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1 | jq . Or use the built-in shortcut jcurl which does both steps at once: jcurl https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1 You can also use xh (a friendlier HTTP tool): xh https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1 Check what ports are listening When your app is running, you might want to see what ports are in use: ports This lists every port that has something listening on it. Customizing Your Terminal You can add your own aliases, functions, and environment variables without touching any shared files and without restarting the container. Open the file .bashrc.user in your workspace root (VS Code's Explorer panel, it is a hidden file, so look for it there or open it from the terminal). Add your customizations. The terminal is a completely different way of talking to your computer, and it requires a different mental model. This primer explains what the terminal is, why it exists, why it matters for a course like this one, and what you need to know to use it without confusion. What the Terminal Is Your operating system — macOS, Windows, Linux — is a layer of software that manages the hardware underneath your applications. Every time you create a file, open a browser, or install a program, the operating system is doing the actual work. A graphical interface gives you buttons and menus to make requests to the operating system. The terminal does the same thing, but through text. When you open a terminal, you see a cursor waiting for input. That interface is called the command line. You type a command, press Enter, and the operating system executes it. The output, if there is any, appears as text below your command. Then the cursor reappears and waits for the next one. That is the entire interaction model. The program that reads your input and coordinates with the operating system is called a shell. On macOS and Linux, the default shell is usually bash or zsh. On Windows with WSL, you also get bash. The shell is not the terminal window itself — the terminal is the visual container, and the shell is the program running inside it. The distinction rarely matters in practice, but you will see both words used in documentation. Why the Terminal Exists and Why It Matters The terminal is not a relic from before graphical interfaces were invented. It is still the primary tool for technical work because it is fast, precise, scriptable, and universal. Most of the tools used in professional software development — version control, build systems, test runners, package managers, servers, deployment scripts — are built to be operated from the command line. They have no graphical interface at all, or their graphical interface exposes far less than the command line does. git, npm, node, docker, psql: every tool you will use in this course is a command-line program. You will install packages by typing npm install. You will run your server by typing node server.js. You will interact with a database by typing commands. None of this happens through a menu. There is a second reason the terminal matters: it is the same everywhere. A command that works on your laptop works on your classmates' laptops and on a remote server in a data center. When you deploy an application to production, there is no graphical interface available — there is only a shell. Learning to work in the terminal now means the jump to professional environments is not a surprise later. Terminology You Need to Know Before touching any commands, you need a shared vocabulary. The file system is the structure your operating system uses to organize all stored data. Everything — your documents, your code, your programs — lives somewhere in the file system. A directory is a container that holds files and other directories. You may know this concept as a "folder." In the terminal, the word "directory" is standard. Directories nest inside each other, forming a tree. The root directory is the top of that tree. On macOS and Linux it is written as /. On Windows with WSL it is also / inside the Linux environment. Everything else in the file system is inside the root directory, directly or indirectly. Your home directory is the directory assigned to your user account. On macOS it is typically /Users/yourname. On Linux it is typically /home/yourname. The ~ character is shorthand for your home directory in most shells. The working directory is the directory the terminal is currently "inside." When you open a terminal, it starts in your home directory. When you run a command, the command executes relative to the working directory unless you specify otherwise. Understanding what your working directory is at any moment is one of the most important habits in terminal use. A path is the address of a file or directory in the file system. An absolute path starts from the root and describes the full address: /home/yourname/cs326/project/server.js. A relative path starts from the current working directory: if your working directory is /home/yourname/cs326, then project/server.js is a relative path to the same file. A command is a text instruction you give to the shell. Commands are usually short programs that live somewhere on your file system. When you type a command name, the shell searches a list of known locations to find and run it. An argument is additional information passed to a command. When you type node server.js, node is the command and server.js is an argument telling it which file to run. A flag (also called an option) is a special kind of argument that modifies a command's behavior. Flags usually start with - or --. For example, ls -l runs ls with the -l flag, which changes the output format. A script is a text file containing a sequence of commands. Instead of typing ten commands manually, you put them in a script file and run the whole file at once. Scripts are how automation works in the terminal. Permissions control who is allowed to read, write, or execute a file. Every file and directory in the file system has a set of permissions attached to it. Permissions matter when you try to run a script or access a file and the operating system refuses — understanding permissions tells you why and how to fix it. Standard output (stdout) is where a command sends its normal output — the text you see printed in the terminal after a command runs. Standard error (stderr) is a separate channel for error messages. Both appear in the terminal by default, but they can be separated and redirected independently. A process is a running instance of a program. When you run node server.js, you start a process. That process runs until it finishes or you stop it. Pressing Ctrl+C in the terminal sends a signal to the current process telling it to stop. The Commands You Need First These are the commands you will use constantly. Learn what they do before you need them in an activity. pwd: Print the working directory. Outputs the absolute path of the directory the terminal is currently in. When you are disoriented, run this first. pwd ls: List files and directories. Shows the files and directories inside the working directory. Running ls -l shows a detailed view including permissions, owner, size, and modification date. ls ls -l cd: Change directory. Moves the terminal's working directory to the path you specify. cd cs326 cd .. cd ~ cd /home/yourname/cs326 cd .. moves up one level to the parent directory. cd ~ moves to your home directory. cd with no argument also moves to your home directory. mkdir: Make a directory. Creates a new directory with the name you provide. mkdir project mkdir -p project/src/routes The -p flag creates intermediate directories as needed. Without it, mkdir project/src/routes fails if project or project/src do not already exist. touch: Creates an empty file if it does not exist, or update the modification timestamp. Commonly used to create placeholder files. touch server.ts cp: Copy file or directory. Copies a file from one location to another. cp server.ts server.backup.ts cp -r src src-backup The -r flag copies recursively, which is required when copying a directory. mv: Move file or directory. Moves a file to a new location, or renames it if the destination is in the same directory. mv server.ts app.ts mv server.js src/server.js rm: Remove file or directory. Deletes a file or directory. This is permanent — there is no trash or undo. rm server.backup.ts rm -r src-backup The -r flag removes a directory and everything inside it recursively. Use it carefully. cat: Concatenate a file. Prints the contents of a file to the terminal. Used constantly for quickly reading short files. cat package.json less: Pages content from a file. Shows the contents of a file one screen at a time, letting you scroll through output that is too long to read in a single terminal view. Unlike cat, it does not dump everything at once. Use the arrow keys or j/k to scroll, space to jump a full page, and q to exit. less server.ts less package.json You will use less any time a file is long enough that cat makes it scroll past before you can read it. It is also how man displays its pages internally, the same navigation keys apply (see below). echo: Print text to standard output. Useful in scripts and for quick checks. echo "hello" echo $PATH clear: Clear the terminal screen. Your command history is not deleted; the display is just scrolled. It clears things up. man: Manual. Open the manual page for a command. On macOS and Linux, nearly every command has a manual page. Use the arrow keys or j/k to scroll, space to jump a full page, and q to exit. Press q to exit. man ls man cp Running a Script Basics A script is an executable text file. To run one, you call it like a command: node server.js Some scripts are written for the shell directly, not for a runtime like Node. Those files typically end in .sh. To run a shell script, you first need to make sure it has execute permission, then call it: chmod +x setup.sh ./setup.sh chmod +x adds execute permission to the file. The ./ prefix tells the shell to look for the file in the current directory — without it, the shell only searches its known program locations and will not find your script. The Shebang (#!) The first line of a shell script that tells the operating system which interpreter to use to run the file. When you execute a script, the operating system reads the first two characters. If they are #!, it treats the rest of that line as the path to the program that should run the script. #!/bin/bash #!/usr/bin/env bash #!/usr/bin/env node #!/usr/bin/env python3 Without a shebang, the operating system does not know what kind of script it is looking at. It may refuse to run it, or it may guess wrong. With a shebang, running ./setup.sh works exactly the same as running bash setup.sh — the shebang makes the file self-describing. The second form, #!/usr/bin/env node, is more portable than a hardcoded path like #!/usr/local/bin/node. The env program searches your PATH for the named interpreter, so the script works regardless of where Node is installed on a given machine. You will see this form in most modern scripts that target Node or Python. The shebang line is ignored as a comment by the interpreter itself, # starts a comment in bash, Python, and most scripting languages, so it causes no errors when the interpreter processes the rest of the file. Here is a simple Node script that prints a greeting to the terminal: #!/usr/bin/env node const name = process.argv[2] ?? "stranger"; console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`); Save this as greet.js, make it executable, and run it: chmod +x greet.js ./greet.js ./greet.js Alice Output: Hello, stranger! Hello, Alice! process.argv is an array Node populates with the command-line arguments passed to the script. The first two entries are always the path to Node and the path to the script itself, so index 2 is where your first real argument lives. The ?? operator supplies a default if no argument was given. Without the shebang, you would have to type node greet.js Alice every time. With it, ./greet.js Alice works -- the script knows how to run itself. Permissions in Brief When you run ls -l, each entry starts with a string like -rwxr-xr--. That string encodes the permissions on the file. The characters map to three groups: the owner, the group, and everyone else. For each group, there are three possible permissions: read (r), write (w), and execute (x). A - means that permission is not granted. You will encounter permissions issues most often when trying to run a script that the operating system refuses to execute. The fix is usually chmod +x filename, which adds execute permission for the owner. The course activities will tell you when this is necessary. What Happens When Something Goes Wrong The terminal is unforgiving in one specific way: it does what you say, not what you meant. If you mistype a filename, it will tell you the file does not exist. If you run a command in the wrong directory, the results will be wrong. If you delete something with rm, it is gone. Developing three habits will prevent most problems. First, always know your working directory. Run pwd whenever you are uncertain. Second, use ls before and after operations that create or move files. Third, read error messages carefully -- they almost always tell you exactly what went wrong. "No such file or directory" means your path is wrong. "Permission denied" means you do not have the right access level. "Command not found" means the program is not installed or not on your PATH. There is no way to learn the terminal except by using it. The commands above will get you through everything in this course. You will be slow at first and faster within a week. A Note on This Course In this course you will use the terminal constantly. Every activity, every project sprint, every interaction with git, npm, node, and the Gantry container runs through the command line. If you setup the development environment and reach the integrated terminal inside VS Code, you are already in the right place. The shell running there is the same shell described in this primer. Every command here works exactly the same inside that terminal as it would in a standalone terminal application.
