The course uses a constrained subset of the language to keep examples consistent and readable across all units. Read through this before starting the units and return to it when you need a reminder. Two rules apply everywhere in the course: Functions are always defined as arrow functions: const fn = () => ... Classes are never used; objects are plain literals with arrow function methods Variables Use const for values that will not be reassigned. Use let for values that will change. Avoid var. const port = 3000; const name = "Alice"; let count = 0; count = count + 1; Reassigning a const is a runtime error. For objects and arrays, const prevents reassignment of the variable itself, not mutation of its contents. const config = { port: 3000 }; config.port = 4000; // allowed — mutating the object config = {}; // TypeError — reassigning the variable MDN: constLinks to an external site. | MDN: letLinks to an external site. Data Types JavaScript has six primitive types and two compound types. Primitives: string — text: 'hello', "world", `template` number — integers and floats: 42, 3.14, NaN, Infinity boolean — true or false null — explicit absence of a value undefined — a variable declared but not yet assigned symbol — unique identifiers (rarely used in this course) Compound: object — key/value pairs array — ordered list (technically also an object) Use typeof to inspect a type at runtime: typeof "hello"; // 'string' typeof 42; // 'number' typeof true; // 'boolean' typeof null; // 'object' — a known JS quirk typeof undefined; // 'undefined' typeof {}; // 'object' typeof []; // 'object' Array.isArray([]); // true MDN: JavaScript data typesLinks to an external site. Strings String literals use single quotes, double quotes, or backticks. Backtick strings (template literals) support embedded expressions and multi-line text. const greeting = "Hello"; const name = "world"; const message = `${greeting}, ${name}!`; // 'Hello, world!' const multiline = ` Line one Line two `; Common string methods: const s = " Hello, World! "; s.length; // 17 s.trim(); // 'Hello, World!' s.toLowerCase(); // ' hello, world! ' s.toUpperCase(); // ' HELLO, WORLD! ' s.includes("World"); // true s.startsWith(" Hello"); // true s.endsWith("! "); // true s.indexOf("World"); // 9 s.slice(2, 7); // 'Hello' s.replace("World", "Alice"); // ' Hello, Alice! ' s.split(", "); // [' Hello', 'World! '] "abc".repeat(3); // 'abcabcabc' "5".padStart(3, "0"); // '005' MDN: StringLinks to an external site. | MDN: Template literalsLinks to an external site. Numbers JavaScript uses 64-bit floating-point for all numbers. Integer arithmetic behaves as expected for typical values. const a = 10; const b = 3; a + b; // 13 a - b; // 7 a * b; // 30 a / b; // 3.3333... a % b; // 1 (remainder) a ** b; // 1000 (exponentiation) The Math object provides common utilities: Math.floor(3.9); // 3 Math.ceil(3.1); // 4 Math.round(3.5); // 4 Math.abs(-5); // 5 Math.min(1, 2, 3); // 1 Math.max(1, 2, 3); // 3 Math.sqrt(16); // 4 Math.pow(2, 10); // 1024 Math.random(); // random float in [0, 1) Convert between strings and numbers: Number("42"); // 42 Number("abc"); // NaN parseInt("42px"); // 42 parseFloat("3.14"); // 3.14 String(42)( // '42' 42, ).toString(); // '42' Check for special values: Number.isNaN(NaN); // true Number.isFinite(Infinity); // false Number.isInteger(4.0); // true MDN: NumberLinks to an external site. | MDN: MathLinks to an external site. Booleans and Comparison true && false; // false (logical AND) true || false; // true (logical OR) !true; // false (logical NOT) Use === (strict equality) and !== (strict inequality). Avoid == and !=, which coerce types in surprising ways. 1 === 1; // true 1 === "1"; // false — different types 1 == "1"; // true — type coercion (avoid this) Truthy and falsy: false, 0, '', null, undefined, and NaN are falsy. Everything else is truthy. if (0) { /* never runs */ } if ("") { /* never runs */ } if (null) { /* never runs */ } if ([]) { /* runs — empty array is truthy */ } if ({}) { /* runs — empty object is truthy */ } MDN: Equality comparisonsLinks to an external site. | MDN: Logical operatorsLinks to an external site. Arrow Functions Arrow functions are the only function syntax used in this course. // no arguments const greet = () => "Hello!"; // one argument — parentheses are optional, but include them for consistency const double = (n) => n * 2; // multiple arguments const add = (a, b) => a + b; // multi-line body — braces required, return must be explicit const clamp = (value, min, max) => { if (value < min) return min; if (value > max) return max; return value; }; // implicit return of an object — wrap in parentheses to avoid ambiguity const makePoint = (x, y) => ({ x, y }); Default parameters: const connect = (host = "localhost", port = 3000) => `${host}:${port}`; connect(); // 'localhost:3000' connect("example.com", 443); // 'example.com:443' Async arrow functions: const fetchData = async (url) => { const response = await fetch(url); return response.json(); }; Arrow functions do not have their own this binding. In this course that is rarely relevant because we reference objects by name rather than via this. MDN: Arrow function expressionsLinks to an external site. | MDN: Default parametersLinks to an external site. Arrays Arrays are ordered lists. Indices start at 0. const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]; fruits[0]; // 'apple' fruits.length; // 3 fruits[fruits.length - 1]; // 'cherry' (last element) Mutating methods (modify the array in place): const a = [1, 2, 3]; a.push(4); // appends 4; returns new length (4) a.pop(); // removes and returns last element (4) a.unshift(0); // prepends 0; returns new length a.shift(); // removes and returns first element (0) a.splice(1, 1); // removes 1 element at index 1; returns removed elements a.reverse(); // reverses in place a.sort(); // sorts in place (lexicographic by default) Non-mutating methods (return a new value, original unchanged): const nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]; nums.slice(2, 5); // [4, 1, 5] — copy from index 2 up to (not including) 5 nums.concat([7, 8]); // [3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6,7,8] nums.includes(4); // true nums.indexOf(1); // 1 — first occurrence nums .join(", ") // '3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6' [(1, [2, [3]])].flat() // [1, 2, [3]] — one level deep [(1, [2, [3]])].flat(Infinity); // [1, 2, 3] — fully flattened Sorting with a comparator: const sorted = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 1, 3, 4, 5] MDN: ArrayLinks to an external site. Functional Array Methods These are the primary iteration tools in this course. Each takes an arrow function as its argument and does not modify the original array. .map() Transforms every element; returns a new array of the same length. const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]; const doubled = numbers.map((n) => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6, 8] const labels = numbers.map((n) => `item-${n}`); // ['item-1', 'item-2', ...] .filter() Keeps elements for which the callback returns true; returns a new (possibly shorter) array. const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]; const evens = numbers.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0); // [2, 4, 6] const big = numbers.filter((n) => n > 3); // [4, 5, 6] .reduce() Accumulates a single value from all elements. Patterns, Trade-Offs, and the Design Mindset Introduction A scalable web system is a distributed system. The terms are nearly synonymous because web applications are almost always the systems that reach the scale at which a single machine can no longer keep up. When that happens, you add more machines, and those machines coordinate over HTTP: the same protocol users use to reach the application in the first place. Chapter 1 of the textbook makes this case directly: modern always-on, instantly scalable services are built from many independent services working in coordination, all presenting to the user the appearance of a single unified application. The patterns this course covers, sidecars, ambassadors, queues, and the rest, are the toolkit for building and maintaining that appearance. Before those patterns can be useful, though, you need to feel the problem they exist to solve. A web application that serves one request at a time will eventually stop keeping up. The obvious fix is to handle requests concurrently: start the next request before the previous one finishes. This speeds things up, but it introduces a coordination problem that does not exist when only one request is in flight. You will watch this happen in about 30 lines of Node.js code. The tension it reveals is the one every pattern in the textbook exists to manage: more concurrency means more speed, but it also means more coordination, and coordination has its own cost and its own failure modes. Before You Start This chapter sets up the vocabulary and motivation for everything that follows, so it's worth reading closely even though it has no code of its own. Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 1 (Introduction) References Promise.all — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/allLinks to an external site. setTimeout — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/setTimeoutLinks to an external site. Node.js event loop — https://nodejs.org/en/docs/guides/event-loop-timers-and-nexttickLinks to an external site. Express API — https://expressjs.com/en/4x/api.htmlLinks to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here is a program that handles five requests, one at a time. const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); const handleRequest = async (userId) => { console.log(`Handling request from user ${userId}`); await delay(1000); // stands in for real work: a database lookup, a computation, a file read console.log(`Finished request from user ${userId}`); }; const main = async () => { const start = Date.now(); for (const userId of [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]) { await handleRequest(userId); } const end = Date.now(); console.log(`Total time: ${(end - start) / 1000} seconds`); }; main(); Run it and you'll see it take about five seconds. That should not be surprising: each await in the loop waits for the request before it to finish before starting the next one. This is the simplest possible web service, and for a long time it's also a perfectly fine one. The problem only shows up once enough users show up at once that "one at a time" stops being fast enough. Extending the example The obvious fix is to stop waiting for each request to finish before starting the next. Promise.all lets you kick off all five requests at once and let the event loop interleave them. const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); let sharedCounter = 0; const handleRequest = async (userId) => { await delay(1000); const current = sharedCounter; await delay(1); // widens the window enough to see the problem sharedCounter = current + 1; }; const main = async () => { const start = Date.now(); await Promise.all([0, 1, 2, 3, 4].map(handleRequest)); const end = Date.now(); console.log(`Total time: ${(end - start) / 1000} seconds`); console.log(`Expected counter value: 5, actual: ${sharedCounter}`); }; main(); The total time drops to about one second, which is the win you'd expect. But run it a few times and look at the printed counter value. It is frequently not 5. Two calls to handleRequest both read sharedCounter, both see the same value, and both write back the same incremented result, so one of the increments is silently lost. This is worth pausing on, because JavaScript is single-threaded. There is no OS-level thread switching happening here, and yet the problem still shows up. The event loop can still suspend handleRequest at the await delay(1) line and let a different call to handleRequest run in the gap, which is enough interleaving to lose an update. Notice what happened: the original problem was "handle requests fast enough." Running them concurrently solved that, but it created a new problem that didn't exist when there was only one request in flight at a time: now the in-flight requests have to agree on the value of something they all touch. Naming the pattern That second problem, getting independent units of work to agree on shared state, is not a bug in this particular program. It is the central tension underneath every pattern in this course. The moment you have more than one unit of work in flight, whether that's threads, processes, async tasks on a single event loop, containers, or machines on a network, you gain speed and resilience, but you take on the job of coordinating those units, and coordination has its own cost and its own failure modes. The JavaScript example above is a useful reminder that this has nothing to do with literal parallelism. It shows up the moment work can interleave, even on a single thread. This is also what the course description means by describing web applications as "a large collection of coordinated services... working in coordination to present to the user the illusion of a single program." A distributed system is not one program. It's several independent units of work arranged so carefully that users can't tell the difference. Every pattern you'll meet in this course, sidecar, ambassador, scatter/gather, consistent hashing, is a named, reusable answer to some version of the trade-off you just watched play out: more concurrency means more speed, but it also means more coordination. This is the design mindset the course title refers to: instead of asking "is this program correct," you start asking "what am I trading away to get this property," because in a distributed system you are always trading something. Exercise JavaScript doesn't have a built-in lock the way some languages do, but you can build an equivalent out of a single chained promise. Here is a small helper: const createLock = () => { let chain = Promise.resolve(); return (fn) => { const result = chain.then(fn); chain = result.catch(() => {}); return result; }; }; Task: Use createLock to wrap the critical section in handleRequest (the read, the delay, and the write) so the five calls run that part one at a time instead of interleaving. Starting point: The second code block in the Notes section above, plus the createLock helper. You'll know it works when: running the program ten times in a row always prints actual: 5. Once it does, add a one-line comment in your code noting whether the total runtime changed compared to the unsynchronized version, and a short guess at why. Real World The JavaScript examples above run in Node.js and use setTimeout to stand in for real work. A real web server does the same thing structurally: it receives requests, does some work (database queries, downstream calls), and sends back responses. The coordination problem is identical. Express is the most widely used Node.js HTTP framework. Here is the same sequential-vs-concurrent pattern, but now it's a real server that a real HTTP client can hit. import express from 'express'; const app = express(); let sharedCounter = 0; const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); app.get('/increment', async (req, res) => { const current = sharedCounter; await delay(10); // simulate async work: a database read, a downstream call sharedCounter = current + 1; res.json({ counter: sharedCounter }); }); app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000')); Rather than reloading browser tabs to generate concurrent requests, write a small bash script using curl in a file called sequ.sh. Start with the sequential version to confirm the server is working correctly: #!/usr/bin/env bash for i in $(seq 1 5); do curl -s http://localhost:3000/increment echo done Make sure to run chmod +x sequ.sh to make the script executable. Then run ./sequ.sh. This should print counter values 1 through 5 in order. Now write the concurrent version in conc.sh that backgrounds each request with & and waits for all of them to finish: #!/usr/bin/env bash for i in $(seq 1 5); do curl -s http://localhost:3000/increment & done wait echo Restart the server between runs to reset the counter to zero. The concurrent script frequently prints duplicate counter values — two responses both reporting {"counter":3}, for example — which is the lost update visible at the HTTP level. The same lost-update problem from the Notes section appears, now in a form you could unfortunately accidentally deploy. This is the very primitive and manual version of what a load testing tool like k6 does automatically, with configurable concurrency, duration, and built-in result reporting — you will use it in later units. The fix in production is to never use an in-memory variable for shared mutable state across concurrent requests. State that multiple requests can race to update belongs in a system that supports atomic operations — a database with transactions, or a cache like Redis that has an INCR command which reads, increments, and writes in a single uninterruptible step. Those tools appear in later units. For now, the takeaway is that the problem from the Notes is not academic: it shows up in the first real server you write. Home Exercise The race condition is easier to study if you don't have to restart the server to reset the counter. Add two new endpoints to the Express server: GET /reset — sets the counter back to zero and returns { "counter": 0 } GET /counter — returns the current counter value without incrementing it Then write a single bash script called compare.sh that: Calls /reset Sends 20 requests sequentially using a for loop Calls /counter and prints the result Calls /reset again Sends 20 requests concurrently using & and wait Calls /counter and prints the result The sequential run should reliably print 20. An SLO is a formal statement of how a service performs, capturing two things separately: how fast it responds under normal and worst-case conditions, and how often it succeeds at all. In a scalable web system, where many services call each other over HTTP, SLOs are what allow one team's service to become a reliable building block for another team's work. Without them, "fast" and "reliable" remain assumptions rather than commitments. Unit 1 showed that concurrency creates a speed-versus-coordination trade-off but left "faster" as a word rather than a number. This unit supplies the measurements that make SLOs concrete: latency percentiles, which reveal what a typical and a worst-case response actually look like, and a reliability rate, which captures how often calls succeed. Notes The starting problem Here's a function that stands in for calling a weather API. In the real world, calls like this don't all take the same amount of time, so this version picks a random delay each time, mostly fast, occasionally slow. const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); const randomLatency = () => Math.random() < 0.95 ? 5 + Math.random() * 15 // fast path: 5 to 20 ms : 100 + Math.random() * 200; // slow path: 100 to 300 ms const callWeatherApi = async () => { const latency = randomLatency(); await delay(latency); return latency; }; const main = async () => { const latencies = []; for (const _ of Array.from({ length: 100 })) { latencies.push(await callWeatherApi()); } const average = latencies.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l, 0) / latencies.length; console.log(`Average latency: ${average.toFixed(1)} ms`); }; main(); Run it and you'll probably see an average somewhere around 15 to 25 ms, which sounds fine. But that single number is hiding something: a small number of those 100 calls took 100 to 300 ms, and the average doesn't tell you how many users had that worse experience, or how much worse it was. Extending the example Two things are missing from the picture above. First, an average flattens out the slow calls instead of showing them to you. Second, real calls don't just run slow, they sometimes fail outright, and that's a different problem than slowness. Let's track both. const percentile = (sortedLatencies, p) => { const index = Math.ceil((p / 100) * sortedLatencies.length) - 1; return sortedLatencies[index]; }; const callWeatherApi = async () => { const latency = randomLatency(); await delay(latency); if (Math.random() < 0.03) { throw new Error("weather service unavailable"); } return latency; }; const main = async () => { const latencies = []; let failures = 0; for (const _ of Array.from({ length: 100 })) { try { latencies.push(await callWeatherApi()); } catch (err) { failures++; } } latencies.sort((a, b) => a - b); const average = latencies.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l, 0) / latencies.length; console.log( `Average latency (successful calls only): ${average.toFixed(1)} ms`, ); console.log(`p50 latency: ${percentile(latencies, 50).toFixed(1)} ms`); console.log(`p95 latency: ${percentile(latencies, 95).toFixed(1)} ms`); console.log(`p99 latency: ${percentile(latencies, 99).toFixed(1)} ms`); console.log(`Failures: ${failures} of 100 calls`); }; main(); Now look at the gap between p50 and p99. p50 looks a lot like the average did before, but p99 is much higher, because it's showing you the slow path that the average was smoothing over. And the failure count is tracked completely separately from latency, because a call that throws an error didn't have a latency at all. It just didn't work. Naming the pattern Three ideas are sitting inside the code you just wrote. Resiliency. The function callWeatherApi is an API: a contract between the caller and whatever does the work. Most API contracts describe the happy path, what comes back when things go well, but they often leave out exactly the two properties you just measured: how long a call might take, and how often it might fail outright. A well designed API contract says something about both, not just about the shape of the return value. Latency is the raw measurement you collected in the latencies array, the time between making a call and getting a response. A percentile is a way of summarizing a pile of latency measurements honestly. The p50, or median, is roughly "what a typical call looks like." The p95 and p99 describe the tail: the experience of the unluckiest 5% or 1% of calls. Real systems are usually judged by their tail, not their median, because a typical user doesn't notice the median, they notice when their own request happens to land in the slow 1%. Reliability is the third idea, and it's independent of latency. A system can be fast and unreliable, slow and reliable, or any combination. That's why production systems usually publish two separate numbers, something like "99.9% of calls succeed" and "p99 latency under 300 ms," rather than a single combined score. Designing an API well means deciding, on purpose, what you're promising for each of these, instead of letting them fall out of whatever the implementation happens to do. In a scalable web system, any HTTP call between services can fail: the network drops a packet, the server processes a request but the response never arrives, a connection resets mid-flight. Chapter 2 introduces delivery semantics to describe what systems can guarantee in those situations: at-least-once delivery ensures nothing is silently lost but allows duplicates; at-most-once delivery prevents duplicates but can lose requests entirely. Idempotency is what resolves that tension. An operation that produces the same result whether it runs once or ten times can safely use at-least-once delivery, because repeating it on failure costs nothing. Unit 2 measured how often calls fail. This unit asks what callers should do about it. The intuitive answer is to retry until the call succeeds, but without idempotency that is dangerous: if the server processed the request and only the response was lost, retrying causes a duplicate effect. You will watch this happen with a simulated payment API, then fix it with an idempotency key, a design decision made before writing the first retry loop that transforms retries from a source of corruption into a reliable recovery mechanism. Before You Start Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 2 References Map — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/MapLinks to an external site. Idempotency keys (Stripe) — https://stripe.com/docs/api/idempotent_requestsLinks to an external site. express.json() — https://expressjs.com/en/4x/api.html#express.jsonLinks to an external site. HTTP status codes — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/StatusLinks to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here's a function that simulates charging a credit card. The network is flaky: 30% of the time, the charge actually succeeds on the server, but the response never makes it back to the client. From the client's point of view, that looks exactly like a failed request, so the client retries. let totalCharged = 0; const chargeCard = (amount) => { totalCharged += amount; const responseArrives = Math.random() > 0.3; if (!responseArrives) { throw new Error("timed out waiting for a response"); } return { status: "charged", amount }; }; const chargeWithRetry = async (amount) => { for (const attempt of [1, 2, 3]) { try { return chargeCard(amount); } catch (err) { console.log(`Attempt ${attempt} failed: ${err.message}, retrying...`); } } throw new Error("all retries failed"); }; const main = async () => { await chargeWithRetry(20).catch(() => {}); console.log(`Total charged: $${totalCharged}`); }; main(); Run this a handful of times. Sometimes totalCharged is $20, like you'd expect. Other times it's $40 or $60. The retry logic did exactly what you'd want from a client that doesn't want to give up too early — it kept trying until it got a real response — but chargeCard had already taken effect on earlier attempts that the client thought had failed. The client and the true state of the world disagree, and the client has no way to tell from the outside. Extending the example The fix isn't to retry less. It's to make the operation safe to repeat. Give each logical charge a unique key, generated once per operation rather than once per attempt, and have the server remember which keys it has already handled. let totalCharged = 0; const processedKeys = new Map(); const chargeCard = (amount, idempotencyKey) => { if (processedKeys.has(idempotencyKey)) { return processedKeys.get(idempotencyKey); } totalCharged += amount; const result = { status: "charged", amount }; processedKeys.set(idempotencyKey, result); const responseArrives = Math.random() > 0.3; if (!responseArrives) { throw new Error("timed out waiting for a response"); } return result; }; const chargeWithRetry = async (amount, idempotencyKey) => { for (const attempt of [1, 2, 3]) { try { return chargeCard(amount, idempotencyKey); } catch (err) { console.log(`Attempt ${attempt} failed: ${err.message}, retrying...`); } } throw new Error("all retries failed"); }; const main = async () => { const idempotencyKey = "order-48213"; // generated once for this logical operation, not once per attempt await chargeWithRetry(20, idempotencyKey).catch(() => {}); console.log(`Total charged: $${totalCharged}`); }; main(); Run this several times. totalCharged stays at $20 no matter how many of the three attempts time out, because the server recognizes the key on every retry and hands back the result it already computed instead of charging again. Naming the pattern An operation is idempotent if doing it once and doing it five times leave the world in the same state. chargeCard on its own was not idempotent: each call had its own effect. What you built was an idempotent API around a non-idempotent action, by attaching an identity to the operation (the key) and having the server deduplicate on that identity rather than trusting the client to only ask once. This connects directly to delivery semantics — the promises a system makes about how many times an operation might actually run: At-most-once: never duplicates an effect, but can silently lose one. Giving up after a single failed attempt means a true failure and a lost response look identical. At-least-once: never silently loses an effect, but can duplicate one unless the operation is idempotent. This is what the retry loop above does. Exactly-once: the thing everyone wants and almost no real network can promise end to end. In practice it is approximated by combining at-least-once delivery with an idempotent operation — often called effectively-once behavior — which is exactly the combination you just built. Notice how this differs from the coordination problem in Unit 1. There, multiple workers disagreed with each other about shared state. Here, it is a single client and a single server that can disagree about whether something happened, purely because the network in between is unreliable. That disagreement is itself a data consistency problem: in the broken version, the client believed one charge had happened while the stored totalCharged reflected two or three. Consistency is not only about concurrent writers stepping on each other — it is also about a delivery layer that cannot fully tell the truth about what already happened. Exercise Task: Add a second, legitimate charge of $20 using a new idempotency key ("order-48214"), then call chargeWithRetry for "order-48213" a second time to simulate a client that didn't hear back and retried. Starting point: The second code block in the Notes section above. You'll know it works when: totalCharged reliably ends at $40 no matter how many internal retries happen on either call. Add a one-line comment explaining why the idempotency key — not the dollar amount — is what determines whether two calls count as "the same" operation. Real World The Notes example runs entirely in memory. A real payment API uses the same concept: the client sends an Idempotency-Key HTTP header with each request, and the server deduplicates on it. This is exactly how Stripe works. Express is already set up from earlier units. Add express.json() middleware to parse the request body. Create server.js: import express from 'express'; const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); let totalCharged = 0; const processedKeys = new Map(); app.post('/charge', (req, res) => { const idempotencyKey = req.headers['idempotency-key']; if (!idempotencyKey) { return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key header is required' }); } if (processedKeys.has(idempotencyKey)) { return res.json({ ...processedKeys.get(idempotencyKey), duplicate: true }); } const { amount } = req.body; totalCharged += amount; const result = { status: 'charged', amount, totalCharged }; processedKeys.set(idempotencyKey, result); res.json(result); }); app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000')); npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module && npm install express Start the server (node server.js) and test it with two curl commands — one original charge and one retry using the same key: # First attempt curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/charge \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: order-48213" \ -d '{"amount": 20}' # Retry — same key, should not double-charge curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/charge \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: order-48213" \ -d '{"amount": 20}' The first response has no duplicate field. The second has "duplicate": true and the same totalCharged value — the server recognized the key and returned the stored result without touching totalCharged again. Looking Ahead Unit 4 shifts from the logical challenges of concurrency, measurement, and safe retries to the practical one of packaging a service so it runs the same way everywhere. Before containers, the patterns the book describes existed as ideas but not as reusable, portable artifacts: you could implement a sidecar in code, but the deployment unit was just "some process" that had to be configured, versioned, and reproduced by hand on every machine it ran on. Containers changed that. When a service and everything it depends on are packaged into a single image, you have something that runs identically anywhere Docker is installed, that can be composed with other services by name, and that other teams can depend on without knowing what it is built from. Units 1 through 3 covered the logical challenges of distributed services: concurrency, measurement, and safe retries. Before any of those patterns can run in production, each service needs to be packaged as an image. A Node.js server that works on your machine may fail on a teammate's machine, in CI, or in production, because none of its dependencies are written down anywhere. This unit fixes that. You will write a Dockerfile, build it into an image, and run it as a container. By the end, those words stop being vocabulary and become two specific things you watched happen. Before You Start Read: Docker's overview of images and containers — https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/Links to an external site. References Dockerfile reference — https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/builder/Links to an external site. docker build — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/image/build/Links to an external site. docker run — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/Links to an external site. docker ps / docker logs / docker rm — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/Links to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here's a tiny web server. // server.js import http from 'node:http'; http.createServer((req, res) => { res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' }); res.end('Hello from a plain Node process\n'); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000')); You also need a package.json so Node treats the file as an ES module: { "type": "module" } Run it with node server.js, then visit localhost:3000 or run curl localhost:3000. It works, but notice everything it's quietly depending on: this exact machine has Node installed, at some version, with nothing else conflicting. None of that is written down anywhere. If you sent server.js to a teammate, it would either work by luck or fail in some way that has nothing to do with the code itself. Extending the example Write down exactly what this code needs to run, in a file called a Dockerfile, then build that description into an image. # Dockerfile FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY . . EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "server.js"] Each line does one specific thing. FROM node:24 starts from a base image that already has Node 24 installed. WORKDIR sets the directory inside the image where the following commands run. COPY . . brings everything from your current directory into the image. EXPOSE documents which port the container expects to be reached on. CMD is the command that runs when a container starts from this image. Build it, then run it: docker build -t hello-server . docker run -p 3000:3000 hello-server docker build reads the Dockerfile and produces an image named hello-server. docker run starts a container — a running instance of that image — and -p 3000:3000 connects port 3000 on your machine to port 3000 inside the container. Visit localhost:3000 again. Same response as before, but now it's coming from inside an isolated container built from a file that says exactly what it needs. Managing containers and images docker run blocks your terminal because the container's output goes there. To start a container in the background, add -d (detached mode). Give it a name with --name so you can refer to it by something other than its ID: docker run -d --name my-server -p 3000:3000 hello-server Check what's running: docker ps docker ps lists every running container: its ID, image, when it started, and the port mapping. To include containers that have stopped, use docker ps -a. To see the output from a detached container: docker logs my-server When you're done, stop the container and remove it: docker stop my-server docker rm my-server docker stop sends a signal that gives the process a moment to shut down cleanly. docker rm removes the stopped container — until you do this, the container still exists on disk (visible in docker ps -a) even after it stops. To skip the two steps, docker rm -f my-server stops and removes in one command. Images accumulate too. To see what images are installed on your machine: docker images To remove an image (only works if no containers — running or stopped — are using it): docker rmi hello-server To remove all unused images at once: docker image prune Naming the pattern An image is a packaged, read-only blueprint: your code plus everything it depends on to run, frozen into a single artifact. A container is a running instance of that image, the way a process is a running instance of a program. You can start several containers from the same image at once, and they won't interfere with each other — each one gets its own isolated filesystem and process space. The Dockerfile is the recipe that produces the image, and each instruction in it becomes a layer that Docker can cache. That's why rebuilding an image after a small code change is usually much faster than the first build: Docker reuses unchanged layers and only reruns the steps that changed. Two things worth keeping straight: EXPOSE just documents intent inside the Dockerfile. The -p flag on docker run is what actually connects a port on your machine to a port inside the running container. EXPOSE without -p doesn't open anything. This is the foundation everything from Unit 6 onward sits on top of. Multi-container patterns — sidecars, proxies, workers — are just multiple containers, each one a running instance of some image, deliberately sharing a little while staying isolated in every other way. You'll know it works when: docker run -d --name server-3000 -e PORT=3000 -p 3000:3000 hello-server docker run -d --name server-3001 -e PORT=3001 -p 3001:3001 hello-server docker ps — both containers are listed as running docker logs server-3000 — shows "Listening on port 3000" docker logs server-3001 — shows "Listening on port 3001" curl localhost:3000 and curl localhost:3001 both return a response Cleanup: docker stop server-3000 server-3001 then docker rm server-3000 server-3001 Real World Most Node.js projects have npm dependencies. That changes the Dockerfile in one important way: you need to install them inside the image before copying your source code. Create an Express app: // server.js import express from 'express'; const app = express(); const port = process.env.PORT || 3000; app.get('/', (req, res) => { res.send('Hello from Express in a container\n'); }); app.listen(port, () => console.log(`Listening on port ${port}`)); { "type": "module", "dependencies": { "express": "^4.18.0" } } Run npm install once locally to generate package-lock.json. Then write the Dockerfile: FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY package*.json . RUN npm install COPY . . EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "server.js"] The key change is the order: copy package*.json first, run npm install, then copy the rest of the source. Docker caches each layer — so as long as package.json doesn't change, npm install is skipped on every subsequent rebuild. If you copied everything first and then ran npm install, any change to any file would invalidate the install layer and force a full reinstall. In production, that role is played by Kubernetes. At the scale of a single developer or a small team, Docker Compose fills the same conceptual role. Instead of a sequence of imperative commands that must be typed in the right order with the right flags every time, Compose lets you declare what containers you want, how they are connected, and what volumes they share, then brings the whole arrangement up or down with a single command. Unit 4 built one container from a Dockerfile and ran it with docker run. The moment you need two containers sharing a volume, that one command becomes four, each one with flags that must match exactly, in the right order, every time you want to bring the system up. This unit introduces Compose as the tool that replaces that sequence with a file you can read, share, and check into version control. Every multi-container setup from Unit 6 onward will be expressed as a docker-compose.yml, so the goal here is to make that format completely familiar before the patterns begin. Before You Start Read: Docker's Compose overview — https://docs.docker.com/compose/Links to an external site. References Compose file reference — https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/Links to an external site. docker compose CLI — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/Links to an external site. Named volumes — https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/Links to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here are two small scripts. One writes a timestamp to a shared file every five seconds. The other serves whatever is currently in that file over HTTP. // writer.js import fs from 'node:fs'; setInterval(() => { fs.writeFileSync( '/data/message.txt', `Last updated: ${new Date().toISOString()}\n`, ); }, 5000); // reader-server.js import http from 'node:http'; import fs from 'node:fs'; http.createServer((req, res) => { const message = fs.existsSync('/data/message.txt') ? fs.readFileSync('/data/message.txt', 'utf8') : 'no data yet\n'; res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' }); res.end(message); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on port 3000')); Using what you learned in Unit 4, running both of these as containers that share a volume takes a sequence like this: docker build -t demo-app . docker volume create shared-data docker run -d --name writer -v shared-data:/data demo-app node writer.js docker run -d --name reader -p 3000:3000 -v shared-data:/data demo-app node reader-server.js That's already four commands, each one easy to get slightly wrong, and you'd have to remember this exact sequence, in this exact order, every single time you wanted to bring this up again. Tearing it down means stopping and removing two containers and a volume by hand too. Extending the example Describe the same two containers and the volume they share in a single file instead. # docker-compose.yml services: writer: build: . command: node writer.js volumes: - shared-data:/data reader: build: . command: node reader-server.js ports: - "3000:3000" volumes: - shared-data:/data volumes: shared-data: Now bring both containers up with one command: docker compose up Visit localhost:3000 a few times over thirty seconds and watch the timestamp update. When you're done, docker compose down removes both containers and cleans up after itself. Same two containers, same shared volume, same result as the four commands above — but now the whole arrangement lives in a file you can read top to bottom, hand to a teammate, and check into version control. You also need a Dockerfile so Compose knows how to build the image: FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY . . There's no CMD here — each service in docker-compose.yml provides its own command, so the Dockerfile just handles the image and leaves the command to Compose. Managing a Compose project docker compose up runs in the foreground — all service output streams to your terminal. To start in the background instead, add -d: docker compose up -d Check the status of every service in the project: docker compose ps To stream logs as they arrive: docker compose logs -f # all services docker compose logs -f writer # one service only To restart a single service without touching the others: docker compose restart writer To stop all services without removing the containers: docker compose stop docker compose down goes further — it stops and removes all containers. By default it leaves named volumes alone. To remove volumes too and wipe all stored data: docker compose down --volumes To open a shell inside a running service for debugging: docker compose exec reader sh Naming the pattern docker-compose.yml is a declarative description of a multi-container application. Each entry under services is one container's blueprint: where to build it from, what command to run, which ports to expose, which volumes to mount. A named volume like shared-data is declared once under volumes and referenced by any service that needs it — which is how two otherwise unrelated containers end up sharing the same files. Compose itself isn't a new pattern. It's a tool for describing an arrangement of containers that you've already decided on, the same way a recipe describes a dish without being the dish. The patterns themselves — sidecar, ambassador, and the ones still ahead — are about why containers are arranged a certain way. Compose is just how that arrangement gets written down in one place instead of typed by hand every time. From Unit 6 onward, every multi-container example in this course will be expressed as a docker-compose.yml. It shares the shared-data volume but doesn't expose any port — it only reads from the shared file and logs to its own console. // logger.js import fs from 'node:fs'; setInterval(() => { const message = fs.existsSync('/data/message.txt') ? fs.readFileSync('/data/message.txt', 'utf8') : 'no data yet'; console.log(message.trim()); }, 5000); Starting point: The docker-compose.yml and Dockerfile from the Notes above, plus the logger.js file. Add a logger service to docker-compose.yml. You'll know it works when: docker compose up -d --build docker compose ps — all three services listed as running docker compose logs logger — shows the same timestamp the reader is serving over HTTP, updating every five seconds curl localhost:3000 — the reader responds with that same timestamp Cleanup: docker compose down Real World Volume sharing is one way containers cooperate. Another is the network: every service in a Compose project can reach every other service by its service name as a hostname. Here's a two-service example. One service generates data; the other fetches from it and serves it externally. // data.js — internal service, port 3001, not exposed to the host import http from 'node:http'; http.createServer((req, res) => { res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(JSON.stringify({ message: 'data from internal service', timestamp: new Date().toISOString() })); }).listen(3001, () => console.log('Data service on port 3001')); // app.js — calls data by service name, serves on port 3000 import http from 'node:http'; http.createServer(async (req, res) => { const response = await fetch('http://data:3001/'); const body = await response.json(); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(JSON.stringify(body)); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('App on port 3000')); The URL http://data:3001/ uses the service name data as the hostname. Docker Compose creates a private network for the project and registers each service's name as a DNS entry on that network. No IP addresses, no service discovery configuration — just service names. # docker-compose.yml services: app: build: . command: node app.js ports: - "3000:3000" depends_on: - data data: build: . command: node data.js depends_on: data tells Compose to start the data container before starting app. The data service has no ports: entry — it's internal to the Compose network. Nothing on your host machine can reach it directly; only app can. Run it: docker compose up --build curl localhost:3000 curl localhost:3000 hits the app container, which calls http://data:3001/ on the internal network, gets a response, and forwards it. The data service is invisible to the outside world. Home Exercise Task: Make the data service's message configurable without rebuilding the image. Chapter 1 explains why patterns matter: they give practitioners a shared vocabulary for describing arrangements that would otherwise have to be described from scratch every time. The sidecar solves a problem that appears as soon as a service acquires a second job: a process that serves HTTP and also syncs content has two reasons to change, two teams that might need to edit it, and two separate failure modes to worry about at once. The pattern's answer is a second container, attached to the first, that handles the second job without either container needing to know much about the other. Unit 5 introduced Docker Compose as the tool for declaring and running multi-container systems. This unit uses that foundation to implement the sidecar: two containers sharing a named volume, where one serves and one syncs, and neither calls the other directly. It is the first unit where the unit of execution is a whole container rather than a function call, and the first where the coordination mechanism is a shared volume rather than a shared variable. Before You Start Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 3 (Sidecar Pattern) References Node.js fs module — https://nodejs.org/api/fs.htmlLinks to an external site. setInterval — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/setIntervalLinks to an external site. Compose volumes — https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/volumes/Links to an external site. docker compose restart — https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/restart/Links to an external site. Notes The starting problem Here's a tiny Node.js server that serves a content directory. To keep that content fresh, it also syncs new content into that directory on a timer, right inside the same file. // app.js import http from 'node:http'; import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; const syncContent = () => { // stands in for pulling the latest content: a git repo, a CMS, an S3 bucket fs.writeFileSync( path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'), `

Updated at ${new Date().toISOString()}

`, ); }; fs.mkdirSync(CONTENT_DIR, { recursive: true }); syncContent(); setInterval(syncContent, 10000); http.createServer((req, res) => { const html = fs.readFileSync(path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html')); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' }); res.end(html); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Serving on port 3000')); This works fine. But notice that app.js now has two jobs that have nothing to do with each other: serving HTTP requests, and knowing how content gets refreshed. If you wanted to change where content comes from, how often it refreshes, or swap in a completely different sync mechanism, you'd have to edit and redeploy the exact same file that handles requests — even though the request-handling logic never changed. Extending the example Split the two jobs into two separate processes that agree on nothing except a shared directory. One serves. One syncs. Neither calls the other directly. // app.js — serves only import http from 'node:http'; import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; http.createServer((req, res) => { const html = fs.readFileSync(path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html')); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' }); res.end(html); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('Serving on port 3000')); // sync.js — syncs only import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; const syncContent = () => { fs.writeFileSync( path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'), `

Updated at ${new Date().toISOString()}

`, ); console.log('Content synced'); }; fs.mkdirSync(CONTENT_DIR, { recursive: true }); syncContent(); setInterval(syncContent, 10000); Create a package.json so Node.js treats these as ES modules: { "type": "module" } Open two terminals. In the first, run node app.js. In the second, run node sync.js. Open http://localhost:3000 and reload every few seconds. The timestamp keeps updating, exactly like before, but app.js and sync.js never call each other. They cooperate purely by reading and writing the same directory. Naming the pattern What you just built is the sidecar pattern: a second process attached to a primary process, sharing a local resource with it so it can add a capability the primary needs without modifying the primary's code. The primary (app.js) has no dependency on the sidecar's implementation. You could replace sync.js with something that pulls from a git repo, fetches from S3, or syncs on a completely different schedule, and app.js would never need to change. The sidecar runs as its own independent process, but is deployed and managed together with its primary as one unit. That independence is what makes the pattern work cleanly: app.js only reads the shared file, sync.js only writes it, so there is no shared mutable state being raced over the way there was in Unit 1. The coordination happens through a resource built for exactly this — a shared file — rather than through memory two processes are racing to update. Exercise Task: Change the sync interval in sync.js from 10 seconds to 3 seconds, and add a counter that increments on every sync so the page shows both a timestamp and a sync count. Starting point: The two-file version from the Notes above (the app.js + sync.js split). You'll know it works when: refreshing http://localhost:3000 shows the sync count climbing roughly every 3 seconds, and you were able to make this entire change inside sync.js without touching app.js at all. Real World The Notes version runs both processes on your local machine sharing a directory. In production, the primary service and its sidecar run as separate containers — but the coordination mechanism is exactly the same: a shared volume that both containers can read and write. Docker Compose lets you define the two containers and their shared volume in a single file. Create Dockerfile: FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY . . RUN mkdir -p content Create docker-compose.yml: services: app: build: . command: node app.js ports: - "3000:3000" volumes: - content:/usr/src/app/content sync: build: . command: node sync.js volumes: - content:/usr/src/app/content volumes: content: Run docker compose up. Open http://localhost:3000 and reload every few seconds. The timestamp keeps updating. app and sync are now isolated containers — different process namespaces, different filesystems — but they cooperate through the content named volume exactly the way the two local processes cooperated through ./content/. To verify the independence: run docker compose restart sync while the page is open. The app container keeps serving without interruption; only the sync pauses and resumes. Home Exercise The sidecar pattern composes: you can attach more than one sidecar to a primary container. Add a second sidecar, monitor.js, that polls index.html every 2 seconds and logs a message whenever the file changes: // monitor.js import fs from 'node:fs'; import path from 'node:path'; const CONTENT_DIR = './content'; const FILE = path.join(CONTENT_DIR, 'index.html'); let lastContent = ''; setInterval(() => { try { const current = fs.readFileSync(FILE, 'utf8'); if (current !== lastContent) { console.log(`[monitor] content changed at ${new Date().toISOString()}`); lastContent = current; } } catch { // file not yet written } }, 2000); Add a monitor service to docker-compose.yml that uses the same image, runs node monitor.js, and mounts the same content volume. You'll know it's working when docker compose logs monitor shows a line every time sync updates the file — and you added this capability without touching app.js or sync.js at all. Traffic grows to the point where one instance cannot keep up, so your team splits the data across two servers: even-numbered user IDs go to one, odd-numbered IDs go to another. You update app.js to route each call to the right server. Three months later a third server is added, and you update app.js again. A second internal service also looks up users, so the routing logic is duplicated there too. Whenever the sharding strategy changes, every service that calls users-service has to change with it. This is the problem Chapter 4 of the textbook targets with the ambassador pattern: routing decisions, retries, and traffic shaping belong in the infrastructure, not inside every application that happens to make a call. The ambassador is a proxy container that intercepts a primary container's outgoing calls and makes those decisions on its behalf, while the primary keeps calling a fixed local address as if nothing has changed. Unit 6 introduced the sidecar: a helper container that adds capability beside the primary by sharing a named volume with it. The ambassador keeps the two-container shape but flips the concern: instead of adding something the primary was missing, it intercepts something the primary was already doing, its outgoing calls to other services, and takes over the routing. This unit uses network_mode: "service:..." in Docker Compose to give the ambassador container access to the primary container's localhost interface. By the end you will have a working sharding ambassador that routes traffic to two backend instances based on user ID, and you will extend it to run a canary experiment on top of the existing routing logic. Before You Start Read: Designing Distributed Systems, Ch. 4 (Ambassador Pattern) References Node.js http module: https://nodejs.org/api/http.htmlLinks to an external site. fetch global (Node.js 18+): https://nodejs.org/api/globals.html#fetchLinks to an external site. Compose network_mode: https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/#network_modeLinks to an external site. Caddy reverse_proxy directive: https://caddyserver.com/docs/caddyfile/directives/reverse_proxyLinks to an external site. Notes The starting problem Your application calls users-service to look up user data. There is one instance, one hostname, and the call is direct. // app.js import http from 'node:http'; const getUser = async (userId) => { const res = await fetch(`http://users-service:5000/users/${userId}`); return res.json(); }; http.createServer(async (req, res) => { const userId = req.url.split('/').pop(); const user = await getUser(userId); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(JSON.stringify(user)); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('App listening on port 3000')); This works as long as there is exactly one users-service to call. The moment you want to split requests across two backend instances, or send a fraction of traffic to a new version you are testing, you have nowhere to put that decision except inside app.js, mixed into code whose job is to handle requests, not manage routing. Extending the example Change one line: instead of calling the real backend's hostname, app.js calls localhost. A separate container, the ambassador, listens on that same localhost interface and decides where each request actually goes. // app.js — now calls localhost instead of the real backend import http from 'node:http'; const getUser = async (userId) => { const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:5000/users/${userId}`); return res.json(); }; http.createServer(async (req, res) => { const userId = req.url.split('/').pop(); const user = await getUser(userId); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(JSON.stringify(user)); }).listen(3000, () => console.log('App listening on port 3000')); // ambassador.js import http from 'node:http'; const forwardTo = async (host, userId, res) => { const r = await fetch(`http://${host}/users/${userId}`); const data = await r.text(); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(data); }; http.createServer((req, res) => { const userId = parseInt(req.url.split('/').pop(), 10); const host = userId % 2 === 0 ? 'users-service-a:5000' : 'users-service-b:5000'; console.log(`Routing user ${userId} to ${host}`); forwardTo(host, userId, res); }).listen(5000, () => console.log('Ambassador listening on port 5000')); // backend.js — used by both users-service-a and users-service-b import http from 'node:http'; http.createServer((req, res) => { const userId = req.url.split('/').pop(); res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); res.end(JSON.stringify({ id: userId, servedBy: process.env.LABEL })); }).listen(5000, () => console.log(`Backend ${process.env.LABEL} listening on port 5000`)); Create a package.json to enable ES modules: { "type": "module" } # docker-compose.yml services: app: build: . command: node app.js ports: - "3000:3000" ambassador: build: . command: node ambassador.js network_mode: "service:app" users-service-a: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=A users-service-b: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=B # Dockerfile FROM node:24 WORKDIR /usr/src/app COPY . . network_mode: "service:app" puts the ambassador inside the same network namespace as app, so they share localhost the same way containers in the same pod would in production. Run docker compose up, then try: curl localhost:3000/users/42 curl localhost:3000/users/43 One comes back with "servedBy": "A" and the other with "servedBy": "B", even though app.js only ever called localhost:5000 and has no idea two backends exist. Naming the pattern This is the ambassador pattern: a proxy container placed in the path of a primary container's outgoing calls, making routing decisions on its behalf, while the primary container keeps calling a fixed local address and stays completely unaware of sharding, retries, or anything else the ambassador might be doing. The primary container's code does not change when you add sharding, retry logic, or an experiment. It is worth comparing this directly to Unit 6's sidecar. Both patterns deploy a helper container alongside a primary one and share a local resource with it. But a sidecar sits beside the primary doing auxiliary work the primary would otherwise have to do itself, like syncing content into a shared volume. An ambassador sits in the path of calls the primary was already going to make, intercepting and reshaping them. Sharding, what you just built, routes requests across multiple backend instances based on a key. The same shape supports a second use case called a canary deployment. The name comes from the mining practice of sending a canary into a coal mine ahead of workers: if the canary was harmed by toxic gas, miners knew to stay out. A canary deployment works the same way. When you have a new version of a service that you are not yet confident in, you route a small percentage of real production traffic to it, say 10%, and leave the rest on the stable version. If the new version has a bug or a performance problem, only that fraction of users is affected, and you can pull it back immediately. Ninety percent of traffic never touched it. Once you gain confidence, you raise the percentage until the new version handles everything. An ambassador makes this straightforward: instead of routing by user ID, it rolls a random number on each incoming request and sends a configurable fraction to the new version. The primary container's code never changes. The experiment can be started, adjusted, or cancelled by modifying the ambassador alone. Exercise Task: Add a canary experiment to ambassador.js. On top of the existing even-or-odd sharding, make 20% of all requests, regardless of user ID, go to users-service-b instead, chosen at random. Starting point: The ambassador.js and docker-compose.yml from the Notes above. You'll know it works when: sending 20 requests for the same even-numbered user ID results in most responses showing "servedBy": "A", but a noticeable fraction showing "servedBy": "B", and app.js did not need a single line changed. Real World The Notes version builds its own ambassador in JavaScript. In production, most teams use an existing reverse proxy for this role. This section replaces ambassador.js with Caddy, a lightweight web server and reverse proxy, to show that the ambassador pattern is not a coding exercise: it is an arrangement that already exists inside tools you can drop in. Create a Caddyfile that configures Caddy to listen on port 5000 and round-robin between two backends: :5000 { reverse_proxy users-service-a:5000 users-service-b:5000 { lb_policy round_robin } } Replace the ambassador service in docker-compose.yml with a Caddy container. The network_mode entry stays the same: services: app: build: . command: node app.js ports: - "3000:3000" caddy: image: caddy:2 volumes: - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile network_mode: "service:app" users-service-a: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=A users-service-b: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=B Run docker compose up, then send several requests: for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -s localhost:3000/users/2 | grep servedBy; done You should see alternating A and B responses. app.js is unchanged; the only thing that changed is which container acts as the ambassador. Caddy's reverse_proxy directive handles round-robin distribution, health checking, and connection pooling that you would otherwise have to implement yourself. Home Exercise Caddy's reverse_proxy accepts additional upstream addresses alongside the existing two. Add a third backend, users-service-c, to both the Caddyfile and docker-compose.yml: Update the Caddyfile: :5000 { reverse_proxy users-service-a:5000 users-service-b:5000 users-service-c:5000 { lb_policy round_robin } } Add to docker-compose.yml: users-service-c: build: . command: node backend.js environment: - LABEL=C You'll know it works when: sending 30 requests for the same user ID produces a mix of A, B, and C responses in roughly equal proportions, and you made this change entirely in Caddyfile and docker-compose.yml without touching app.js or backend.js. Looking Ahead Unit 8 introduces the third shape for a helper container. Unlike the sidecar, which adds capability beside the primary, or the ambassador, which intercepts the primary's outgoing calls, the adapter intercepts what the primary already produces and transforms it into a format that something else expects. Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing Schedule: Week 2 (Jul 13–17) Grade entry: Sprint 2 (half weight) Purpose Week 1 introduced the vocabulary of distributed systems: why latency and reliability are the two properties you measure first, what idempotency means and why it matters when services retry, and how concurrency creates coordination problems that do not exist on a single machine. Sprint 1 asks your team to apply that vocabulary to your chosen domain. No code is expected in this sprint. This is design thinking grounded in the concepts just studied. The deliverables are written artifacts that demonstrate you can reason about your system before you build it. Deliverables All three deliverables are committed to the team repository under a docs/ directory and linked from the README.md. 1. Refined project description (docs/PROJECT.md) Write a short document called docs/PROJECT.md (roughly one page) that refines the domain paragraph from Sprint 0 into a complete project description. It must address: Domain: What kind of system is this, and who does it serve? Scalability problem: What specific load or coordination challenge makes this domain require a scalable distributed web system? Be concrete: what happens when demand spikes, when a service goes down, or when data must be shared across multiple nodes? Computing for the Common Good framing: Who benefits when this system works correctly? Who is harmed when it fails or is slow?
