Also note like what goes into the course and what to be on\\n\\nany extra information you need access to from this leave in 'syllabus.md' \\nSkip To Content\\nDashboard\\nAustin Fairbanks\\nAccount\\nDashboard\\nCourses\\nGroups\\nCalendar\\nInbox\\nHistory\\nStudio\\nPortfolio\\n4 unread release notes.4\\nHelp\\nCOMPSCI 426 (170735) SUM26Pages⚖️ 426 U26 Syllabus (Summer Session II)\\n\\nSummer 2026\\nHome\\nAnnouncements\\nModules\\nGradescope\\nAssignments\\nQuizzes\\nDiscussions\\nPeople\\nIgniteAI Search\\n⚖️ 426 U26 Syllabus (Summer Session II)\\nCOMPSCI 426 Scalable Web Systems\\nNumber: COMPSCI 426\\nTitle: Scalable Web Systems\\nInstructor: Tim Richards\\nCanvas: https://umamherst.instructure.com/courses/38093\\nSemester: Summer Session II 2026\\nMode: Online, Asynchronous\\nScheduled Meetings: There are no scheduled meetings for this course. It is online and asynchronous.\\nExams: There are no exams in this course\\nGroups: There is group work in this course\\nCredits: 3\\nPrerequisites: COMPSCI 320 or COMPSCI 326 with a grade of C or better. If you are from another academic institution or have unique circumstances, you must submit an override requestLinks to an external site. to be considered for enrollment.\\nDescription\\nThe web has become a large and complex area for application development. Access to an abundance of open source languages, libraries, and frameworks has led to the quick and easy construction of a variety of applications with several moving parts working in coordination to present to the user the illusion of a single program. In reality, web applications are extremely difficult to get right. They involve a large collection of coordinated services, multiple databases, complicated user interfaces, security and performance issues, and ever changing third party services, spread across physical and virtual machines. These complications are further stressed by the large number of concurrent users that access these applications every second. This course investigates several well known web-based applications and the technology and software architecture used to scale them. We will also study specific topics related to scalability in software design in the context of web application architecture. This course is hands-on and heavily project-based; students will build, monitor, and load test a distributed system composed of coordinated services. This course counts as an Elective for the CS and INFORM Majors.\\n\\nThis course is concept-first and experiential. You will build and break real scalable systems before we put names to the patterns you discover. The vocabulary of the field, sidecars, ambassadors, sharding, scatter/gather, comes after you have already felt why each pattern exists.\\n\\nStaff\\nInstructor: Tim Richards\\nEmail: tdr@umass.edu\\nOffice Hours: By appointment, via Google Meet\\nTeaching Assistant: Miles (Mingzhe) Li\\nEmail: mingzhel@umass.edu\\nLearning Objectives\\nBy the end of this course, students will be able to:\\n\\nConfigure and use a devcontainer-based development environment with Docker and VS Code for a reproducible, team-consistent workspace.\\n\\nExplain the core properties of distributed systems, including latency, reliability, idempotency, and delivery semantics, and reason about the trade-offs between them.\\n\\nContainerize an application with Docker and orchestrate multiple coordinated services with Docker Compose.\\n\\nApply single-node patterns, including the sidecar, ambassador, and adapter patterns, to extend services without modifying them.\\n\\nDesign and reason about serving patterns, including replication, caching, sharding with consistent hashing, and scatter/gather.\\n\\nMeasure system behavior under load using k6, and interpret latency percentiles, throughput, and error rates.\\n\\nBuild event-driven and queue-based systems, including work queues, pub/sub pipelines, and dead letter queues.\\n\\nReason about distributed coordination, including locks, leases, ownership election, and concurrent data manipulation.\\n\\nInstrument a system for observability using structured logging, metrics, and tracing.\\n\\nDiagnose common distributed failure patterns, including thundering herd, versioning errors, and cascading failure.\\n\\nUse Git and GitHub for version control, branching, and pull request workflows on a shared team repository.\\n\\nPlan, build, and present a complete, scalable web system simulation as a team.\\n\\nTime Commitment\\nA three credit course does not get smaller when you compress it into six weeks; it gets denser. Plan for roughly twenty-two to twenty-three hours a week.\\n\\nUMass Amherst defines course workload by a standard credit hour rule. The guiding rule is forty five hours of work per semester for each unit of credit, on the assumption that each credit hour generates two hours of assigned work for every hour of in class contact. By that rule a three credit course represents about one hundred thirty five hours of total work, and the University expects the total workload for a three credit course to be at least 135 hours. That total is fixed. It is the same whether the course runs across a full semester or across a summer.\\n\\nWhat changes is how those hours are distributed. In a normal fifteen week semester, one hundred thirty five hours works out to about nine hours per week. This section is taught asynchronously over six weeks, so the same one hundred thirty five hours are compressed into roughly six weeks of effort, which comes to about twenty-two to twenty-three hours per week. There is no reduction in scope to go with the shorter calendar; you are doing a full three credit course in forty percent of the usual time, so the weekly pace is about two and a half times what the same course would demand in the fall or spring.\\n\\nTwenty-two hours a week is a serious commitment, and you should plan your summer around that reality. Spread across six working days it is just under four hours a day. Because each day's material builds directly on the day before, and because this is a systems course where one misconfigured service can block everything downstream, the work does not compress well into a weekend burst. Students who treat this as a part time effort fall behind quickly, and in a six week term there is very little room to recover. For that reason I strongly advise against pairing this course with another demanding summer course or with full time employment. If your situation makes twenty-two hours a week difficult, email me at tdr@umass.edu before the term begins so we can be honest about whether the timing works for you.\\n\\nTo make the number concrete, your weekly hours go toward the same components described elsewhere in this syllabus: working through several Knowledge Units, since the eighteen KUs are spread across the six weeks, including their preparatory reading, the activity, and the exercises; and steadily advancing your team's sprint project, which on its own accounts for a substantial share of your time over the term. The weekly quizzes are the clearest early signal of whether you are keeping pace. If you find yourself consistently spending far more than this, or far less and still finishing everything, let me know, because that is useful feedback on the course and may also be a sign we should look at how you are approaching the work.\\n\\nCourse Structure Synopsis\\nAsynchronous Delivery\\nThis course is offered in an online, asynchronous format. All course materials will be available online on the course website. You are expected to engage with the content and complete assignments on your own schedule within the given deadlines. This course is designed to be experiential, meaning that you will learn by doing, and the course structure is built around active participation and hands-on activities.\\n\\nKnowledge Units (KUs)\\nThe primary way in which learning takes place is through knowledge units (KUs). Each KU is a self-contained module that includes preparatory reading, hands-on activities, and exercises. You are expected to complete each KU in order, as they build upon one another. The course is deliberately concept-first: most units ask you to build or observe something before the underlying pattern is named, so that the name lands on an experience you already have rather than on an abstraction. Each KU will have a set of activities that you must complete, including coding and load-testing exercises.\\n\\nCanvas\\nCanvas is where you will find links to all of the course material. The syllabus and schedule can be found on Canvas. All assignments will be posted on Canvas. Grades will be posted to Canvas. Announcements will be posted on Canvas. If in doubt, go to Canvas to find what you are looking for and follow links from there.\\n\\nGradescope\\nHomework assignments are submitted through Gradescope and graded automatically. When you submit, an autograder runs your code against a test suite and reports a score immediately; you do not have to wait for manual review to see how you did. If a test fails, the output includes enough information to diagnose and fix the issue before the deadline. You may resubmit as many times as you like before the deadline, and only your final submission is graded. Gradescope is accessible through Canvas.\\n\\nCommunication\\nEmail the instructor at tdr@umass.edu for all course-related questions and requests. Every email must include [426] at the start of the subject line — for example, [426] Sprint 3 question. Emails without this prefix may be missed. See the full Communication section for guidance on what to include in your message.\\n\\nSpire\\nFinal grades will be posted to Canvas before they are submitted to Spire. You are expected to check your grades in both places to ensure that everything adds up. You are responsible for ensuring that your grades are accurate and that you have received credit for all assignments that you submitted by the posted deadline. If you notice any discrepancies, you should contact the course staff immediately.\\n\\nRequired Books, Equipment, and Technology\\nOne textbook, one container that carries the entire stack, and a machine capable of running it.\\n\\nThis course uses one textbook: Designing Distributed Systems, 2nd EditionLinks to an external site., by Brendan Burns (O'Reilly). You have free access to the book by logging in using your UMass credentials under “Other login options” and selecting “Affiliated with a school or institution?” The book frames containers as the vehicle for every pattern we study, and its treatment of patterns like the sidecar, the work queue, and dead letter queues is unusually thorough. Preparatory reading for the Knowledge Units draws directly from it. Beyond the textbook, everything you need to read is provided through as Knowledge Units, primers, and linked documentation. Where you need a reference for a specific tool, the course points you to that tool's official documentation.\\n\\nWhat this course also requires is a computer you control and that is capable of running a containerized development environment. You need a reasonably current laptop or desktop running macOS, Windows, or Linux, with enough memory and disk space to run Docker comfortably; eight gigabytes of RAM is a practical minimum and sixteen is more comfortable, along with several gigabytes of free disk space for container images and your project. A Chromebook or a tablet is not sufficient for this course, because neither can run the local development environment. If your only computer cannot meet these requirements, email the course staff at tdr@umass.edu during the first few days so we can help you find an alternative such as a loaner machine through the University. We will try, but we can't guarantee.\\n\\nNearly all of the software for this course is delivered through a single prepared development environment, a Dev Container that bundles the entire technology stack so you do not have to install or configure each piece by hand.\\n\\nDevelopment Environment\\nThis course uses development containers (devcontainers) to provide a uniform and consistent development environment for all students. Devcontainers are a way to package and distribute development environments using Docker containers. This allows you to have a consistent environment across different machines and operating systems, and ensures that you have all the necessary tools and dependencies installed.\\n\\nYou are not required to know much about Docker or devcontainers to begin, but you will need to have Docker installed on your machine, and over the course of the term you will come to understand containers deeply, since they are the central building block of the entire course. You will be required to use the devcontainer for all course-related work, including coding exercises, load tests, and the project.\\n\\nThe core software you will need to install is VS Code, Docker Desktop, and the VS Code Remote Containers extension. The devcontainer is configured to include the tools and dependencies for the course, including Node.js, npm, the Docker CLI and Compose, the k6 load testing tool, and Caddy as a reverse proxy and load balancer. Services and worker processes in this course are written in Node.js and JavaScript. You should not install this software right now, as you will be instructed on how to do so as part of the course setup unit.\\n\\nAssignments\\nWe use several different methods to scaffold your learning and assess your understanding of the material covered in this course. We outline the various methods and the kind of assessment below so you can better understand and plan your learning path. We categorize assignments as either being formative (F), summative (S), or a combination (FS). A purely formative assignment is designed to build your understanding, low stakes, and doesn't have any or very little impact on your grade. A summative assignment is designed to measure your understanding of the material. A combination of formative/summative contains aspects of low stakes assessment with measurement.\\n\\nAssessment Type\\tCount\\tWeight\\nExercises\\tShort practice exercises\\tF\\t>10\\t0%\\nParticipation\\tWeekly discussions and reflections\\t\\t6\\t5%\\nQuizzes\\t\\t\\t\\t20%\\nWeekly Quiz\\tF\\t6\\t\\nHomework\\t\\t\\t\\t30%\\nHomework\\tF\\t4\\t\\nSprints\\t\\t\\t\\t25%\\nSprint 1\\tFS\\t1\\t\\nSprint 2\\tFS\\t1\\t\\nSprint 3\\tFS\\t1\\t\\nSprint 4\\tFS\\t1\\t\\nSprint 5\\tS\\t1\\t\\nProject\\t\\t\\t\\t20%\\nGitHub Repository URL\\tS\\t1\\t\\nRecorded Video Demonstration\\tS\\t1\\t\\nProject Poster\\tS\\t1\\t\\nReflection\\tS\\t1\\t\\nExercises\\nPractice embedded in every unit, not graded, but expected.\\n\\nExercises are short activities built into each Knowledge Unit. They are not submitted and they do not count toward your grade. Many ask you to run a service under load with k6, observe a latency percentile or an error rate, and interpret what you see. The goal is practice: try something, get it wrong safely, and learn from it. You are expected to do the exercises; they exist to make the hands-on work in the Knowledge Units land rather than to generate a score.\\n\\nParticipation\\nSmall, low-stakes tasks spread across the term that keep you engaged with the course and your teammates-to-be.\\n\\nEach of the six weeks, Week 0 through Week 5, carries one participation task delivered natively on Canvas: Week 0 is a public discussion where you introduce yourself before project teams form; Weeks 1 through 5 are a short, private reflection survey connecting that week's Knowledge Units to your own experience. Both are graded on completion, not correctness or length, and both are generated directly from this repository rather than written by hand in Canvas. Together the six tasks make up five percent of your final grade.\\n\\nWeekly Quizzes\\nA timed, summative check on the week's material, taken at your own pace within 3 days after the week's completion.\\n\\nAfter each of the six content weeks you complete a timed quiz covering that week's Knowledge Units. Each quiz is multiple choice, approximately twenty questions, and you have forty-five minutes. You may take each quiz up to three times; your highest score is recorded. The quiz for the final week is cumulative across the full course. Together the six quizzes make up twenty percent of your final grade. Quizzes are available on Canvas.\\n\\nHomework\\nFour hands-on assignments that build the skills the project depends on.\\n\\nThere are four homework assignments across the term, one roughly every week and a half. Each is a hands-on task that involves creating parts of a simulated distributed system using real tools and services: k6 for load testing, JavaScript for building services, and existing services such as Caddy, Redis, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Prometheus, and Grafana. Homework is submitted through Gradescope and graded automatically against a rubric; you will see your score as soon as the autograder runs. Together the four assignments make up thirty percent of your final grade. Your scores from Gradescope will be periodically synced to Canvas.\\n\\nSprints\\nA simulated scalable system built incrementally: each sprint applies only what the previous week taught.\\n\\nThe Sprints are the team project itself, carried forward in stages rather than assembled at the end. Each sprint is due during the week after the Knowledge Units that inform it are covered, so the system grows in lockstep with the course material. You cannot design the full architecture at the start; you do not yet know the patterns. Instead the simulation is extended one layer at a time: Sprint 0 forms the team and stakes out a domain idea; Sprint 1 frames the scalability problem using the distributed systems vocabulary from Week Sprint 1: Project Definition and Scalability Framing\nSchedule: Week 2 (Jul 13–17)\n\nGrade entry: Sprint 2 (half weight)\n\nPurpose\nWeek 1 introduced the vocabulary of distributed systems: why latency and reliability are the two properties you measure first, what idempotency means and why it matters when services retry, and how concurrency creates coordination problems that do not exist on a single machine. Sprint 1 asks your team to apply that vocabulary to your chosen domain.\n\nNo code is expected in this sprint. This is design thinking grounded in the concepts just studied. The deliverables are written artifacts that demonstrate you can reason about your system before you build it.\n\nDeliverables\nAll three deliverables are committed to the team repository under a docs/ directory and linked from the README.md.\n\n1. Refined project description (docs/PROJECT.md)\nWrite a short document called docs/PROJECT.md (roughly one page) that refines the domain paragraph from Sprint 0 into a complete project description. It must address:\n\nDomain: What kind of system is this, and who does it serve?\nScalability problem: What specific load or coordination challenge makes this domain require a scalable distributed web system? Be concrete: what happens when demand spikes, when a service goes down, or when data must be shared across multiple nodes?\nComputing for the Common Good framing: Who benefits when this system works correctly? Who is harmed when it fails or is slow? This framing should motivate the latency and reliability requirements you will define below.\n2. Initial service list (docs/SERVICES.md)\nWrite a document called docs/SERVICES.md containing a bulleted list of the services your simulation will likely include, with one sentence describing what each service does. This is a first guess and will change as you learn more patterns in subsequent weeks.\n\nEach service entry should name the service and describe its role in one sentence:\n\ninventory-service: Manages stock levels for each pantry location and accepts update and query requests from the coordinator.\ncoordinator-service: Routes incoming distribution requests to the appropriate pantry location based on availability.\nThe target is team_size + 1 custom services: 3 for 2-person teams, 4 for 3-person teams, and one more per additional member. The extra service beyond per-member ownership is a shared component — a coordinator, gateway, or API layer that multiple members contribute to. Infrastructure containers (Caddy, Redis, Prometheus, Grafana) do not count. This list is a projection — you will not build all services in Sprint 1. Sprint 2 begins with 2; Sprint 4 adds at least one more.\n\n3. Service level objectives (docs/SLO.md)\nWrite a document called docs/SLO.md. It should be roughly half a page and define the system's service level objectives: the specific, measurable targets that describe what \"good enough\" looks like for your domain.\n\nFor each service you listed above, define at least two SLOs:\n\nLatency SLO: A percentile target and a threshold. For example: \"The inventory lookup endpoint must respond within 500 ms at the 95th percentile.\" Tie the target to the domain: name who is waiting and what happens when the threshold is exceeded.\nReliability SLO: A success rate target. For example: \"The distribution request endpoint must succeed at least 99% of the time.\" Reason about what at-least-once and at-most-once delivery semantics mean for each operation: a failed lookup is annoying; a double-counted distribution is a data integrity problem.\nThese SLOs do not need to be precise engineering targets yet. They are commitments that will inform your design decisions in later sprints and that you will measure against in Sprint 3 and Sprint 5. Write them as if you intend to hold your system to them.\n\nGrading\nSprint 1 is worth 50 points. It counts as half a sprint grade toward the Sprints total (30%).\n\nTeam (30 pts)\nCriterion\tPoints\ndocs/PROJECT.md, docs/SERVICES.md, and docs/SLO.md all exist in a docs/ directory and are linked from README.md\t5\ndocs/PROJECT.md: names a specific domain and community (5 pts); describes a concrete scalability problem with at least one named condition (5 pts); CFTCG framing names specific beneficiaries and a specific harm — not a restatement of the domain (5 pts)\t15\ndocs/SERVICES.md: lists team_size + 1 services; every entry has a formatted name (service-name) and a one-sentence role description\t5\ndocs/SLO.md: contains at least one latency SLO and at least one reliability SLO\t5\nAward 0 pts for a docs/PROJECT.md criterion if the content is absent or entirely generic (e.g. \"high traffic\" without a named condition). For docs/SERVICES.md, deduct 1 pt per entry missing a name or description, down to 0.\n\nIndividual (20 pts)\nGraded per student based on commit history and service ownership.\n\nCriterion\tPoints\nStudent has authored at least one commit to any of the three Sprint 1 documents before the deadline\t5\ndocs/SERVICES.md includes a service this student owns (identifiable by commit authorship in Sprint 2 onward) with a formatted name and one-sentence description\t5\ndocs/SLO.md contains both a latency SLO and a reliability SLO for their service; latency SLO names an endpoint, a percentile, and a threshold with units\t10\nA latency SLO without a percentile scores 5/10. Sprint 4 adds an asynchronous processing path to your simulation and introduces controlled failures that demonstrate the system can degrade gracefully rather than collapse completely. The distinction between synchronous and asynchronous processing matters for your domain. Some operations in your system should complete before a response is sent; others, particularly those that are expensive, retryable, or durable, belong in a queue. Sprint 4 asks you to identify at least one operation in your domain that fits the async pattern and build it that way. ## Deliverables ### 1. At least one async processing path The producer and consumer of an async path are typically separate services. For teams of 3 or more, the worker is a new standalone service. For 2-person teams, the worker logic can be added to an existing service rather than creating a new one. Either way, this sprint advances your team closer to the target of team_size + 1 custom services. Add at least one work queue or pub/sub channel, using the same tools Unit 14 and Unit 15 built them with: RabbitMQ for a work queue, Kafka for pub/sub. The choice of pattern should be motivated by your domain: Work queue (RabbitMQ): Use when a task needs to be picked up and processed by exactly one worker, and the result does not need to be returned to the original caller synchronously. Example: sending a notification after a distribution request is logged, or recalculating inventory totals after a batch update. Pub/sub (Kafka): Use when multiple downstream services need to react to the same event independently. Example: broadcasting an alert when a pantry location's stock drops below a threshold, so both the coordinator service and the notification service respond to the same event. The async path must be observable: log when a message is enqueued and when a worker picks it up and processes it. Add a rabbitmq or kafka service to your docker-compose.yml. This is new infrastructure, not the Redis cache from Sprint 3, which stays a cache. Give the broker its own healthcheck, matching the setup from Unit 14 or Unit 15, so any service that depends on it can use depends_on with condition: service_healthy rather than just waiting for the container to start. ### 2. Health check endpoints on all services Add a GET /health endpoint to every service in your system. The endpoint must return a JSON response indicating the service is running: { "status": "ok" } Wire these health check endpoints into the Docker Compose healthcheck configuration for each service so that Docker knows when a service is ready to receive traffic. Services that depend on other services must use depends_on with a condition: service_healthy check. ### 3. At least one scripted failure scenario Add a mechanism to one of your services that allows it to be made to fail or slow down on demand. This could be an environment variable that toggles a fault injection mode, an endpoint that forces the service to return errors or inject extra latency, or a script that kills a worker process. Write a short description (roughly half a page) committed to the repository as results/sprint-4-failure.md. The description must explain: What the failure scenario is How to trigger it How the system responds (does it degrade gracefully, queue up work, return errors, or something else?) What a real system would do differently in production ### 4. Updated system diagram (`docs/SERVICES.md`) Update the diagram in docs/SERVICES.md to add the async path: the producer, the RabbitMQ- or Kafka-backed queue or pub/sub channel, and the consumer or worker. As with Sprint 3, this should be the complete system diagram, not just the new pieces. ## Example Repository Structure This sprint adds the async path. For teams of three or more, the worker is a new standalone service and gets its own top-level directory, shown below as alert-worker/. For two-person teams, the worker logic can instead live inside an existing service’s code rather than a new directory. Either way, this sprint also adds results/sprint-4-failure.md alongside the load test summary from Sprint 3. 426-project-pantry-network/ ├── README.md ├── docker-compose.yml ├── docs/ │ ├── PROJECT.md │ ├── SERVICES.md │ └── SLO.md ├── results/ │ ├── sprint-3-load-test.md │ └── sprint-4-failure.md ├── load-tests/ │ └── sprint-3-load.js ├── caddy/ │ └── Caddyfile ├── inventory-service/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ ├── package.json │ └── src/ │ └── index.js ├── coordinator-service/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ ├── package.json │ └── src/ │ └── index.js ├── coordinator-sidecar/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ ├── package.json │ └── src/ │ └── index.js └── alert-worker/ ├── Dockerfile ├── package.json └── src/ └── index.js Health check endpoints do not add new files here since they are additions to each existing service’s own code and to the healthcheck blocks already in docker-compose.yml. ## Checking Your Work You'll know this sprint is complete when: docker compose up starts all services, including the RabbitMQ or Kafka broker, and all health checks pass. Submit the repository URL through Canvas by the Sprint 4 deadline. # 426-project--Team-9- Blue Light ## Team Roster | GitHub Username | UMass Email | |-----------------|-------------| |austinfairbanks|afairbanks@umass.edu| |Dos0n|bdo@umass.edu |ShriRadhakrishnan1|sradhakrishn@umass.edu| | | | ## Domain Description Our system simulates a distributed mobile blue-light emergency response network that routes emergency requests across multiple regions, including university campuses, transit hubs, stadiums, shopping centers, and other public venues. Users submit requests through a mobile application, and the system is responsible for determining the appropriate response, routing the request to the correct regional service, and keeping responders and users updated throughout the incident. A single server becomes insufficient when the system experiences sudden spikes in demand, such as during large public events, severe weather, or multiple simultaneous emergencies. During these periods, the system must rapidly process incoming requests, determine user locations, prioritize incidents based on severity, and notify the appropriate local responders without introducing delays. Distributing the workload across multiple servers allows the system to remain responsive and available even under heavy load. From a Computing for the Common Good perspective, a reliable emergency response system directly improves public safety. Students, commuters, event attendees, employees, and other members of the public all benefit from fast and dependable access to emergency services. When the system performs well, people receive timely police, medical, security, or crisis-response assistance. When it fails or becomes overloaded, delayed or misrouted requests can increase response times and potentially place people in dangerous situations. Each response exposes `servedBy` so replica selection is observable. `GET /route` is Redis-cached: the cache key normalizes `latitude`/`longitude` to six decimal places and combines it with `emergencyType`, so an exact repeated lookup (e.g. many requests during an event at the Mullins Center) becomes a cache hit shared across all three replicas, without merging distinct nearby venues into the same key. Each response's `cache` field reports `"HIT"` or `"MISS"`, and every replica logs the cache key and outcome for each request. If Redis is unreachable, a lookup falls back to computing the route directly rather than failing the request. - `regional-routing-load-balancer`: Caddy load balancer that checks each routing replica's `/health` endpoint and distributes requests across healthy replicas using round-robin selection. - `redis`: Shared Redis cache used by all three `regional-routing-service` replicas for `GET /route` results, keyed by rounded location and emergency type with a 30-second TTL (`ROUTE_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS`). - `regional-routing-ambassador` (Owner: `@ShriRadhakrishnan1`): Ambassador proxy in front of the routing load balancer; forwards lookups, applies timeout/retry under load, and logs each upstream attempt. - `incident-ambassador` (Owner: `@Dos0n`): Ambassador proxy in front of `incident-service`; forwards `GET` and `POST` requests, retries safe (`GET`/`HEAD`) requests on timeout or 5xx, never retries `POST /incidents` to avoid duplicate incident creation, applies a simulated request-inspection delay via `setTimeout` before replying, and logs each upstream attempt. - `responder-dispatch-service` (Owner: `@Dos0n`): Simulates notifying and assigning the appropriate security, medical, police, or crisis-response team via `POST /dispatches` (body: `incidentId`, `teamId`), tracks dispatch status through `GET /dispatches/:dispatchId` and `PATCH /dispatches/:dispatchId/status`, and lists the response-team roster via `GET /teams`. ## Current Sprint 4 Container Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR client[Phone / Web Client] subgraph compose[Docker Compose] incident[incident-service

GET /incidents/:incidentId| incidentAmbassador incidentAmbassador -->|Forward through Compose DNS| incident incident -->|Persistent job after valid POST /incidents| rabbitmq rabbitmq -->|Deliver to one consumer| notificationWorker client -->|GET /route
GET /regions| routingAmbassador routingAmbassador -->|One stable upstream| routingLoadBalancer routingLoadBalancer -->|Healthy upstream| routingA routingLoadBalancer -->|Healthy upstream| routingB routingLoadBalancer -->|Healthy upstream| routingC routingA -->|Cache GET/SET on /route| redis routingB -->|Cache GET/SET on /route| redis routingC -->|Cache GET/SET on /route| redis client -->|POST /dispatches
GET /dispatches/:dispatchId
GET /teams| dispatch ``` The primary HTTP services remain separate client-facing paths in Sprint 4; `incident-service`, `regional-routing-service`, and `responder-dispatch-service` do not call each other directly. A valid incident creation now branches into asynchronous work: `incident-service` publishes a persistent job to RabbitMQ and returns after broker confirmation without waiting for `emergency-notification-worker` to process it. RabbitMQ holds jobs while the worker is unavailable and redelivers a job when a worker disconnects before acknowledging it. Two primary services remain reachable through their observable ambassador containers: `incident-ambassador` is the public path to `incident-service`, and `regional-routing-ambassador` reaches the routing replicas through Caddy. `responder-dispatch-service` is reached directly, with no ambassador in front of it. Redis remains exclusively the shared routing cache and does not carry Sprint 4 notification work. The regional routing service is replicated because routing is naturally stateless. Every replica receives the location and emergency type, loads the same synthetic regional map, and computes the answer independently. No request depends on mutable state held by a particular replica. Caddy can therefore send a request to any healthy replica and remove a failed replica without changing routing results. ## Sprint 3 Routing Replication and Caddy Verification Run these commands from the Gantry devcontainer. Start the complete system and validate Caddy's loaded configuration: ```bash docker compose up --build -d docker compose exec regional-routing-load-balancer \ caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile docker compose ps ``` Send nine requests through the public routing ambassador. All three `servedBy` values should appear: ```bash for request_number in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9; do curl -fsS \ 'http://localhost:3002/route?latitude=42.3868&longitude=-72.5301&emergencyType=medical' \ | jq -r '.servedBy' done ``` Stop replica B, wait longer than Caddy's two-second health-check interval, and repeat the requests. Every request should still succeed, and only replicas A and C should appear: ```bash docker compose stop regional-routing-service-b sleep 3 for request_number in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -fsS \ 'http://localhost:3002/route?latitude=42.3868&longitude=-72.5301&emergencyType=medical' \ | jq -r '.servedBy' done ``` Restore replica B and confirm that the full system returns to a healthy state: ```bash docker compose start regional-routing-service-b docker compose ps ``` Regression-check the other existing service paths: ```bash curl -fsS http://localhost:3003/health | jq curl -fsS http://localhost:3004/health | jq ``` ### Recorded Validation: July 30, 2026 The complete system built and started with `docker compose up --build -d`, and every service with a configured health check reported healthy. Some operations in your system should complete before a response is sent; others, particularly those that are expensive, retryable, or durable, belong in a queue. Sprint 4 asks you to identify at least one operation in your domain that fits the async pattern and build it that way.\n\n## Deliverables\n### 1. At least one async processing path\nThe producer and consumer of an async path are typically separate services. For teams of 3 or more, the worker is a new standalone service. The choice of pattern should be motivated by your domain:\n\nWork queue (RabbitMQ): Use when a task needs to be picked up and processed by exactly one worker, and the result does not need to be returned to the original caller synchronously. Example: sending a notification after a distribution request is logged, or recalculating inventory totals after a batch update.\nPub/sub (Kafka): Use when multiple downstream services need to react to the same event independently. Example: broadcasting an alert when a pantry location's stock drops below a threshold, so both the coordinator service and the notification service respond to the same event.\nThe async path must be observable: log when a message is enqueued and when a worker picks it up and processes it. Add a rabbitmq or kafka service to your docker-compose.yml. This is new infrastructure, not the Redis cache from Sprint 3, which stays a cache. Give the broker its own healthcheck, matching the setup from Unit 14 or Unit 15, so any service that depends on it can use depends_on with condition: service_healthy rather than just waiting for the container to start.\n\n### 2. # Sprint 5 Summary: Observability, Final Measurement, and Delivery

Use this summary when finishing, measuring, demonstrating, or submitting the final project system and its four capstone artifacts.

## Timing and Grading Context

- Schedule: Week 6, August 10–14, 2026, the final course week.
- This instruction page is not separately graded and receives no submission.
- The graded work is split across four separate Project assignments worth 20% of the course grade, separate from the 25% Sprints category.
- All four artifacts are due by the course end date with no late window; check each Canvas assignment for its exact due date and time.
- There is no separate Week 6 reflection; the Project Individual Reflection replaces it.

These category weights agree with the saved syllabus.

## Required Final System State

Complete all instrumentation and measurement work before recording the video or writing the poster. Sprint 5 adds no new service.

### Metrics and Prometheus

Every custom service must:

- expose `GET /metrics` in Prometheus text format;
- count requests received; and
- record response time in milliseconds in a histogram.

Add Prometheus to root `docker-compose.yml` and configure it to scrape every custom service.

### Grafana

Add Grafana to root `docker-compose.yml`, connect it to Prometheus, and provision a committed dashboard that loads automatically without manual demo setup. At minimum, the main service path must display:

- request rate in requests per second;
- error rate as the percentage of non-2xx responses; and
- p95 latency.

### Structured Logging

Every custom service must output JSON log objects containing at least `timestamp`, `level`, and `message`. Request logs must also include HTTP method, path, status code, and response time.

### Final k6 Evidence

Run the final k6 test against the fully instrumented primary request path for at least 60 seconds with at least 10 virtual users. Commit the script near the other load tests and write `results/sprint-5-load-test.md` containing:

1. The complete k6 summary output.
2. A pass/fail comparison against every relevant target in `docs/SLO.md`.
3. A comparison with Sprint 3 latency and error rate after async processing, health checks, and observability were added.
4. A bottleneck interpretation and what the team would change with another sprint.

## Capstone Artifacts

| Artifact | Submission responsibility | Points |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Project: GitHub Repository | Once per team | 100 |
| Project: Recorded Video Demonstration | Once per team | 60 |
| Project: Poster | Once per team | 50 |
| Project: Individual Reflection | Each team member | 40 |

The repository and video are graded against the completed, instrumented system. The video, poster, and reflection are submitted directly through Canvas rather than committed to the repository.

See `course-docs/pages/project-github-repository/summary.md` for the final repository acceptance criteria, `course-docs/pages/project-recorded-video-demonstration/summary.md` for the live demo and participation requirements, `course-docs/pages/project-poster/summary.md` for the poster's content, format, and rubric requirements, and `course-docs/pages/project-individual-reflection/summary.md` for the individual evidence and writing requirements.

## Recommended Sequence

1. Instrument every service, provision Prometheus and Grafana, and verify a fresh clone starts cleanly with one `docker compose up`.
2. Run the final load test, write the report, and finalize `docs/SERVICES.md`.
3. Freeze the stable system, then record the video and prepare the poster.
4. Have each member write the individual reflection using actual commit and pull-request links.

# Sprint 5: Observability, Final Measurement, and Delivery

Schedule: Week 6 (Aug 10–14) · This page: instructions only, not graded, see the four Project assignments below

## Overview

Week 6 is the final delivery week. There is no new unit and no new service to build. Your team instruments the system you have built across the previous five sprints, produces the final load test evidence, and delivers the four capstone artifacts that together make up the Project category of your grade.

Sprint 5 introduces no new services. It asks a different question than every sprint before it: does what you already built actually hold up when it is measured under load, watched through a dashboard, and handed to someone who has never seen it before?

Note: this page carries no separate score. It is the set of instructions for the week. The work is graded through the four Project assignments listed below, each its own Canvas assignment, which together are worth 20% of your course grade, separate from the Sprints total (25%). Nothing on this page is submitted here.

## What "Finished" Means

Before you record anything or write anything, get the system into the state the rest of the week assumes. Work through this list first:

### 1. Prometheus metrics on all custom services

Add Prometheus metrics to all of your team's custom services. At minimum, each service must expose:

- A counter tracking the number of requests received
- A histogram tracking response time in milliseconds

Expose these metrics at a GET /metrics endpoint in the Prometheus text format. Add a Prometheus service to docker-compose.yml that scrapes those endpoints.

### 2. Grafana dashboard

Add a Grafana service to docker-compose.yml connected to your Prometheus instance. Configure a dashboard that displays, at minimum:

- Request rate (requests per second) for the main service path
- Error rate (percentage of requests that return a non-2xx status)
- p95 latency for the main service path

SOURCE # Sprint 5: Observability, Final Measurement, and Delivery Schedule: Week 6 (Aug 10–14) · This page: instructions only, not graded, see the four Project assignments below ## Overview Week 6 is the final delivery week. There is no new unit and no new service to build. Your team instruments the system you have built across the previous five sprints, produces the final load test evidence, and delivers the four capstone artifacts that together make up the Project category of your grade. Sprint 5 introduces no new services. It asks a different question than every sprint before it: does what you already built actually hold up when it is measured under load, watched through a dashboard, and handed to someone who has never seen it before? Note: this page carries no separate score. It is the set of instructions for the week. The work is graded through the four Project assignments listed below, each its own Canvas assignment, which together are worth 20% of your course grade, separate from the Sprints total (25%). Nothing on this page is submitted here. ## What "Finished" Means Before you record anything or write anything, get the system into the state the rest of the week assumes. Work through this list first: ### 1. Prometheus metrics on all custom services Add Prometheus metrics to all of your team's custom services. At minimum, each service must expose: - A counter tracking the number of requests received - A histogram tracking response time in milliseconds Expose these metrics at a GET /metrics endpoint in the Prometheus text format. Add a Prometheus service to docker-compose.yml that scrapes those endpoints. ### 2. Grafana dashboard Add a Grafana service to docker-compose.yml connected to your Prometheus instance. Configure a dashboard that displays, at minimum: - Request rate (requests per second) for the main service path - Error rate (percentage of requests that return a non-2xx status) - p95 latency for the main service path The dashboard must be committed to the repository as a JSON export so it loads automatically when Grafana starts. Do not require manual dashboard configuration as part of the demo. ### 3. Structured log output from all custom services Add structured JSON logging to all of your team's custom services. Each log line must be a JSON object that includes at minimum: a timestamp, a log level, and a message. For request logs, include the HTTP method, path, status code, and response time. ### 4. Final k6 load test with written interpretation Run a final k6 load test against your system in its fully instrumented state. The load test must exercise the primary request path of your system and run for at least 60 seconds with at least 10 virtual users. Write a final load test report committed to the repository as results/sprint-5-load-test.md. The report must include: - The full k6 summary output (copy it into the document) - A comparison against your docs/SLO.md targets: which SLOs is the final system meeting, and which are not? - A comparison with the Sprint 3 load test results: how did latency and error rate change after adding async processing, health checks, and observability instrumentation? - An interpretation: where is the bottleneck in the final system? What would you change if you had another sprint? Do all four of these before you record the video or write the poster. The GitHub Repository and Video artifacts below are graded on this state of the system, not on a promise that it exists. ## The Four Capstone Artifacts Each artifact is its own Canvas assignment with its own rubric, linked from this Week 06 module. Three are submitted once per team; the reflection is submitted individually by every team member, and takes the place of a Week 6 Reflection, there is no separate weekly reflection this week. | Artifact | Submitted | Points | | --- | --- | ---: | | Project: GitHub Repository | Once per team | 100 | | Project: Recorded Video Demonstration | Once per team | 60 | | Project: Poster | Once per team | 50 | | Project: Individual Reflection | By each team member | 40 | All four are due by the course end date. There is no late window on the final deliverables, because grades are due to the university shortly afterward. See each assignment's own due date on Canvas. ## Example Repository Structure This is the final technical structure, adding a prometheus/ directory for the scrape configuration and a grafana/ directory holding the dashboard JSON export so it loads automatically, alongside the final load test report and script. As in every prior sprint, this is the same illustrative food pantry example; your team's actual layout will differ in names, service count, and organization. ```text 426-project-pantry-network/ ├── README.md ├── docker-compose.yml ├── docs/ │ ├── PROJECT.md │ ├── SERVICES.md │ └── SLO.md ├── results/ │ ├── sprint-3-load-test.md │ ├── sprint-4-failure.md │ └── sprint-5-load-test.md ├── load-tests/ │ ├── sprint-3-load.js │ └── sprint-5-load.js ├── caddy/ │ └── Caddyfile ├── prometheus/ │ └── prometheus.yml ├── grafana/ │ └── provisioning/ │ └── dashboards/ │ └── system-overview.json ├── inventory-service/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ ├── package.json │ └── src/ │ └── index.js ├── coordinator-service/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ ├── package.json │ └── src/ │ └── index.js ├── coordinator-sidecar/ │ ├── Dockerfile │ ├── package.json │ └── src/ │ └── index.js └── alert-worker/ ├── Dockerfile ├── package.json └── src/ └── index.js ``` The video, poster, and individual reflection are submitted directly through Canvas, not committed to the repository, so they do not appear in this tree. ## A Suggested Order for the Week Teams that leave the video and poster until the last day usually end up recording a demo of a system they were still changing an hour earlier. A workable order: - Early in the week. Instrument every service (Prometheus metrics, structured logging), stand up Grafana with the committed dashboard, and confirm docker compose up starts everything cleanly from a fresh clone. - Mid week. Run the final k6 load test against the fully instrumented system, write results/sprint-5-load-test.md, and bring docs/SERVICES.md to its final, complete state. - Late in the week. Record the video against the now-stable, instrumented system, and write the poster while the architecture is fresh in your head. - Last. # AI: This file was generated with AI assistance. See AI-DISCLOSURE.md and ai/chats/2026-08-06-201302-austinf-sprint4-rabbitmq.jsonl.
set -euo pipefail

readonly queue_name="${NOTIFICATION_QUEUE:-incident-notification-jobs}"
readonly normal_processing_ms="${NOTIFICATION_PROCESSING_MS:-500}"
readonly health_wait_attempts="${HEALTH_WAIT_ATTEMPTS:-180}"
readonly worker_service="emergency-notification-worker"
readonly -a compose=(docker compose)

restore_mode="none"

fail() {
  printf 'FAIL %s\n' "$1" >&2
  exit 1
}

phase() {
  printf '\n==> %s\n' "$1"
}

restore_normal_worker() {
  case "$restore_mode" in
    start)
      printf '\nRestarting previously running %s...\n' "$worker_service" >&2
      "${compose[@]}" start "$worker_service" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      ;;
    recreate)
      printf '\nRestoring %s with %s ms processing delay...\n' \
        "$worker_service" "$normal_processing_ms" >&2
      NOTIFICATION_PROCESSING_MS="$normal_processing_ms" \
        "${compose[@]}" up -d --force-recreate "$worker_service" \
        >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      ;;
  esac
}

trap restore_normal_worker EXIT

wait_for_health() {
  local service="$1"
  local container_id
  local health_status

  for ((_attempt = 1; _attempt <= health_wait_attempts; _attempt += 1)); do
    container_id="$("${compose[@]}" ps -q "$service")"

    if [[ -n "$container_id" ]]; then
      health_status="$(
        docker inspect \
          --format '{{if .State.Health}}{{.State.Health.Status}}{{else}}missing{{end}}' \
          "$container_id" 2>/dev/null || true
      )"

      if [[ "$health_status" == "healthy" ]]; then
        return
      fi
    fi

    sleep 2
  done

  "${compose[@]}" ps "$service" >&2 || true
  "${compose[@]}" logs --no-color "$service" >&2 || true
  fail "$service did not become healthy"
}

queue_ready_count() {
  "${compose[@]}" exec -T incident-service \
    node --input-type=module -e '
      import amqp from "amqplib";

      const connection = await amqp.connect({
        protocol: "amqp",
        hostname: process.env.RABBITMQ_HOST,
        port: Number(process.env.RABBITMQ_PORT),
        username: process.env.RABBITMQ_USER,
        password: process.env.RABBITMQ_PASSWORD,
        heartbeat: Number(process.env.RABBITMQ_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS),
      });
      const channel = await connection.createChannel();
      const queue = await channel.checkQueue(process.env.NOTIFICATION_QUEUE);

      console.log(queue.messageCount);
      await channel.close();
      await connection.close();
    '
}

assert_queue_empty() {
  local ready

  ready="$(queue_ready_count)"

  if [[ "$ready" != "0" ]]; then
    fail "queue $queue_name already contains ready=$ready"
  fi
}

wait_for_queue_ready() {
  local expected_ready="$1"
  local ready

  for _attempt in {1..45}; do
    ready="$(queue_ready_count)"

    if [[ "$ready" == "$expected_ready" ]]; then
      return
    fi

    sleep 1
  done

  fail "queue $queue_name did not reach ready=$expected_ready"
}

wait_for_log() {
  local service="$1"
  local pattern="$2"
  local logs

  for _attempt in {1..45}; do
    logs="$("${compose[@]}" logs --no-color --no-log-prefix "$service" 2>/dev/null || true)"

    if printf '%s\n' "$logs" | rg -q "$pattern"; then
      return
    fi

    sleep 1
  done

  "${compose[@]}" logs --no-color "$service" >&2 || true
  fail "$service logs did not match: $pattern"
}

enqueue_log_count() {
  local logs
  local count

  logs="$("${compose[@]}" logs --no-color --no-log-prefix incident-service 2>/dev/null || true)"
  count="$(printf '%s\n' "$logs" | rg -c '"event":"incident_notification_enqueued"' || true)"
  printf '%s\n' "${count:-0}"
}

published_port() {
  local service="$1"
  local container_port="$2"
  local mapping
  local port

  mapping="$("${compose[@]}" port "$service" "$container_port" | tail -n 1)"
  port="${mapping##*:}"

  [[ "$port" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || fail "could not resolve host port for $service"
  printf '%s\n' "$port"
}

create_incident() {
  local base_url="$1"
  local venue="$2"

  curl -fsS -X POST "$base_url/incidents" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data "{\"emergencyType\":\"medical\",\"severity\":\"critical\",\"location\":{\"latitude\":42.3868,\"longitude\":-72.5301,\"venue\":\"$venue\"}}"
}

phase "Start the Sprint 4 asynchronous subsystem"
existing_worker_id="$("${compose[@]}" ps -q "$worker_service")"

if [[ -n "$existing_worker_id" ]]; then
  restore_mode="start"
  "${compose[@]}" stop "$worker_service"
fi

"${compose[@]}" up -d rabbitmq
wait_for_health rabbitmq

"${compose[@]}" build \
  "$worker_service" \
  incident-service \
  incident-ambassador

"${compose[@]}" up --force-recreate -d incident-service
wait_for_health incident-service
assert_queue_empty

"${compose[@]}" up --force-recreate -d \
  "$worker_service" \
  incident-ambassador

wait_for_health "$worker_service"
restore_mode="none"
wait_for_health incident-ambassador

readonly incident_port="$(published_port incident-ambassador 3000)"
readonly incident_base_url="http://127.0.0.1:$incident_port"

wait_for_queue_ready 0

phase "Verify normal enqueue, delivery, processing, and acknowledgment"
normal_response="$(create_incident "$incident_base_url" "Gate 4 normal flow")"
normal_incident_id="$(jq -er '.incidentId' <<<"$normal_response")"

wait_for_log incident-service \
  "\"event\":\"incident_notification_enqueued\".*\"incidentId\":\"$normal_incident_id\""
wait_for_log "$worker_service" \
  "\"event\":\"incident_notification_received\".*\"incidentId\":\"$normal_incident_id\""
wait_for_log "$worker_service" \
  "\"event\":\"incident_notification_completed\".*\"incidentId\":\"$normal_incident_id\""
wait_for_queue_ready 0
printf 'PASS normal enqueue and consume\n'

phase "Verify invalid and read-only requests do not enqueue"
enqueue_count_before="$(enqueue_log_count)"
invalid_status="$(
  curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
    -X POST "$incident_base_url/incidents" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data '{}'
)"

[[ "$invalid_status" == "400" ]] || fail "invalid incident returned HTTP $invalid_status instead of 400"
curl -fsS "$incident_base_url/health" >/dev/null
curl -fsS "$incident_base_url/incidents/$normal_incident_id" >/dev/null

enqueue_count_after="$(enqueue_log_count)"
[[ "$enqueue_count_after" == "$enqueue_count_before" ]] || \
  fail "invalid or read-only request unexpectedly enqueued work"
wait_for_queue_ready 0
printf 'PASS invalid and read-only requests do not enqueue\n'

phase "Verify RabbitMQ retains work while the worker is stopped"
restore_mode="start"
"${compose[@]}" stop "$worker_service"

queued_response="$(create_incident "$incident_base_url" "Gate 4 queued flow")"
queued_incident_id="$(jq -er '.incidentId' <<<"$queued_response")"

# Blue Light

A simulated distributed emergency-response system built by Team 9 for COMPSCI
426. The system accepts incident reports, routes requests to an appropriate
regional response group, assigns responder teams, and publishes asynchronous
notification work.

## Team Roster

| GitHub Username | UMass Email |
| --- | --- |
| austinfairbanks | afairbanks@umass.edu |
| Dos0n | bdo@umass.edu |
| ShriRadhakrishnan1 | sradhakrishn@umass.edu |

## Domain Description

Our system simulates a distributed mobile blue-light emergency response network that routes emergency requests across multiple regions, including university campuses, transit hubs, stadiums, shopping centers, and other public venues. Users submit requests through a mobile application, and the system is responsible for determining the appropriate response, routing the request to the correct regional service, and keeping responders and users updated throughout the incident.

A single server becomes insufficient when the system experiences sudden spikes in demand, such as during large public events, severe weather, or multiple simultaneous emergencies. During these periods, the system must rapidly process incoming requests, determine user locations, prioritize incidents based on severity, and notify the appropriate local responders without introducing delays. Distributing the workload across multiple servers allows the system to remain responsive and available even under heavy load.

From a Computing for the Common Good perspective, a reliable emergency response system directly improves public safety. Students, commuters, event attendees, employees, and other members of the public all benefit from fast and dependable access to emergency services. When the system performs well, people receive timely police, medical, security, or crisis-response assistance. When it fails or becomes overloaded, delayed or misrouted requests can increase response times and potentially place people in dangerous situations. There are also inherent flaws with physical blue light alarms as they may not always be accessible during times of need, which makes being able to use blue light systems from one's phone the natural way to improve accessibility.

## Start the Complete System

Requirements:

- Docker with Docker Compose
- The course Gantry devcontainer

From the repository root:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up --build
```

The `.env` copy is optional because every Compose variable has a local default,
but keeping one makes overrides explicit. Wait until `docker compose ps` shows
the services as healthy before sending requests. Stop the system with:

```bash
docker compose down
```

## Service Endpoints

| Component | Default host URL | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regional routing ambassador | `http://localhost:3002` | Public routing path, including `GET /route` |
| Incident ambassador | `http://localhost:3003` | Public incident path, including `POST /incidents` |
| Responder dispatch service | `http://localhost:3004` | Dispatch creation, lookup, and status updates |
| Notification worker HTTP server | `http://localhost:3005` | Worker health and metrics endpoints |
| Prometheus | `http://localhost:9090` | Metrics targets, queries, and graphs |
| RabbitMQ management | `http://localhost:15672` | Local queue administration |

The incident service, three routing replicas, Caddy, Redis, and RabbitMQ's
service ports are connected through Compose DNS and do not need public HTTP
ports. See [docs/SERVICES.md](docs/SERVICES.md) for the complete architecture.

## Prometheus Metrics

Every custom service exposes `GET /metrics` in Prometheus text format. The
endpoint includes:

- `http_requests_total`, labeled by service, method, normalized route, and
  status code.
- `http_request_duration_milliseconds`, a response-time histogram using
  millisecond buckets.

Prometheus scrapes eight running targets: the incident service and ambassador,
all three routing replicas, the routing ambassador, the dispatch service, and
the notification worker. Inspect their status at
`http://localhost:9090/targets`.

The main routing path can be queried with these PromQL expressions:

```promql
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="regional-routing-ambassador",route="/route"}[1m]))
```

```promql
100 * (sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="regional-routing-ambassador",route="/route",status_code!~"2.."}[1m])) or vector(0))
  / clamp_min(sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="regional-routing-ambassador",route="/route"}[1m])), 0.000001)
```

```promql
histogram_quantile(
  0.95,
  sum by (le) (
    rate(http_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket{service="regional-routing-ambassador",route="/route"}[1m])
  )
)
```

The last expression returns milliseconds because the underlying histogram is
recorded in milliseconds.

## Environment Variables

All variables are optional. When a variable is missing, Compose uses the local
default shown below.

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `INCIDENT_LATENCY_MS` | `200` | Simulated incident-service response latency |
| `ROUTING_AMBASSADOR_PORT` | `3002` | Routing ambassador host port |
| `ROUTING_LATENCY_MS` | `200` | Simulated routing-service miss latency |
| `ROUTING_UPSTREAM_URL` | `http://regional-routing-load-balancer:3000` | Routing ambassador upstream |
| `ROUTING_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS` | `2000` | Routing ambassador upstream timeout |
| `ROUTING_MAX_RETRIES` | `2` | Safe routing request retries |
| `ROUTE_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS` | `30` | Redis route-cache lifetime |
| `INCIDENT_AMBASSADOR_PORT` | `3003` | Incident ambassador host port |
| `INCIDENT_UPSTREAM_URL` | `http://incident-service:3000` | Incident ambassador upstream |
| `INCIDENT_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS` | `2000` | Incident ambassador upstream timeout |
| `INCIDENT_MAX_RETRIES` | `2` | Safe incident request retries |
| `INCIDENT_AMBASSADOR_PROCESSING_DELAY_MS` | `50` | Simulated ambassador processing overhead |

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# AI: This file was generated with AI assistance. See AI-DISCLOSURE.md and ai/chats/2026-08-06-201302-austinf-sprint4-rabbitmq.jsonl.
set -euo pipefail

readonly queue_name="${NOTIFICATION_QUEUE:-incident-notification-jobs}"
readonly normal_processing_ms="${NOTIFICATION_PROCESSING_MS:-500}"
readonly health_wait_attempts="${HEALTH_WAIT_ATTEMPTS:-180}"
readonly worker_service="emergency-notification-worker"
readonly -a compose=(docker compose)

restore_mode="none"

fail() {
  printf 'FAIL %s\n' "$1" >&2
  exit 1
}

phase() {
  printf '\n==> %s\n' "$1"
}

restore_normal_worker() {
  case "$restore_mode" in
    start)
      printf '\nRestarting previously running %s...\n' "$worker_service" >&2
      "${compose[@]}" start "$worker_service" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      ;;
    recreate)
      printf '\nRestoring %s with %s ms processing delay...\n' \
        "$worker_service" "$normal_processing_ms" >&2
      NOTIFICATION_PROCESSING_MS="$normal_processing_ms" \
        "${compose[@]}" up -d --force-recreate "$worker_service" \
        >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      ;;
  esac
}

trap restore_normal_worker EXIT

wait_for_health() {
  local service="$1"
  local container_id
  local health_status

  for ((_attempt = 1; _attempt <= health_wait_attempts; _attempt += 1)); do
    container_id="$("${compose[@]}" ps -q "$service")"

    if [[ -n "$container_id" ]]; then
      health_status="$(
        docker inspect \
          --format '{{if .State.Health}}{{.State.Health.Status}}{{else}}missing{{end}}' \
          "$container_id" 2>/dev/null || true
      )"

      if [[ "$health_status" == "healthy" ]]; then
        return
      fi
    fi

    sleep 2
  done

  "${compose[@]}" ps "$service" >&2 || true
  "${compose[@]}" logs --no-color "$service" >&2 || true
  fail "$service did not become healthy"
}

queue_ready_count() {
  "${compose[@]}" exec -T incident-service \
    node --input-type=module -e '
      import amqp from "amqplib";

      const connection = await amqp.connect({
        protocol: "amqp",
        hostname: process.env.RABBITMQ_HOST,
        port: Number(process.env.RABBITMQ_PORT),
        username: process.env.RABBITMQ_USER,
        password: process.env.RABBITMQ_PASSWORD,
        heartbeat: Number(process.env.RABBITMQ_HEARTBEAT_SECONDS),
      });
      const channel = await connection.createChannel();
      const queue = await channel.checkQueue(process.env.NOTIFICATION_QUEUE);

      console.log(queue.messageCount);
      await channel.close();
      await connection.close();
    '
}

assert_queue_empty() {
  local ready

  ready="$(queue_ready_count)"

  if [[ "$ready" != "0" ]]; then
    fail "queue $queue_name already contains ready=$ready"
  fi
}

wait_for_queue_ready() {
  local expected_ready="$1"
  local ready

  for _attempt in {1..45}; do
    ready="$(queue_ready_count)"

    if [[ "$ready" == "$expected_ready" ]]; then
      return
    fi

    sleep 1
  done

  fail "queue $queue_name did not reach ready=$expected_ready"
}

wait_for_log() {
  local service="$1"
  local pattern="$2"
  local logs

  for _attempt in {1..45}; do
    logs="$("${compose[@]}" logs --no-color --no-log-prefix "$service" 2>/dev/null || true)"

    if printf '%s\n' "$logs" | rg -q "$pattern"; then
      return
    fi

    sleep 1
  done

  "${compose[@]}" logs --no-color "$service" >&2 || true
  fail "$service logs did not match: $pattern"
}

enqueue_log_count() {
  local logs
  local count

  logs="$("${compose[@]}" logs --no-color --no-log-prefix incident-service 2>/dev/null || true)"
  count="$(printf '%s\n' "$logs" | rg -c '"event":"incident_notification_enqueued"' || true)"
  printf '%s\n' "${count:-0}"
}

published_port() {
  local service="$1"
  local container_port="$2"
  local mapping
  local port

  mapping="$("${compose[@]}" port "$service" "$container_port" | tail -n 1)"
  port="${mapping##*:}"

  [[ "$port" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || fail "could not resolve host port for $service"
  printf '%s\n' "$port"
}

create_incident() {
  local base_url="$1"
  local venue="$2"

  curl -fsS -X POST "$base_url/incidents" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data "{\"emergencyType\":\"medical\",\"severity\":\"critical\",\"location\":{\"latitude\":42.3868,\"longitude\":-72.5301,\"venue\":\"$venue\"}}"
}

phase "Start the Sprint 4 asynchronous subsystem"
existing_worker_id="$("${compose[@]}" ps -q "$worker_service")"

if [[ -n "$existing_worker_id" ]]; then
  restore_mode="start"
  "${compose[@]}" stop "$worker_service"
fi

"${compose[@]}" up -d rabbitmq
wait_for_health rabbitmq

"${compose[@]}" build \
  "$worker_service" \
  incident-service \
  incident-ambassador

"${compose[@]}" up --force-recreate -d incident-service
wait_for_health incident-service
assert_queue_empty

"${compose[@]}" up --force-recreate -d \
  "$worker_service" \
  incident-ambassador

wait_for_health "$worker_service"
restore_mode="none"
wait_for_health incident-ambassador

readonly incident_port="$(published_port incident-ambassador 3000)"
readonly incident_base_url="http://127.0.0.1:$incident_port"

wait_for_queue_ready 0

phase "Verify normal enqueue, delivery, processing, and acknowledgment"
normal_response="$(create_incident "$incident_base_url" "Gate 4 normal flow")"
normal_incident_id="$(jq -er '.incidentId' <<<"$normal_response")"

wait_for_log incident-service \
  "\"event\":\"incident_notification_enqueued\".*\"incidentId\":\"$normal_incident_id\""
wait_for_log "$worker_service" \
  "\"event\":\"incident_notification_received\".*\"incidentId\":\"$normal_incident_id\""
wait_for_log "$worker_service" \
  "\"event\":\"incident_notification_completed\".*\"incidentId\":\"$normal_incident_id\""
wait_for_queue_ready 0
printf 'PASS normal enqueue and consume\n'

phase "Verify invalid and read-only requests do not enqueue"
enqueue_count_before="$(enqueue_log_count)"
invalid_status="$(
  curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
    -X POST "$incident_base_url/incidents" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    --data '{}'
)"

[[ "$invalid_status" == "400" ]] || fail "invalid incident returned HTTP $invalid_status instead of 400"
curl -fsS "$incident_base_url/health" >/dev/null
curl -fsS "$incident_base_url/incidents/$normal_incident_id" >/dev/null

enqueue_count_after="$(enqueue_log_count)"
[[ "$enqueue_count_after" == "$enqueue_count_before" ]] || \
  fail "invalid or read-only request unexpectedly enqueued work"
wait_for_queue_ready 0
printf 'PASS invalid and read-only requests do not enqueue\n'

phase "Verify RabbitMQ retains work while the worker is stopped"
restore_mode="start"
"${compose[@]}" stop "$worker_service"

queued_response="$(create_incident "$incident_base_url" "Gate 4 queued flow")"
queued_incident_id="$(jq -er '.incidentId' <<<"$queued_response")"
wait_for_log incident-service \
  "\"event\":\"incident_notification_enqueued\".*\"incidentId\":\"$queued_incident_id\""
wait_for_queue_ready 1

# Blue Light

A simulated distributed emergency-response system built by Team 9 for COMPSCI
426. The system accepts incident reports, routes requests to an appropriate
regional response group, assigns responder teams, and publishes asynchronous
notification work.

## Team Roster

| GitHub Username | UMass Email |
| --- | --- |
| austinfairbanks | afairbanks@umass.edu |
| Dos0n | bdo@umass.edu |
| ShriRadhakrishnan1 | sradhakrishn@umass.edu |

## Domain Description

Our system simulates a distributed mobile blue-light emergency response network that routes emergency requests across multiple regions, including university campuses, transit hubs, stadiums, shopping centers, and other public venues. Users submit requests through a mobile application, and the system is responsible for determining the appropriate response, routing the request to the correct regional service, and keeping responders and users updated throughout the incident.

A single server becomes insufficient when the system experiences sudden spikes in demand, such as during large public events, severe weather, or multiple simultaneous emergencies. During these periods, the system must rapidly process incoming requests, determine user locations, prioritize incidents based on severity, and notify the appropriate local responders without introducing delays. Distributing the workload across multiple servers allows the system to remain responsive and available even under heavy load.

From a Computing for the Common Good perspective, a reliable emergency response system directly improves public safety. Students, commuters, event attendees, employees, and other members of the public all benefit from fast and dependable access to emergency services. When the system performs well, people receive timely police, medical, security, or crisis-response assistance. When it fails or becomes overloaded, delayed or misrouted requests can increase response times and potentially place people in dangerous situations. There are also inherent flaws with physical blue light alarms as they may not always be accessible during times of need, which makes being able to use blue light systems from one's phone the natural way to improve accessibility.

## Start the Complete System

Requirements:

- Docker with Docker Compose
- The course Gantry devcontainer

From the repository root:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up --build
```

The `.env` copy is optional because every Compose variable has a local default,
but keeping one makes overrides explicit. Wait until `docker compose ps` shows
the services as healthy before sending requests. Stop the system with:

```bash
docker compose down
```

## Service Endpoints

| Component | Default host URL | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regional routing ambassador | `http://localhost:3002` | Public routing path, including `GET /route` |
| Incident ambassador | `http://localhost:3003` | Public incident path, including `POST /incidents` |
| Responder dispatch service | `http://localhost:3004` | Dispatch creation, lookup, and status updates |
| Notification worker HTTP server | `http://localhost:3005` | Worker health and metrics endpoints |
| Prometheus | `http://localhost:9090` | Metrics targets, queries, and graphs |
| RabbitMQ management | `http://localhost:15672` | Local queue administration |

The incident service, three routing replicas, Caddy, Redis, and RabbitMQ's
service ports are connected through Compose DNS and do not need public HTTP
ports. See [docs/SERVICES.md](docs/SERVICES.md) for the complete architecture.

## Prometheus Metrics

Every custom service exposes `GET /metrics` in Prometheus text format. The
endpoint includes:

- `http_requests_total`, labeled by service, method, normalized route, and
  status code.
- `http_request_duration_milliseconds`, a response-time histogram using
  millisecond buckets.

Prometheus scrapes eight running targets: the incident service and ambassador,
all three routing replicas, the routing ambassador, the dispatch service, and
the notification worker. Inspect their status at
`http://localhost:9090/targets`.

The main routing path can be queried with these PromQL expressions:

```promql
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="regional-routing-ambassador",route="/route"}[1m]))
```

```promql
100 * (sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="regional-routing-ambassador",route="/route",status_code!~"2.."}[1m])) or vector(0))
  / clamp_min(sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="regional-routing-ambassador",route="/route"}[1m])), 0.000001)
```

```promql
histogram_quantile(
  0.95,
  sum by (le) (
    rate(http_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket{service="regional-routing-ambassador",route="/route"}[1m])
  )
)
```

The last expression returns milliseconds because the underlying histogram is
recorded in milliseconds.

## Environment Variables

All variables are optional. When a variable is missing, Compose uses the local
default shown below.

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `INCIDENT_LATENCY_MS` | `200` | Simulated incident-service response latency |
| `ROUTING_AMBASSADOR_PORT` | `3002` | Routing ambassador host port |
| `ROUTING_LATENCY_MS` | `200` | Simulated routing-service miss latency |
| `ROUTING_UPSTREAM_URL` | `http://regional-routing-load-balancer:3000` | Routing ambassador upstream |
| `ROUTING_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS` | `2000` | Routing ambassador upstream timeout |
| `ROUTING_MAX_RETRIES` | `2` | Safe routing request retries |
| `ROUTE_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS` | `30` | Redis route-cache lifetime |
| `INCIDENT_AMBASSADOR_PORT` | `3003` | Incident ambassador host port |
| `INCIDENT_UPSTREAM_URL` | `http://incident-service:3000` | Incident ambassador upstream |
| `INCIDENT_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS` | `2000` | Incident ambassador upstream timeout |
| `INCIDENT_MAX_RETRIES` | `2` | Safe incident request retries |
